questions.stem: When purlins are placed between panel points, the principal rafter is to be designed for:
questions.solution:
**Axial compression AND bending moment.**

**Why.** A truss is idealised on the assumption that **loads are applied ONLY at the joints (panel points)**. Under that assumption every member carries **pure axial force** and nothing else.

> **A purlin placed BETWEEN panel points breaks that assumption.** It applies a **transverse load partway along the rafter**, which therefore acts as a **beam as well as a strut**.

| Action | Source |
|---|---|
| **AXIAL COMPRESSION** | The rafter's normal role as a truss member |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | The purlin load applied **between** the joints |

> **The member becomes a BEAM-COLUMN**, and must be checked for the **combined** effect — not for either action alone.

**The interaction check:**

> **A beam-column is verified by an INTERACTION equation**, roughly of the form:

> **(P/P_allowable) + (M/M_allowable) ≤ 1**

> **Neither action alone may reach its own limit**, because each consumes part of the section's capacity. A rafter safe in pure compression and safe in pure bending can still fail under the two together.

**Why purlins are normally placed AT panel points:**

> Precisely to avoid this. **Loading only at the joints keeps every member in pure axial force**, which is simpler, more efficient, and what the truss was conceived to do.

> **Where the purlin spacing required by the roof sheeting does not match the panel spacing**, the designer must either **change the panel layout** or **accept the bending and design for it.**

**The truss idealisation and what it assumes:**

| Assumption | Consequence if violated |
|---|---|
| **Frictionless PIN joints** | Real bolted/welded joints carry some moment — **secondary stresses** |
| **Loads only at joints** | **Bending in members** — this question |
| Members straight and weightless | Self-weight causes minor bending |

> **Secondary stresses from joint rigidity are usually accepted as small**, because the members are slender and the moments they attract are correspondingly modest. **A purlin load between panel points is NOT small**, and cannot be treated the same way.

**The principal rafter's role** in a roof truss:

> It is the **top chord**, in **COMPRESSION** under gravity loading — which is why its **effective length and slenderness matter**, and why an unexpected bending moment is particularly unwelcome in a member already carrying compression.

> **Compression plus bending is the most demanding combination in steelwork**, because the axial load amplifies the deflection caused by the moment, which in turn increases the moment (**the P-δ effect**).

**Roof truss types and their compression members**, for context: in a **PRATT** truss the long **diagonals are in TENSION** and the short verticals take compression — putting the buckling problem in the shortest members, which is why Pratt suits steel. **HOWE** is the reverse, which suited timber, strong in compression along the grain.

examTip.trick: A truss assumes **loads only at the JOINTS** — that is what keeps members in pure axial force. A purlin **between** panel points breaks the assumption and adds **bending**.
examTip.trap: The rafter is a **top chord in COMPRESSION**, so the answer must combine compression with bending. Options naming tension have the axial sense wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **A beam-column is checked by an INTERACTION equation — neither action may reach its own limit alone.** And compression amplifies the bending deflection (**P-δ**), making the combination the most demanding in steelwork.

questions.stem: For sandy soils the most common method of stabilization is:
questions.solution:
**Soil-cement.**

**Why cement suits sand:**

> **Cement hydrates INDEPENDENTLY of the soil.** It needs only water, and it forms a cementitious matrix that binds the sand grains together — regardless of the soil's own mineralogy.

> **That independence is the whole point.** Sand contributes nothing chemically to the reaction; it is simply the aggregate being bound.

**The essential pairing, which is the reverse of what most people assume:**

| Soil | Stabiliser | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **GRANULAR / SANDY** | **CEMENT** | **Hydrates on its own** — needs no contribution from the soil |
| **CLAYEY** | **LIME** | **Needs the clay's own SILICA and ALUMINA** for the pozzolanic reaction |

> **LIME for CLAY, CEMENT for SAND.** Getting it backwards is the standard error — and **lime in a clean sand does almost nothing**, because there is no clay mineral for it to react with.

**How cement stabilisation works:**

| Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Hydration** | Forms **C-S-H gel** binding the particles |
| **Reduces plasticity** (if any fines present) | — |
| **Increases strength and durability** | Substantially |
| **Reduces permeability** | — |
| Resists water | The stabilised layer no longer softens when wet |

> **Typical cement content is 3–10% by weight**, and the mixture is compacted at **optimum moisture content** like any fill.

**Why the other options are wrong here:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | **Blending two or more soils** to obtain a better grading. Genuine and cheap, but it improves grading rather than binding the grains |
| **Soil-lime** | For **CLAYEY** soils — needs clay minerals to react with |
| **Soil-bitumen** | Works by **WATERPROOFING and binding** granular particles. Real for sands, but **cement is the more common and more effective structural stabiliser** |

> **Soil-bitumen is the meaningful near-miss**: it genuinely suits sandy soils, and it is used for low-cost roads. **But it binds by adhesion rather than by cementation**, giving a flexible, water-resistant layer rather than a rigid strong one — and the question asks for the **most common** method.

**The stabilisation methods generally:**

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical** (blending, compaction) | Improving grading |
| **CEMENT** | **Granular and sandy soils** |
| **LIME** | **Clayey and expansive soils** |
| **Bitumen** | Sandy soils; waterproofing |
| Chemical (sodium silicate, resins) | Specialised grouting |
| **Geosynthetics** | Reinforcement and separation |

**Why stabilisation is worth doing:**

> **It converts an unsuitable local material into a usable one** — avoiding the cost of importing selected fill, which on a remote site can dominate the earthworks budget.

> **In Nepal's hill roads, where haulage of good material is extremely expensive, in-situ stabilisation is often the difference between a viable and an unviable project.**

**And the caution about sulphates:** cement (and lime) stabilisation can fail where the soil contains **sulphates**, because these react to form **expansive ETTRINGITE** — the same mechanism that attacks concrete foundations in sulphate-bearing ground. **A sulphate test on the soil is a sensible precaution before specifying either stabiliser.**

examTip.trick: **Cement hydrates INDEPENDENTLY of the soil** — it needs only water, so it works in clean sand. **Lime needs the CLAY's own silica and alumina** and does almost nothing in sand.
examTip.trap: **LIME for CLAY, CEMENT for SAND** — the reverse of what most people assume, and the single most-tested point in soil stabilisation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Soil-bitumen is the near-miss** — genuine for sands, but it binds by **adhesion and waterproofing** rather than cementation. And watch for **SULPHATES**: they turn either stabiliser into expansive ettringite.

questions.stem: The rate of stretching of bitumen in the ductility test is:
questions.solution:
**5 cm/min — that is, 50 mm per minute.**

> **Note that options (a) and (b) are the same number in different units**, and only one is right: **5 cm/min = 50 mm/min**, not 5 mm/min. **The unit is doing all the work in this question.**

**The ductility test:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Rate of pulling** | **50 mm/min (5 cm/min)** |
| **Temperature** | **27 °C** |
| **Minimum ductility** | **50 cm** for paving bitumen |
| Specimen | A briquette of standard cross-section, pulled until it breaks |

> **The ductility is the distance in centimetres to which the specimen stretches before breaking.**

**What ductility measures, and why it matters:**

> **The binder's ability to STRETCH and deform without cracking** — its capacity to accommodate movement in the pavement.

| Consequence of low ductility | Note |
|---|---|
| **CRACKING** under traffic and thermal movement | The binder cannot follow the aggregate's movement |
| **Loss of adhesion** to the aggregate | Brittle binder debonds |
| Poor performance in cold weather | Ductility falls as temperature drops |

> **A pavement flexes continuously under traffic and expands and contracts with temperature.** A binder that cannot stretch simply cracks — and once cracked, water enters and the failure cascades.

**Note that both 27 °C and the rate are specified**, and both matter:

> **Bitumen is VISCOELASTIC** — its behaviour depends on **both temperature and rate of loading**. Pull it faster, or colder, and it behaves more brittly; slower or warmer, and it flows.

> **That is why the test conditions are fixed so precisely.** A ductility figure without its temperature and rate would be meaningless.

> **The same viscoelasticity explains why bitumen behaves as a solid under a fast wheel load but flows under sustained load in hot weather** — the source of rutting.

**The full set of bitumen tests:**

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **Hardness — in TENTHS of a millimetre** (grades 60/70, 80/100) |
| **Softening point** | Temperature susceptibility — **ring and ball** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **Stretch without cracking — minimum 50 cm** |
| **Flash and fire point** | Safety in handling |
| Viscosity | Mixing and laying temperatures |
| **Water content** | **Maximum 0.2%** |
| Specific gravity | ~0.97–1.02 |
| Loss on heating | Volatility |

> **No single test characterises bitumen.** A binder can pass penetration and still be unsuitable — which is why the specification lists all of them.

**The relationship between the main two** is worth knowing:

> **A binder with HIGH penetration (soft) has a LOW softening point**, and vice versa. **The PENETRATION INDEX** combines the two into a single measure of **temperature susceptibility** — how much the binder's consistency changes with temperature.

> **A binder with low temperature susceptibility is the ideal**: stiff enough not to rut in summer, soft enough not to crack in winter. **That is precisely what polymer modification aims to achieve.**

**And why the moisture limit is so tight (0.2%):** bitumen is handled at about **150 °C**, far above water's boiling point. **Even a little water flashes to steam and the boiler froths over** — a serious safety hazard as well as a bond problem.

examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are the SAME number in different units.** The rate is **5 cm/min = 50 mm/min**, not 5 mm/min — a tenfold difference hidden in the unit.
examTip.trick: Both the **rate (50 mm/min) and the temperature (27 °C)** are specified because bitumen is **VISCOELASTIC** — it behaves differently at different rates and temperatures. A figure without both would be meaningless.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ductility ≥ 50 cm; penetration in TENTHS of a millimetre; water ≤ 0.2%.** And the **PENETRATION INDEX** combines penetration and softening point into a measure of temperature susceptibility — the property polymer modification targets.

questions.stem: The CG of a cone from its base is:
questions.solution:
**h/4 from the base** — equivalently **3h/4 from the apex**.

> **Note that options (b) and (d) are the SAME point measured from opposite ends**, which is exactly what the question's phrase "from its base" resolves. **Read the datum before answering.**

**The centroid positions worth carrying:**

| Shape | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Triangle (lamina)** | **h/3 from the base** |
| **CONE (solid)** | **h/4 from the base** |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8 from the base** |
| Hollow hemisphere | r/2 |
| **Semicircular AREA** | **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r** |
| **Semicircular ARC** | **2r/π** |
| Solid pyramid | h/4 from the base |

> **The triangle gives h/3 and the cone h/4** — and option (a) is offered precisely because the triangle's value is the more familiar one.

**Why the cone's centroid sits LOWER than the triangle's:**

> A triangle is a **plane lamina**: its width falls **linearly** with height, so the area at height y goes as **(1 − y/h)**.

> A cone is a **solid of revolution**: its cross-sectional **AREA falls as the SQUARE** of the distance from the apex, so the volume is concentrated even more strongly toward the base.

> **More of the volume is near the base, so the centroid is nearer the base — h/4 rather than h/3.**

> **That reasoning generalises**: the same argument gives **h/4 for any pyramid**, whatever its base shape, because the area still falls as the square.

**The general method:**

> **ȳ = ∫y dV / ∫dV**

> For a cone with the apex at the origin, the radius at distance x from the apex is **r x/h**, so **dV = π(rx/h)² dx**, and integrating gives **x̄ = 3h/4 from the apex = h/4 from the base** ✓

**For a COMPOSITE body:**

> **ȳ = Σ(V_i ȳ_i)/ΣV_i** — treating each part's volume as concentrated at its own centroid.

> **A REMOVED portion (a hole) is taken as a NEGATIVE volume**, which is the neatest way of handling a body with a cavity.

**Where centroids matter in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Second moment of area** | Via the **parallel axis theorem: I = I_c + Ad²** |
| **Stability of floating bodies** | **Metacentric height GM** depends on the centroid and the centre of buoyancy |
| **Retaining wall and dam stability** | The **line of action of the self weight** |
| Earthwork volumes | The prismoidal and mean area formulae |
| Composite sections | Locating the neutral axis |

> **For a gravity dam or retaining wall, the centroid fixes where the self-weight acts** — and since stability against overturning depends on that lever arm, an error in the centroid is an error in the safety factor.

**And the check worth remembering:** since **I = I_centroid + Ad²** always **adds**, the **centroidal axis gives the MINIMUM second moment**. A computed value smaller than the centroidal one is arithmetically impossible.

examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) are the SAME point from opposite ends** — h/4 from the base is 3h/4 from the apex. The phrase "from its base" is what resolves it, so read the datum.
examTip.trick: **Triangle h/3, CONE h/4** — the cone's centroid is lower because its cross-sectional **area falls as the SQUARE** of distance from the apex, concentrating volume near the base. The same gives **h/4 for any pyramid**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Semicircular AREA 4r/3π; semicircular ARC 2r/π; solid hemisphere 3r/8.** A lamina is not a wire and a solid is not a lamina — the three are constantly swapped.

questions.stem: A bending moment M acts at each support of a simply supported beam. The SFD has ordinates:
questions.solution:
**Zero at all sections.**

**Why.** The beam carries **only applied COUPLES at its ends — no transverse loads at all.**

> **A couple applies NO NET VERTICAL FORCE.** So for vertical equilibrium of the whole beam, the **support reactions must sum to zero.**

> With **equal moments M at each end**, the reactions form an equal and opposite pair — and if the moments are applied so as to balance, **the reactions are zero entirely.** Either way, **there is no vertical force anywhere along the beam, so the shear force is zero at every section.**

> The source puts it in one line: **"There is no force to contribute to SFD."**

**The general principle, which is the substance here:**

| Applied | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **POINT LOAD W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** — slope changes, value continuous |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change at all** | **JUMPS by M** |
| UDL w | Linear | Parabolic |

> **A point load jumps the shear and kinks the moment; a couple does nothing to the shear and jumps the moment.** They are exact opposites, and this question is the pure case of the second.

**What the BMD looks like here:**

> With equal end moments and no transverse load, **the bending moment is CONSTANT at M along the entire beam** — a rectangular BMD.

> **That follows directly from V = dM/dx**: if V = 0 everywhere, then dM/dx = 0 everywhere, so **M cannot change.**

> **The shear diagram and the moment diagram are consistent**, and each confirms the other.

**This is the case of PURE BENDING**, and it is important beyond this question:

> **Pure bending means constant moment with zero shear** — exactly the condition assumed in the derivation of the **flexure formula σ = My/I.**

> **The simple bending theory is strictly valid only in pure bending**, which is why the **middle third of a four-point bending test** is used for measuring flexural strength: **that region has constant moment and zero shear**, matching the theory's assumptions.

> **A cantilever or a beam under a central point load has shear everywhere except at one section**, so the flexure formula is an approximation there — a very good one for slender beams, but an approximation.

**The governing relations:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Shear is the **SLOPE** of the moment diagram | **V = 0 → M constant** ✓ |
| **V = 0 marks a moment peak** | Here the whole beam is at the peak |
| **Change in M = AREA of the SFD** | Zero area → no change ✓ |

**Where end moments actually arise:**

| Situation | Source |
|---|---|
| **A BRACKET or corbel** framing into the beam | An eccentric load **P at eccentricity e = P plus a couple Pe** |
| A column framing eccentrically | Eccentric axial load |
| Continuity with adjacent spans | Support moments |
| Prestressing with eccentric tendons | — |

> **The bracket case is the everyday one**: a load P at eccentricity e is statically equivalent to **P on the axis PLUS a couple Pe**, and **BOTH must be applied.** Analysing only the transferred force understates the moment — a genuine and common error in the design of brackets and eccentric connections.

examTip.trick: **A couple applies NO net vertical force**, so there is nothing to produce shear anywhere. And since **V = dM/dx = 0**, the moment must be **constant** — a rectangular BMD.
examTip.trap: **Point load: jumps V, kinks M. Couple: nothing to V, jumps M.** Exact opposites — and this question is the pure case of the second.
examTip.mnemonic: **Constant moment with zero shear IS pure bending** — the condition the flexure formula σ = My/I assumes. Which is why flexural strength is measured in the **middle third of a four-point test**.

questions.stem: The equation of continuity for a fluid that is compressible and flow that is steady is:
questions.solution:
**ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.**

**The principle:** continuity is the **CONSERVATION OF MASS**. For steady flow, the **mass flow rate must be the same at every section** — whatever enters must leave.

> **Mass flow rate = ρ A V** (density × area × velocity)

> So **ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂** ✓ — the **general form, valid for compressible AND incompressible fluids.**

**The familiar form is a special case:**

> **If the fluid is INCOMPRESSIBLE, ρ₁ = ρ₂**, and the densities cancel:

> **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** — which is option (a), and the form used in virtually all civil engineering.

> **Option (a) is therefore not wrong in general — it is wrong HERE**, because the question specifies a **compressible** fluid. **The word "compressible" is doing all the work.**

**Why option (d) fails on dimensions:**

> **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ρ** has **volume flow on one side and mass flow on the other** — dimensionally inconsistent, and impossible whatever the fluid.

> **A dimensional check kills it instantly**, which is worth doing on any equation offered as an option.

**When compressibility matters:**

| Condition | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **Liquids, at ordinary pressures** | **Incompressible** — water's bulk modulus is 2.1 GPa |
| **Gases at low speed (Mach < 0.3)** | **Treated as incompressible** — density changes under 5% |
| **Gases at high speed (Mach > 0.3)** | **COMPRESSIBLE** — density changes matter |
| **WATER HAMMER** | **Compressible even for water** |

> **Water hammer is the one case where a civil engineer must treat water as compressible.** The pressure wave **Δp = ρcΔV** travels at the speed of sound in the fluid–pipe system (**c ≈ 1000 m/s**), and that wave exists **only because the water and the pipe are slightly elastic.**

> **In a truly incompressible fluid in a rigid pipe, closing a valve would generate infinite pressure instantly.** The finite wave speed — and therefore the finite pressure rise — is a consequence of compressibility.

**The general differential form:**

> **∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρu) = 0**

> For **constant density** this reduces to **∇·u = 0** — the incompressibility condition in the Navier–Stokes equations.

> **The elementary A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ used in every pipe problem IS ∇·u = 0, integrated over a cross-section.** Seeing that connection makes the vector statement far less abstract.

**The three conservation equations** that govern all fluid flow:

| Equation | Conserves |
|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY** | **MASS** |
| **Momentum (Navier–Stokes / Euler)** | **MOMENTUM** — Newton's second law |
| **Energy (Bernoulli)** | **ENERGY** |

> **Continuity is the only one of the three with no exceptions** — mass is conserved whatever the losses, whatever the turbulence, however abrupt the transition.

> **That is why continuity can always be applied**, while **Bernoulli must not be used across a hydraulic jump or a sudden expansion**, where the energy loss is large and unknown. **In those cases momentum is used — and continuity always.**

examTip.trick: Continuity is **conservation of MASS**, and mass flow is **ρAV**. The familiar A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ is the special case where **ρ cancels** — valid only for an incompressible fluid.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is not wrong in general — it is wrong HERE**, because the question says **compressible**. And option (d) is **dimensionally impossible**: volume flow on one side, mass flow on the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **Continuity is the ONLY conservation law with no exceptions** — mass is conserved whatever the losses. Which is why **Bernoulli fails across a hydraulic jump but continuity never does.**

questions.stem: When the barometer reads 740.0 mm of mercury, a pressure of 10 kPa suction at that location is equivalent to:
questions.solution:
**88.72 kPa (absolute).**

**Working.**

> **P_atm = ρ_Hg × g × h = 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.740 = 98 720 Pa = 98.72 kPa**
>
> **Suction (vacuum) means BELOW atmospheric:**
> **P_abs = P_atm − P_suction = 98.72 − 10 = 88.72 kPa (abs)** ✓

> **Note the barometer reads 740 mm, not the standard 760 mm** — so the local atmospheric pressure is **98.72 kPa, not 101.3 kPa.** Using the standard value would give 91.3 kPa, which is not an option. **Reading the given barometric value rather than assuming the standard one is the first trap.**

**The relations, and which applies:**

| Relation | When |
|---|---|
| **P_abs = P_atm + P_gauge** | Pressure **ABOVE** atmospheric |
| **P_abs = P_atm − P_suction** | Pressure **BELOW** atmospheric — **this case** |
| **P_vac = P_atm − P_abs** | Rearranged |

> **Suction is a magnitude measured DOWNWARD from atmospheric**, so it is **subtracted**. Adding it would give 108.72 kPa — the standard error.

**Why the water-column options are wrong:**

> **88.72 kPa in metres of water = 88 720/(1000 × 9.81) = 9.04 m**, not 10.02 or 9.87 m. **Neither water option corresponds to the correct pressure**, so they are not merely alternative units — they are wrong values.

> (For reference, **9.87 m of water = 96.8 kPa** and **10.02 m = 98.3 kPa** — both close to atmospheric, which is what makes them superficially plausible.)

**Barometric pressure varies with altitude**, which matters in Nepal:

| Location | Approximate pressure |
|---|---|
| Sea level | **101.3 kPa (760 mm Hg)** |
| **740 mm Hg** | **98.7 kPa** — a modest elevation or low-pressure weather |
| **Kathmandu (~1400 m)** | **~86 kPa** |
| 3000 m | ~70 kPa |

> **At altitude the atmosphere can support a shorter water column**, so **a suction pump's maximum lift is reduced** — a genuine practical consequence for water supply schemes in the hills.

**The limit this illustrates:**

> **A suction pump cannot lift water more than 10.33 m at sea level, and less at altitude** — and only **6–7 m in practice**.

> **The pump does not pull the water up.** It reduces the pressure at its inlet, and **atmospheric pressure pushes the water up** the suction pipe. **The maximum lift is whatever the atmosphere can support.**

| Loss | Effect |
|---|---|
| Friction and velocity head | Reduce the available lift |
| **VAPOUR PRESSURE** | **The water BOILS before a perfect vacuum is reached** |
| **Cavitation margin (NPSH)** | The binding constraint |

> **A perfect vacuum is impossible because the water vaporises first** — which is why **absolute pressure, not gauge, is used in cavitation and NPSH calculations.**

> **Vapour pressure rises with temperature**, so hot liquids cavitate far more readily.

**Reference values:** **1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 10.33 m of water = 760 mm Hg = 1.013 bar**, and **mercury's density of 13 600 kg/m³ is 13.6 times water's** — which is exactly why a mercury barometer is 760 mm tall while a water one would need to be 10.33 m.

examTip.trap: **The barometer reads 740 mm, not the standard 760.** Local atmospheric pressure is **98.72 kPa**, not 101.3 — assuming the standard value gives 91.3 kPa, which is not an option.
examTip.trick: **Suction is measured DOWNWARD from atmospheric, so SUBTRACT it**: 98.72 − 10 = **88.72 kPa**. Adding gives 108.72 — the standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mercury is 13.6× denser than water** — which is why a barometer is 760 mm and not 10.33 m. And at **Kathmandu's altitude (~86 kPa)** a suction pump's maximum lift is measurably reduced.

questions.stem: e/D is a parameter in the Moody diagram. What is that 'e' in the Moody diagram?
questions.solution:
**The surface roughness height** — the average height of the irregularities on the pipe's inner wall.

> **e/D is the RELATIVE ROUGHNESS** — roughness height divided by pipe diameter, and therefore **dimensionless.**

**What the Moody diagram is:**

> A chart giving the **DARCY FRICTION FACTOR f** as a function of two dimensionless parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Reynolds number Re = VD/ν** | The **flow** regime |
| **Relative roughness e/D** | The **pipe** surface |

> **f is then used in the Darcy–Weisbach equation: h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**

**Why RELATIVE roughness rather than absolute:**

> **A 1 mm irregularity is enormous in a 10 mm capillary and negligible in a 2 m tunnel.** What matters is the roughness **compared with the pipe size** — and dividing by D makes the parameter dimensionless, which is what allows one chart to serve every pipe.

**Reading the diagram — the three regions:**

| Region | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (Re < 2000)** | **f = 64/Re — ROUGHNESS IS IRRELEVANT** |
| **Transitional / smooth turbulent** | f depends on **both Re and e/D** |
| **FULLY ROUGH (high Re)** | **f depends on e/D ONLY — the curves go HORIZONTAL** |

> **In laminar flow the roughness does not appear at all**, because the flow slides over the irregularities without disturbance — a genuinely surprising result, and one worth knowing.

> **At high Reynolds number the curves flatten**, and f stops changing with Re. **The flow is then "fully rough", and the head loss varies simply as V².**

**The physical explanation — the VISCOUS SUBLAYER:**

> A thin layer next to the wall remains **viscous** even in turbulent flow.

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Roughness BURIED within the sublayer** | **Hydrodynamically SMOOTH** — f depends on **Re only** |
| **Roughness PROJECTING through it** | **Fully ROUGH** — f depends on **e/D only** |

> **As Re rises the sublayer THINS**, so the same pipe moves from smooth toward rough behaviour.

> **"Smooth" and "rough" therefore describe the FLOW as much as the PIPE** — the same pipe can be hydrodynamically smooth at low velocity and fully rough at high. **That is the key idea, and it explains the whole shape of the Moody chart.**

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity, kinematic viscosity** | Both enter through the **REYNOLDS NUMBER**, the other axis — not through e |
| **Boundary layer thickness** | A **property of the FLOW** that varies along the pipe; e is a **fixed property of the SURFACE** |

> **Option (d) is the meaningful near-miss**, because the boundary layer (specifically the viscous sublayer) genuinely determines **whether** the roughness matters. **But it is not what e is** — e is the physical height of the wall irregularities, fixed for a given pipe.

**Typical roughness heights:**

| Material | e (mm) |
|---|---|
| **Drawn tubing, glass** | **0.0015** |
| Commercial steel | 0.045 |
| Galvanised iron | 0.15 |
| **Concrete** | **0.3 – 3.0** |
| Riveted steel | 0.9 – 9.0 |

> **Roughness INCREASES with age** — through corrosion, tuberculation and deposits — so an old main has a substantially higher friction factor than when new. **Design for the aged condition, not the new one**, or the capacity will fall short within a few years.

**The COLEBROOK–WHITE equation** is the algebraic form the Moody diagram plots. It is **implicit in f** (f appears on both sides), which is exactly why a chart was drawn in the first place — and why **explicit approximations such as Swamee–Jain** are used in computation today.

examTip.trick: **e/D is RELATIVE roughness — dimensionless.** A 1 mm irregularity is huge in a capillary and nothing in a tunnel; dividing by D is what lets one chart serve every pipe.
examTip.trap: **In LAMINAR flow, f = 64/Re and roughness is IRRELEVANT** — the flow slides over the irregularities. Roughness only matters once the flow is turbulent.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Smooth" and "rough" describe the FLOW as much as the PIPE** — as Re rises the **viscous sublayer thins** and the same pipe becomes rough. And **roughness increases with age**: design for the aged condition.

questions.stem: What is the formula for seepage discharge in a flow net?
questions.solution:
**q = k H (N_f/N_d).**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **k** | **Coefficient of permeability** |
| **H** | **Total head difference** between upstream and downstream |
| **N_f** | **Number of FLOW CHANNELS** (the strips between flow lines) |
| **N_d** | **Number of EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS** |

**Why N_f is on top and N_d beneath — reason it out rather than memorise:**

| More | Effect on seepage |
|---|---|
| **More FLOW CHANNELS (N_f)** | **More paths for water → MORE seepage** → numerator |
| **More EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS (N_d)** | **A LONGER path, so each drop is smaller → LESS seepage** → denominator |

> **More channels means more flow; more drops means more resistance.** That single sentence fixes the formula, and option (d) is simply the ratio inverted.

**What a flow net is:**

> A graphical solution of **LAPLACE's equation** for seepage — two families of curves:

| Line | Property |
|---|---|
| **FLOW LINES** | The paths water particles follow |
| **EQUIPOTENTIAL LINES** | Lines of **equal total head** |

> **They intersect at RIGHT ANGLES**, and a correctly drawn net consists of approximate **"squares"** — figures whose length and breadth are equal.

> **The right-angle intersection and the square shape are the tests of a correctly drawn net**, and they are what make the simple formula valid: each square carries the same flow and drops the same head.

**What else the flow net gives:**

| Quantity | From |
|---|---|
| **Seepage discharge** | **q = kH(N_f/N_d)** |
| **Pore pressure** at any point | The **head remaining** at that equipotential |
| **UPLIFT pressure** on a structure | Integrating the pressure along its base |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i = Δh/Δl** at the **downstream exit** — the smallest square is critical |

> **The exit gradient is the most important output**, because it governs **PIPING** — and piping is the leading cause of earth dam failure.

**The piping mechanism:**

> When the **upward exit gradient reaches the CRITICAL value**, the effective stress at the exit falls to zero and the soil is fluidised:

> **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.0** for most soils

> **Once erosion starts, the channel formed SHORTENS the seepage path, which RAISES the gradient, which erodes faster** — a **self-accelerating** process working backwards toward the reservoir.

> **A factor of safety of 4 to 5 is required against the exit gradient** — far higher than the 1.5–3 used for most geotechnical checks, precisely because the failure is sudden, progressive and gives almost no warning.

**The defences:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Graded FILTER** at the exit | **Retains the soil while passing the water** — the principal defence |
| **Lengthen the seepage path** | Cut-offs, sheet piles, upstream blankets — **reduces i** |
| Loaded (inverted) filter at the toe | Adds weight where the gradient is highest |
| Relief wells | Relieve the pressure directly |

> **The filter criteria** are the two inequalities to carry: **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4–5** (retention) and **D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4–5** (permeability). **They pull in opposite directions and both must be satisfied** — too fine and the filter clogs, too coarse and the soil washes through.

**And for ANISOTROPIC soil** (the usual case, since natural deposits are layered): the section is **TRANSFORMED** by scaling the horizontal dimension by **√(k_v/k_h)**, the net is drawn on the transformed section, and the **equivalent permeability √(k_h k_v)** is used in the discharge formula.

examTip.trick: Reason it out: **more FLOW CHANNELS → more seepage (numerator); more EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS → longer path, more resistance → less seepage (denominator).** Option (d) is simply inverted.
examTip.trap: A correctly drawn net has **flow and equipotential lines meeting at RIGHT ANGLES** forming approximate **SQUARES** — that is what makes the simple formula valid, since each square carries equal flow and drops equal head.
examTip.mnemonic: **The EXIT GRADIENT is the flow net's most important output** — compare it with **i_c ≈ 1.0** using a factor of safety of **4–5**, because **piping is self-accelerating** and gives almost no warning.

questions.stem: The deflection at the centre of a simply supported beam when a concentrated load P is acting at its centre is:
questions.solution:
**PL³/48EI.**

**The standard deflection formulae:**

| Beam | Loading | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **Central point load W** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **Fixed both ends** | Central point load | **WL³/192EI** |
| **Simply supported** | UDL w | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| Fixed both ends | UDL | wL⁴/384EI |
| **Cantilever** | Point load at free end | **WL³/3EI** |
| Cantilever | UDL | wL⁴/8EI |

**The DIMENSIONAL check kills two options instantly:**

> **A point load formula must contain L³; a UDL formula must contain L⁴.**

> The reason is that **w has units of force per unit length**, so a UDL formula needs an extra power of L to give the same dimensions as a point load formula.

| Option | Powers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) **PL³/48EI** | P and **L³** | ✓ Consistent |
| (b) PL³/96EI | P and L³ | Dimensionally fine, but **96 is not a standard coefficient** for any case |
| (c) **PL⁴/24EI** | P with **L⁴** | ✗ **Mismatched — L⁴ belongs with w, not P** |
| (d) **PL²/24EI** | P with **L²** | ✗ **PL²/EI has the dimensions of a SLOPE, not a deflection** |

> **Option (d) is a real quantity in the wrong place**: **PL²/16EI is the SLOPE at the supports** of this very beam. **Deflection formulae carry L³ or L⁴; slope formulae carry L² or L³.**

**The accompanying slope, for completeness:**

> **θ_A = θ_B = PL²/16EI**, and the **slope at the centre is ZERO** — because the beam and its loading are symmetric.

> **The source's own note states the three governing facts**: deflections at the supports are zero while the slope there is maximum; the slope at the centre of a symmetrically loaded beam is zero; and the deflection is maximum at the centre.

> **Where the slope is zero, the deflection is at its extreme** — which is simply calculus, since **slope = dδ/dx**.

**Why deflection matters:**

> It is a **SERVICEABILITY** limit state, checked with **UNFACTORED** loads.

| Limit (IS 456) | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total deflection** | **span/250** |
| **Deflection after partitions are built** | **span/350 or 20 mm**, whichever is less |

> **The second limit is the stricter one in practice**, because it is the movement occurring **after** the finishes are in place that cracks partitions and jams doors.

**And the practical consequence:**

> **Deflection depends on L³ or L⁴** — an extraordinarily steep dependence. **Doubling the span increases the deflection EIGHTFOLD for a point load and SIXTEENFOLD for a UDL.**

> **That is why deflection, not strength, usually governs long-span beams and slabs** — and why the first thing computed in a slab design is the **span/effective depth ratio** (cantilever 7, simply supported 20, continuous 26), not the moment.

> **It also explains why a higher-grade steel or concrete does NOT solve a deflection problem**: **E = 200 GPa for every steel grade**, and concrete's E rises only as **√f_ck**. **Depth is the effective lever, not strength.**

examTip.trick: **Dimensional check: a POINT load formula carries L³; a UDL formula carries L⁴** (because w is force per length). That eliminates options (c) and (d) without any recall.
examTip.trap: **PL²/EI has the dimensions of a SLOPE, not a deflection** — indeed **PL²/16EI is the support slope** of this very beam. A real quantity offered in the wrong place.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deflection goes as L³ or L⁴** — doubling the span multiplies it by 8 or 16. Which is why deflection governs long spans, and why **DEPTH, not a higher grade, is the fix** (E = 200 GPa for every steel).

questions.stem: If σ and τ are normal and shear stress respectively, the minor principal stress is:
questions.solution:
**σ_x/2 − √(σ_x²/4 + τ_xy²).**

**The general expression** (with σ_y = 0, as here):

> **σ_{1,2} = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**
>
> With **σ_y = 0**: **σ_{1,2} = σ_x/2 ± √(σ_x²/4 + τ_xy²)**

> **MINOR principal stress takes the MINUS sign** ✓

**Two signs must BOTH be right, and the four options are exactly the four combinations:**

| Option | Before the radical | Inside the radical | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | **+** | **−** | Wrong both ways |
| **(b)** | **+** | **+** | **The MAJOR principal stress** |
| (c) | **−** | **−** | Right outside, impossible inside |
| **(d)** | **−** | **+** | **✓ The MINOR principal stress** |

> **Option (b) is the MAJOR principal stress** — it differs from the answer only in the sign before the radical, which is the single most instructive confusion in this topic.

> **The plus inside the radical is not a convention — it is geometry.** On Mohr's circle the radical **IS the RADIUS**, and a radius is **√(horizontal² + vertical²)** — a Pythagorean sum, which can only be a plus.

> **A minus inside would allow the radical to become imaginary** whenever τ exceeded σ_x/2, which is physically impossible. **That check alone eliminates (a) and (c).**

**On Mohr's circle:**

| Feature | Value (σ_y = 0) |
|---|---|
| **Centre** | **(σ_x/2, 0)** |
| **Radius R** | **√(σ_x²/4 + τ_xy²)** |
| **Major principal stress** | **Centre + R** |
| **Minor principal stress** | **Centre − R** |
| **τ_max** | **= R** |

> **The radius IS the maximum shear stress** — worth internalising, because it makes τ_max immediate once the circle is drawn.

**Two consequences worth knowing:**

> **1. The minor principal stress can be NEGATIVE (compressive) even when the applied direct stress is purely tensile.** Since R = √(σ_x²/4 + τ²) always exceeds σ_x/2 whenever τ ≠ 0, **σ_x/2 − R is always negative** in that case.

> **Pure shear is equivalent to equal tension and compression at 45°**, so adding shear to a tension always drives one principal stress compressive.

> **2. Principal planes carry ZERO shear**, by definition — they are where the circle crosses the σ axis. **But the plane of maximum shear is NOT free of normal stress**: it carries the centre value σ_x/2.

> **Only principal planes are shear-free; no plane is generally free of normal stress.** That asymmetry catches many candidates.

**The orientation:**

> **tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y)**, and the plane of maximum shear lies at **45°** to the principal planes — because on the circle it is 90° round, and **circle angles are DOUBLE real angles.**

> **Forgetting that factor of two is the standard error** in every Mohr's circle problem.

**Where the principal stresses are used:**

| Material | Failure theory | Governing quantity |
|---|---|---|
| **BRITTLE** (cast iron, concrete) | **Rankine** — maximum principal stress | **σ₁** |
| **DUCTILE** (steel) | **Tresca** — maximum shear | **(σ₁ − σ₃)/2** |
| Ductile | **von Mises** — distortion energy | Best fit to test data |
| **SOIL, rock** | **MOHR–COULOMB: τ = c + σ tan φ** | The failure envelope |

> **Tresca uses the FULL RANGE (σ₁ − σ₃), including a negative σ₃** — and omitting the compressive minor stress is the commonest error in applying it, since it understates the severity.

verification.notes: The source prints options (b) and (d) IDENTICALLY as σ_x/2 − √(σ_x²/4 + τ_xy²), keying (d). A duplicated option is a printing defect: it leaves only three distinct choices and makes (b) unanswerable. Option (b) has therefore been replaced with σ_x/2 + √(σ_x²/4 + τ_xy²) — the MAJOR principal stress — which completes the set of four sign combinations and is the most instructive distractor available, since major and minor differ only in the sign before the radical. The stem and the keyed answer are unchanged.

examTip.trick: **The radical IS the RADIUS of Mohr's circle**, so it must be a **Pythagorean sum — PLUS τ² inside.** A minus would let it go imaginary, which is physically impossible.
examTip.trap: **The source printed options (b) and (d) IDENTICALLY** — a genuine defect, corrected here so the four options are the four sign combinations. **Option (b) is now the MAJOR principal stress**, differing only in the sign before the radical.
examTip.mnemonic: **The minor principal stress goes NEGATIVE whenever shear is present**, even under pure applied tension — because pure shear is equal tension and compression at 45°. And **circle angles are DOUBLE real angles**.

questions.stem: A plane truss has 11 members and 8 joints. How many additional members are needed to make the truss stable?
questions.solution:
**2 additional members.**

**Working.** For a plane truss to be **statically determinate and stable**:

> **m = 2j − 3**
>
> **Required m = 2(8) − 3 = 16 − 3 = 13 members**
> **Provided = 11**
> **Shortfall = 13 − 11 = 2** ✓

**Reading the count:**

| Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **m = 2j − 3** | **Determinate and (usually) stable** |
| **m > 2j − 3** | **Indeterminate** — redundant members |
| **m < 2j − 3** | **A MECHANISM — unstable** |

> **With 11 < 13 the truss is DEFICIENT — it is a mechanism**, and will collapse under load by changing shape rather than by any member failing.

**Where 2j − 3 comes from:**

> Each joint gives **two equilibrium equations** (ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0), so there are **2j equations**.

> The unknowns are the **m member forces plus 3 support reactions**.

> **For a determinate solution: m + 3 = 2j**, hence **m = 2j − 3** ✓

> **Knowing the derivation means never mis-remembering the formula**, and it makes the general form **D_s = m + r − 2j** obvious too — with r = 3 for a simply supported truss.

**The essential caveat, which the count cannot capture:**

> **The formula checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.**

> **A truss can satisfy m = 2j − 3 exactly and still be a mechanism** if its geometry is wrong:

| Faulty geometry | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **A panel with no diagonal** | The rectangle can **rack** into a parallelogram |
| **Three connecting members PARALLEL** | The parts can still **slide** |
| **Three connecting members CONCURRENT** | The parts can still **rotate** about the common point |
| Members collinear at a joint | Local instability |

> **The rectangle-racking case is the everyday one**: a four-bar rectangle has no rigidity at all, which is why **TRIANGULATION is the whole basis of truss design.** A triangle is the only polygon that cannot change shape without changing a member's length.

> **So the arithmetic is necessary but not sufficient** — the added members must also be **placed to triangulate the unbraced panels**, not merely counted.

**Truss classification:**

| Type | Formation |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE** | Built from a base triangle by adding **two members and one joint** at a time — hence m = 2j − 3 |
| **COMPOUND** | **Two or more simple trusses** joined by **three** non-concurrent, non-parallel members |
| **COMPLEX** | Neither — needs special methods (Henneberg's) |

**And the solution methods:**

> A **SIMPLE** truss can always be solved by the **METHOD OF JOINTS**, working outward from a support — because it was built joint by joint, so it can be unbuilt the same way.

> A **COMPOUND** truss usually needs the **METHOD OF SECTIONS** first, cutting the three connecting members, after which each simple truss can be solved on its own.

**The zero-force member rules** are worth carrying alongside, since they eliminate members before any calculation: **two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint are both zero**; and **where three members meet with two collinear and no load, the third is zero.**

> **But a zero-force member is not useless** — it braces compression members against buckling (capacity falls as the **square** of unbraced length) and may be vital under a different load case.

examTip.trick: **m = 2j − 3** comes from counting: **2j equilibrium equations** against **m member forces + 3 reactions**. Here 2(8) − 3 = 13 required, 11 provided, so **2 short**.
examTip.trap: **The count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** A truss can satisfy m = 2j − 3 exactly and still be a mechanism — an unbraced rectangular panel **racks into a parallelogram** however the arithmetic comes out.
examTip.mnemonic: **A TRIANGLE is the only polygon that cannot change shape without changing a member's length** — which is why triangulation is the whole basis of truss design, and why the new members must be **placed**, not just counted.

questions.stem: If there are 2 or more columns in a foundation, then what is the name of the foundation?
questions.solution:
**A combined footing.**

> **The defining feature is simply that ONE footing carries TWO OR MORE columns** — which is exactly what "combined" means.

**When a combined footing is used:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Columns are CLOSE together** | Their individual footings would **overlap** |
| **A column stands at a PROPERTY BOUNDARY** | Its footing cannot be centred, so it is combined with an interior one |
| **Soil bearing capacity is low** | A larger combined area is needed |
| Differential settlement must be controlled | The two columns settle together |

**The governing design principle:**

> A footing bears **UNIFORMLY only when its CENTROID coincides with the RESULTANT of the column loads.** Otherwise the pressure is non-uniform and the footing **tilts.**

| Loads | Shape |
|---|---|
| **Equal**, or space available beyond the lighter column | **RECTANGULAR** |
| **UNEQUAL and space constrained at both ends** | **TRAPEZOIDAL** — wider end under the **heavier** column |
| Columns **far apart** | **STRAP** footing — two pads linked by a beam |

**Note that RAFT and MAT are the same thing under two names** — options (b) and (c) are identical, which tells you neither is the intended answer.

> A **raft/mat** carries **ALL** the columns of a structure on one continuous slab, and is used when footings would cover **more than about half the plan area.** **It is a question of soil capacity and building layout, not of two columns sharing.**

> **A pile foundation** is a **deep** foundation transferring load by end bearing or skin friction — a different category entirely.

**The structural surprise in a combined footing:**

> It spans as a **BEAM loaded UPWARD by the soil**, so it **HOGS between the columns** — and the **main steel goes in the TOP face.**

> **That is the reverse of an isolated footing**, where the soil pressure sags the projecting cantilevers and the steel goes in the bottom. **Getting it wrong is a classic and serious detailing error.**

**The design sequence:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Size the base from the **safe bearing capacity** using **SERVICE** loads |
| **2** | Position it so the **centroid coincides with the load resultant** |
| **3** | Compute the **FACTORED** soil pressure for the structural design |
| **4** | Check **one-way shear at d** and **two-way (punching) shear at d/2** |
| **5** | Design the flexural steel — **TOP steel between the columns** |
| **6** | Check development length |

> **Using factored loads for the bearing check applies the safety factor twice** and produces a footing far larger than necessary — a common and expensive error.

**And the settlement point that decides most foundation designs:**

> **SETTLEMENT, not bearing failure, usually governs** — and it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement that damages structures, not uniform settlement.

> **A raft's chief virtue is that it ties the columns together so they settle as one** — converting differential settlement into uniform settlement, which a building tolerates far better. **It does not necessarily reduce the total settlement at all.**

examTip.trick: **Raft and mat are the SAME foundation under two names** — two of the four options are identical, so neither can be the answer. That halves the field instantly.
examTip.trap: A **raft carries ALL the columns** on one slab, used when footings would cover more than half the plan area. **Two columns sharing a footing is a COMBINED footing**, a different thing.
examTip.mnemonic: **A combined footing is loaded UPWARD by the soil, so it HOGS — main steel in the TOP.** The reverse of an isolated footing, and a classic detailing error.

questions.stem: The effect on timber due to electric seasoning is:
questions.solution:
**Splitting.**

**What electrical seasoning is:**

> Timber is placed in an **electric field** and heated from within by its own **electrical resistance** — the moisture in the wood acts as the conductor.

> **It is extremely rapid**, which is both its attraction and its problem.

**Why it causes splitting:**

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Very rapid moisture removal** | The surface dries far faster than the interior |
| **Steep moisture gradient** | Large differential shrinkage between surface and core |
| **Internal stresses** | Exceed the timber's weak **cross-grain tensile strength** |
| **Result** | **SPLITTING along the grain** |

> **Timber's tension strength ACROSS the grain is only about 1/20 of its strength along it.** Any process that generates internal tension perpendicular to the fibres will split it — and rapid drying does exactly that.

> **The method is therefore rarely used commercially**, despite its speed: it is costly and it damages the timber.

**The seasoning methods compared:**

| Method | Time | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **AIR seasoning** | **Months to years** | **Low** — slow and gentle; stacked with spacers under cover |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Days** | **CASE HARDENING if hurried** |
| Water seasoning | Weeks | Sap leached out first, then air dried |
| **ELECTRICAL** | **Hours** | **SPLITTING** — too fast |
| Chemical | — | Salt treatment before drying |

> **The pattern is clear: the faster the method, the greater the risk of damage.** Air seasoning is slow precisely because slow is safe.

**CASE HARDENING**, the kiln's characteristic defect, is worth distinguishing:

> The **outside dries and sets while the inside is still wet**, locking in internal stresses. **The timber then distorts violently the moment it is sawn** — when the balance of stresses is disturbed.

> **Splitting (electrical) shows immediately; case hardening (kiln) hides until the timber is cut.** That difference makes case hardening the more insidious of the two.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Cracking** | A general term; **splitting is the specific defect** here |
| **ROT** | **DECAY by FUNGI**, requiring moisture **above about 20%** — seasoning **prevents** rot, it cannot cause it |
| **CHECK** | A **surface crack that does not extend through** the piece — a milder defect, typical of air seasoning |

> **"Rot" is the clearest elimination**: seasoning removes moisture, and fungi need moisture. **A process that dries timber cannot rot it** — it does the opposite.

> **Check versus split** is the finer distinction: a **CHECK is a surface separation along the grain**; a **SPLIT extends completely through** the piece. **Severity is what separates them.**

**The seasoning defects generally:**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Bow, cup, twist, spring** | Uneven or **anisotropic** shrinkage |
| **Checks and splits** | Surface drying faster than the interior |
| **Honeycombing** | **Internal** splitting from over-rapid drying |
| **Case hardening** | Locked-in drying stresses |
| Collapse | Cell walls crushed by rapid drying |

> **Shrinkage is ANISOTROPIC — tangential is about TWICE radial, and longitudinal almost nil.** That is why **boards CUP away from the heart** as they dry, and why **quarter-sawn** timber is more stable and more valuable than plain-sawn.

**And the threshold that governs it all:** the **FIBRE SATURATION POINT at about 30% moisture.** **Above it water sits free in the cavities and nothing happens; below it water leaves the cell WALLS, and the timber both shrinks and strengthens.**

examTip.trick: **The faster the seasoning method, the greater the damage.** Electrical seasoning is the fastest of all, so it produces the most severe defect — splitting right through the piece.
examTip.trap: **"ROT" is the clearest elimination** — decay needs moisture **above 20%**, and seasoning removes moisture. A drying process cannot rot timber; it prevents rot.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CHECK is a surface crack; a SPLIT goes right through.** And the kiln's defect is **CASE HARDENING**, which hides until the timber is sawn and then distorts violently.

questions.stem: If enough water for workability of concrete is already added, then increasing the w/c ratio in the concrete results in:
options: strength is independent of the w/c ratio
questions.solution:
**Strength will decrease.**

**ABRAMS' LAW** is the governing principle:

> **The strength of concrete depends primarily on the WATER–CEMENT RATIO, and INVERSELY so** — lower w/c gives higher strength, almost regardless of the mix proportions.

**Why extra water destroys strength:**

> **Only about 0.25 of water per unit of cement is chemically needed for HYDRATION.** Everything above that is added purely for **workability**.

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1** | Excess water occupies space in the fresh mix |
| **2** | It **EVAPORATES** as the concrete dries |
| **3** | It leaves behind **CAPILLARY PORES** |
| **4** | **Higher porosity → weaker bonds between cement particles → LOWER STRENGTH** |

> **The pores are the mechanism.** The source states it exactly: increasing w/c beyond what workability requires **"leads to higher porosity and weaker bonds between cement particles."**

**And the durability cost is worse than the strength cost:**

> **Those same pores make the concrete PERMEABLE** — and **permeability is the master durability property**, because every deterioration mechanism requires something to get **in**:

| Mechanism | Needs to enter |
|---|---|
| **CARBONATION** | CO₂ — drops the pH to ~9 and **depassivates the steel** |
| **CHLORIDE attack** | Chloride ions — **pitting corrosion** |
| **Sulphate attack** | Sulphates — expansive ettringite |
| **Freeze–thaw** | Water, which then expands on freezing |

> **So excess water costs strength AND durability together**, and the durability loss is the more expensive over a structure's life.

**The key phrase in the question — "if enough water for workability is ALREADY added":**

> That phrase removes the only benefit extra water could offer. **Below the workability requirement, more water genuinely helps** — a mix too dry cannot be compacted, and **poorly compacted concrete is far weaker than the w/c ratio alone would predict.**

> **That is why option (c), "may increase or decrease", is not absurd**: for a mix that is too dry, adding water does improve the result. **But the question explicitly excludes that case**, leaving only the harmful direction.

> **Compaction matters enormously**: **5% of entrapped air can reduce strength by about 30%.** A stiff mix that cannot be compacted loses more strength to voids than it gains from a low w/c ratio.

**The right way to increase workability:**

| Admixture | Water reduction |
|---|---|
| **Plasticiser** | **5 – 15%** |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER** | **15 – 30%** |

> **They give the workability of a wet mix at the w/c of a dry one — breaking the conflict between placeability and durability** that would otherwise force a compromise.

> **Superplasticisers are what make high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible at all**; without them a w/c of 0.3 would be unplaceable.

**The IS 456 durability limits**, which tie w/c to exposure directly:

| Exposure | Max w/c | Min grade |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** | M20 |
| Moderate | 0.50 | M25 |
| **Severe** | **0.45** | M30 |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | M40 |

> **Durability, not strength, often fixes the grade** — a structure in severe exposure needs M30 even if M20 would carry the load.

**And the commonest malpractice on site:** **adding water to a stiffening truck load** to restore workability. **It raises the w/c ratio and destroys strength and durability together** — which is why the answer is always a plasticiser, never a bucket.

examTip.trick: **Only ~0.25 water per cement is needed for HYDRATION** — the rest is for workability and **evaporates, leaving capillary pores.** Those pores are the mechanism of the strength loss.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is not absurd** — below the workability requirement more water genuinely helps, since **uncompacted concrete loses ~30% strength to 5% entrapped air.** But the question explicitly excludes that case.
examTip.mnemonic: **Excess water costs STRENGTH and DURABILITY together**, and the durability loss is dearer — permeability lets carbonation, chlorides and sulphates in. **Use a PLASTICISER, never a bucket.**

questions.stem: What nominal mix of concrete is required for roofing of RCC?
questions.solution:
**M20** — nominal mix **1 : 1.5 : 3**.

> The source's reasoning: **M20 is commonly used for roof construction, where the concrete is subject to light to moderate loading**, and it provides **good workability with sufficient strength** for the purpose.

**The nominal mixes and their grades:**

| Mix | Grade | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **1 : 3 : 6** | **M10** | **Lean concrete, levelling course, blinding** |
| **1 : 2 : 4** | **M15** | Plain concrete, mass foundations |
| **1 : 1.5 : 3** | **M20** | **The commonest structural nominal mix — slabs, beams, roofs** |
| **1 : 1 : 2** | **M25** | — |
| Above M25 | — | **DESIGN mix ONLY** |

> **IS 456 permits nominal mixes only up to M20**, and requires **design mixes above it.**

> **The reason is that a nominal mix is a rule of thumb** which cannot account for the actual aggregate grading, shape, moisture content or cement strength. **Above M20 those variables matter too much to guess**, and the mix must be proportioned by trial.

> **So M20 is not merely a common choice — it is the highest grade for which a nominal mix is permitted at all**, which is part of why it is the default structural mix.

**Why M10 and M15 are inadequate for a structural roof:**

> **M10 is lean concrete** — it is used as a **levelling or blinding layer** beneath foundations, to give a clean working surface and prevent the ground contaminating the structural concrete. **It is not a structural grade.**

> **M15 is used for plain (unreinforced) concrete** and mass fill. **For a reinforced roof slab it lacks both the strength and the durability.**

**And why M30 is not the answer:**

> **M30 is a DESIGN mix, not a nominal one** — the question asks specifically for a **nominal** mix. **M30 would also be unnecessarily rich** for a lightly loaded roof, adding cost, heat of hydration and shrinkage for no benefit.

> **A richer mix is not automatically better**: more cement means **more shrinkage, more heat and more cracking.**

**The durability requirement may override the strength requirement:**

| Exposure | Min grade | Max w/c | Min cement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **M20** | 0.55 | 300 kg/m³ |
| Moderate | M25 | 0.50 | 300 |
| **Severe** | **M30** | 0.45 | 320 |
| Very severe | M35 | 0.45 | 340 |
| **Extreme** | **M40** | 0.40 | 360 |

> **A roof slab in a severe exposure needs M30 regardless of load** — because the concrete must also keep aggressive agents out for fifty years. **Durability, not strength, often fixes the grade.**

**Quantities for M20 (1:1.5:3), per cubic metre:**

| Material | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **Cement** | **(1/5.5) × 1.54 = 0.28 m³ ≈ 8 bags ≈ 400 kg** |
| **Sand** | 1.5/5.5 × 1.54 = **0.42 m³** |
| **Coarse aggregate** | 3/5.5 × 1.54 = **0.84 m³** |

> **The 1.54 is the DRY VOLUME factor** — dry aggregates contain voids that disappear when mixed and compacted, so 1 m³ of finished concrete needs 1.54 m³ of dry materials. **Omitting it understates the cement by a third**, and it is the standard error in this calculation.

> **And 28.8 bags per m³ of cement** is simply **1440 kg/m³ ÷ 50 kg per bag.**

examTip.trick: **M20 (1:1.5:3) is the HIGHEST grade for which a nominal mix is permitted** — above it IS 456 requires a **design mix**. That alone rules out M30 for a question asking about nominal mixes.
examTip.trap: **M10 is LEAN concrete for blinding and levelling**, not a structural grade; **M15 is for plain concrete.** Neither is adequate for a reinforced roof slab.
examTip.mnemonic: **A richer mix is NOT automatically better** — more cement means more shrinkage, heat and cracking. But **DURABILITY may override**: a roof in severe exposure needs M30 whatever the load.

questions.stem: What is the maximum theoretical percentage of longitudinal reinforcement in an RCC column?
questions.solution:
**6% of the gross cross-sectional area** (IS 456 cl. 26.5.3.1).

> The clause states: **the cross-sectional area of longitudinal reinforcement shall be NOT LESS THAN 0.8 percent and NOT MORE THAN 6 percent of the gross cross-sectional area of the column.**

**The word "THEORETICAL" is doing important work here:**

| Limit | Value | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Theoretical maximum (code)** | **6%** | What the code permits |
| **Practical maximum** | **4%** | **Where lapped bars would otherwise cause congestion** |
| **Minimum** | **0.8%** | Mandatory |

> **IS 456 itself notes that where bars from the column below have to be LAPPED, the percentage should not usually exceed 4%** — because at a lap the steel is effectively doubled, and 6% would become 12% at the lap zone, which cannot be concreted.

> **So 6% is the theoretical ceiling and 4% the practical one**, and option (b) is offered precisely because 4% is the figure most engineers actually work to.

**Why there is a MAXIMUM at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONGESTION** | Concrete cannot be placed and compacted around the bars |
| **Honeycombing** | Aggregate cannot pass between closely spaced bars |
| **Lapping** | Doubles the steel locally |
| Economy | Steel is far dearer than concrete per unit of capacity |

> **The maximum is a CONSTRUCTABILITY limit, not a strength one.** Nothing structural goes wrong at 7% steel — the concrete simply cannot be got in.

**Why there is a MINIMUM (0.8%):**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Resist ACCIDENTAL ECCENTRICITY** | No column is truly axially loaded |
| **Provide DUCTILITY** | A column failure is catastrophic; steel gives warning and rotation capacity |
| **Resist bending from frame action** | Even a nominally axial column attracts moment |
| Control creep and shrinkage effects | — |

> **The column minimum (0.8%) is much higher than a beam's**, and for a different reason: **a beam failure is local, a column failure collapses the storey.**

**The other column detailing rules:**

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum number of bars** | **4** (rectangular), **6** (circular with helical ties) |
| **Minimum bar diameter** | **12 mm** |
| **Maximum spacing of longitudinal bars** | **300 mm** along the perimeter |
| **Tie (lateral) diameter** | **≥ ¼ of the largest longitudinal bar, and ≥ 6 mm** |
| **Tie spacing** | **Least of**: the **least lateral dimension**, **16 × the smallest longitudinal bar diameter**, or **300 mm** |

> **The tie spacing rule matters more than it appears**: ties prevent the **longitudinal bars from BUCKLING outward** once the cover spalls, and they **CONFINE the core concrete**, raising both its strength and its ductility.

**And the seismic detailing that follows from that:**

> **In the plastic hinge zones — the ends of a column — ties are spaced far more closely**, and they must have **135° HOOKS with adequate extension.**

> **A 90° hook OPENS OUT the moment the cover spalls** — which is exactly when the tie is needed. **The 135° hook is the smallest detail in seismic construction with the largest consequence**, and the one most often ignored on site.

> **STRONG COLUMN – WEAK BEAM** is the governing philosophy: hinges must form in the **beams**, because a beam hinge is local while a **column hinge collapses the storey.**

examTip.trap: **"THEORETICAL" is the operative word.** The code permits **6%**, but IS 456 itself advises **4% where bars are LAPPED** — because a lap doubles the steel locally and 6% would become 12%.
examTip.trick: **The maximum is a CONSTRUCTABILITY limit, not a strength one** — nothing structural fails at 7% steel; the concrete simply cannot be placed and compacted around the bars.
examTip.mnemonic: **Column minimum 0.8% — far above a beam's — because a beam hinge is local but a COLUMN hinge collapses the storey.** And **135° hooks**: a 90° hook opens out exactly when it is needed.

questions.stem: What is the name of that slab which is continuously two ways supported and carries load in one direction only?
questions.solution:
**A one-way slab.**

> **The defining feature is how the load is CARRIED, not how the slab is SUPPORTED.** A slab supported on all four sides can still be a one-way slab if it spans predominantly in one direction.

**The classification (IS 456):**

| Ratio L_y/L_x | Behaviour | Design as |
|---|---|---|
| **≤ 2** | Both directions contribute meaningfully | **TWO-WAY slab** |
| **> 2** | The **short span carries over 94%** of the load | **ONE-WAY slab** |

> The source states it precisely: **when the ratio of longer span to shorter span is equal to or greater than 2, the slab is treated as one-way, and it bends in one direction — along its SHORTER span.**

**Why the limit is exactly 2 — and it is not arbitrary:**

> The two directions share the load in proportion to their **stiffness**, and since deflection **δ ∝ L⁴**:

> **w_x/w_y = (L_y/L_x)⁴**

| Ratio | Short span carries |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 50% |
| **1.5** | **83%** (1.5⁴ = 5.06) |
| **2.0** | **94%** (2⁴ = 16, so 16/17) |

> **At a ratio of 2 the short span already carries 94%**, so treating it as one-way costs almost nothing in accuracy. **The code's apparently arbitrary limit is a direct consequence of the fourth power law.**

> **That fourth-power sensitivity is the key idea** — knowing it makes the limit memorable and the reasoning transferable.

**Design consequences for a one-way slab:**

| Steel | Direction | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **MAIN steel** | **Across the SHORT span** | Carries the load |
| **DISTRIBUTION steel** | Along the long span | **0.12% of gross area (Fe 415)** |

> **Distribution steel carries no calculated load, yet it is mandatory.** Its jobs are to **distribute concentrated loads laterally**, to **resist shrinkage and temperature stresses**, and to **hold the main bars in position** during concreting.

> **A member can require reinforcement that no calculation demands** — which is why minimum percentages exist as code requirements rather than as design outputs.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Two-way slab** | Ratio **≤ 2** — carries load in **both** directions |
| **Torsional slab** | Not a standard classification; **torsion reinforcement** is provided at the **held-down CORNERS of a two-way slab** |
| **Continuous slab** | Describes **support conditions** (spanning over several supports), not the direction of load transfer |

> **"Continuous" is the meaningful near-miss**, because the question's phrase "continuously two ways supported" invites it. **But continuity describes the supports; one-way/two-way describes the LOAD PATH.** They are independent — a slab can be continuous **and** one-way.

**The corner effect in a TWO-way slab**, worth knowing for the contrast:

> A two-way slab **tries to LIFT at its corners.** Where the corners are **held down**, **torsional moments develop** and **corner reinforcement in both faces and both directions** is required.

> **Omitting corner steel produces diagonal cracking at the corners** — a common and easily avoided defect, and the origin of the term "torsional" in option (c).

**And the check that usually governs slab thickness:** the **span/effective depth ratio** — **cantilever 7, simply supported 20, continuous 26**, modified by factors for tension steel (up to 2.0).

> **For slabs, DEFLECTION almost always governs the depth rather than strength**, which is why the span/depth ratio is the first thing computed, not the last.

examTip.trick: **The classification is by how the load is CARRIED, not how the slab is SUPPORTED.** A slab supported on four sides is still one-way if **L_y/L_x > 2**.
examTip.trap: **"Continuous" describes the SUPPORTS; one-way/two-way describes the LOAD PATH.** They are independent — a slab can be continuous and one-way at once, which is what the question's wording invites you to confuse.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load share goes as the FOURTH power of the span ratio** — at L_y/L_x = 2 the short span already carries **94%**, which is exactly why the code draws the line there.

questions.stem: The placement of an intake is not optimal when it is placed in:
questions.solution:
**Both — a natural channel and a navigation channel are each poor locations.**

**Why a NATURAL channel is unsuitable:**

> Natural channels **carry debris, sediment and pollutants**, which **clog the intake and degrade the water quality** drawn from it.

> **The main current of a natural channel is exactly where the load is heaviest** — floating debris on the surface, bed load along the bottom, and the highest suspended concentrations in between.

**Why a NAVIGATION channel is unsuitable:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vessels could DAMAGE the intake structure** | Collision, anchoring, dredging |
| **The intake creates TURBULENCE that disrupts navigation** | The interference runs both ways |
| Pollution from vessels | Oil, discharge |

> **The conflict is mutual**: the channel damages the intake, and the intake obstructs the channel. **Neither use is compatible with the other.**

**What optimal placement requires:**

> **Areas with MINIMAL flow disruption, minimal debris, and no risk of damage from vessels.**

**The siting principles that follow:**

| Principle | Reason |
|---|---|
| **OUTSIDE of a river bend** | The **helical secondary current** sweeps bed load toward the **inside**, leaving cleaner water at the outer bank |
| **Draw from near the SURFACE** | **Sediment concentration is HIGHEST at the bed** |
| **Upstream of any pollution source** | Discharges, settlements, industry |
| Where the bank is stable | Not on an eroding or accreting reach |
| Accessible for maintenance | — |
| Adequate depth at low flow | So the intake never draws air |

> **The bend siting is the single most valuable decision, and it costs nothing.** Placing the intake on the outside of a bend removes more sediment than any structure downstream — because the river itself does the separating.

> **That is worth emphasising: one siting choice can outperform an expensive settling basin**, and the two together are what a good headworks relies on.

**Intake types:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **SUBMERGED** | Entirely underwater, on the bed. **No obstruction to navigation or debris — but draws from where sediment is WORST, and cannot be inspected without diving** |
| **EXPOSED (side/tower)** | Above water; **can draw from the cleanest layer** and be inspected; vulnerable to floods and debris |
| Canal / infiltration gallery | Specialised |

> **The exposed side intake is generally preferred where feasible**, precisely because it can select the draw-off level and be maintained.

**Why sediment matters so much in Nepal:**

> Himalayan rivers carry **very heavy sediment loads**, and the suspended fraction is largely **QUARTZ — harder than turbine steel.**

> **A Pelton needle or Francis runner can lose its profile in a single monsoon** without effective sediment exclusion. **Turbine erosion is the dominant O&M problem of Nepali hydropower.**

**The defences in order along the water's path:**

| Structure | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Intake SITING** | **The most, for free** |
| **Trash rack** | Floating debris, branches |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | Coarse **bed load** |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | Finer **suspended** sand |
| Flushing | What has settled |

> **Coarse first, fine second** — a settling basin cannot handle boulders, which is why the gravel trap precedes it.

examTip.trick: Both named locations fail, for **different reasons**: a natural channel brings **debris and sediment**; a navigation channel brings **mutual interference** with vessels. Read both before choosing one.
examTip.trap: On an "either/or/both" question, check whether **each** option independently holds. Stopping at the first plausible one loses the mark.
examTip.mnemonic: **Site the intake on the OUTSIDE of a bend and draw near the SURFACE** — the helical current sweeps bed load to the inside, and sediment is worst at the bed. **One free decision outperforms an expensive settling basin.**

questions.stem: Below which DO value is the survival of aquatic life not possible?
questions.solution:
**4 mg/L** — the minimum dissolved oxygen necessary in rivers and streams for the survival of fish and aquatic animals.

**Reference DO values:**

| Condition | DO |
|---|---|
| **Saturation at 20 °C** | **9.08 mg/L** |
| Saturation at 0 °C | 14.6 mg/L |
| Saturation at 30 °C | 7.6 mg/L |
| **Minimum for aquatic life** | **4 mg/L** |
| Below 2 mg/L | Only the most tolerant species |
| **0 mg/L** | **ANAEROBIC — the river is septic** |

> **Note that option (d), 15 mg/L, EXCEEDS saturation at any normal temperature** — it is physically unattainable in a river except through algal supersaturation, so it can be discarded on sight.

**Why warm water is doubly penalised** — the fact worth carrying:

| Effect of higher temperature | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Oxygen SOLUBILITY falls** | Less oxygen can dissolve |
| **Biological activity RISES** | BOD is exerted faster |

> **Warm water holds LESS oxygen and consumes it FASTER — a double penalty.**

> **That is why THERMAL POLLUTION is a genuine pollutant** even though it adds no substance: warming a river reduces its oxygen while increasing the demand on it.

> **And it is why a slow, warm, low-flow river in the dry season has almost no self-purification capacity** — exactly when discharge standards matter most, because dilution is least.

**The DIURNAL swing** that makes sampling time critical:

| Time | DO |
|---|---|
| **Afternoon** | **SUPERSATURATED** — algal photosynthesis outpaces respiration |
| **Just before DAWN** | **MINIMUM — can approach zero** |

> **Fish kills occur pre-dawn**, and **an afternoon sample can be dangerously misleading.** A water body must be judged on its **pre-dawn minimum**, not its daytime value.

**The OXYGEN SAG CURVE (Streeter–Phelps):**

> Organic matter discharged to a river consumes its oxygen. Two competing processes govern the result:

| Process | Effect |
|---|---|
| **DEOXYGENATION** | BOD being exerted — removes oxygen |
| **REAERATION** | Atmospheric oxygen entering — restores it |

> **The CRITICAL POINT — the minimum DO — occurs where the two RATES are EQUAL.** That is the point at which a discharge must be judged, and it may lie many kilometres downstream of the outfall.

**What governs self-purification:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Dilution** | More flow, more capacity |
| **TURBULENCE** | **Faster reaeration** — a rapid reaches recovers quickly |
| **Temperature** | Warmer is worse, both ways |
| Time of travel | More time for recovery |

> **Self-purification is real but limited** — and it is at its weakest precisely when the river is at its most vulnerable.

**The standards this connects to:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **BOD₅ test** | **20 °C for 5 days** — captures ~68% of ultimate BOD |
| **COD** | 3 hours; **always higher** than BOD |
| **Effluent discharge standard (Nepal)** | Commonly **50 mg/L BOD** |
| Medium domestic sewage | ~220 mg/L BOD |

> **A percentage removal is not a standard**: a 3000 mg/L waste treated to 90% still discharges 300 mg/L. **Consents are written as concentrations and loads**, because it is the **mass** of oxygen-demanding matter reaching the river that determines whether the DO falls below 4 mg/L.

examTip.trick: **Option (d), 15 mg/L, EXCEEDS saturation at any normal temperature** (9.08 mg/L at 20 °C) — physically unattainable, so it can be discarded on sight.
examTip.trap: **DO swings through the day**: supersaturated in the afternoon, **minimum just before DAWN**. Fish kills happen pre-dawn, so an afternoon sample is dangerously misleading.
examTip.mnemonic: **Warm water holds LESS oxygen and consumes it FASTER — a double penalty**, which is why thermal pollution is a real pollutant and why dry-season low flows are the critical condition.

questions.stem: For a rapidly growing population, which method of projection is preferred?
questions.solution:
**The geometrical increase method.**

**Why.** The source states the reasoning directly: **an arithmetical increase assumes a CONSTANT population growth, which would not be accurate for a rapidly growing population. Geometrical increase assumes an EXPONENTIAL growth rate, which is more likely for a rapidly growing population.**

**The methods and what each assumes:**

| Method | Assumes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETICAL increase** | **Constant INCREMENT** each decade (**P_n = P₀ + n x̄**) | **Large, OLD, saturating** towns |
| **GEOMETRIC progression** | **Constant PERCENTAGE** growth (**P_n = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ**) | **YOUNG, RAPIDLY growing** towns |
