examTip.mnemonic: **Alligator cracking means the pavement is TOO THIN for its traffic** — a structural message, so patching treats only the symptom. And **RUTTING and CRACKING need OPPOSITE remedies**: too soft versus too brittle.

questions.stem: Find the value of radius of curvature if D is given as 23.76.
questions.solution:
**241.16 m.**

**Working.** Using the **degree of curve** relation:

> **R = 5730/D**
> **R = 5730/23.76 = 241.16 m** ✓

**Where 5730 comes from — and it is worth knowing rather than memorising:**

> The **degree of curve D is the angle subtended at the centre by an arc of 30 m** (the metric standard; 100 ft in imperial practice).

> Arc length **s = R θ**, with θ in radians:
> **30 = R × (D × π/180)**
> **R = 30 × 180/(π D) = 5400/(π D) = 1718.9/D**

> **The 5730 constant corresponds to a 100-unit arc**, which is the origin of the number: **R = 100 × 180/π = 5729.6 ≈ 5730.**

> **The formula in use here is the 5730 form**, which is what the source applies and what gives the keyed answer.

**Why degree of curve is used at all:**

> **It is far more convenient for SETTING OUT than the radius.** A surveyor working along a curve with a chain and theodolite deals naturally in **deflection angles per chord**, and the degree of curve expresses exactly that.

> **A large D means a SHARP curve; a small D a flat one** — the inverse relation to radius, which is worth fixing in mind: **R = 5730/D**, so they are reciprocal.

**Where the radius then feeds into design:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Minimum radius** | **R = V²/(127(e + f))** |
| **Superelevation** | **e = V²/(225 R)** — using **75% of design speed** |
| **Extra widening** | **nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** |
| **Grade compensation** | **(30 + R)/R %, max 75/R** |
| Transition length | Greatest of three criteria |

> **Nearly every geometric element depends on R**, which is why establishing it correctly is the first step in curve design.

**The superelevation constant, since it recurs:**

> **225 = 127 ÷ 0.75²** — superelevation is designed for **75% of the design speed**, so that slow vehicles are not made to slide inward on a steeply banked curve.

> **e_max: 7% plain and rolling, 10% hilly (not snow bound), 7% snow bound.**

> **Snow-bound roads are capped at 7% even in the hills**, because a steeply banked icy road makes a **stationary or slow vehicle slide inward off the carriageway.**

**And the transition curve** that connects the straight to the circular arc:

> A **SPIRAL (clothoid)** is used because its **radius decreases uniformly with length** — exactly matching a driver turning the steering wheel at a steady rate.

> **Its length is the GREATEST of three criteria**: the rate of change of radial acceleration (**L = 0.0215V³/CR**), the rate of superelevation application (1 in 150 for hills), and the IRC empirical value.

> **A curve without a transition forces an instantaneous change in radial acceleration** — the driver must jerk the wheel, and the superelevation must appear abruptly. **Both are unsafe and uncomfortable.**

examTip.trick: **R = 5730/D** — and the 5730 is simply **100 × 180/π = 5729.6**, the angle relation for a 100-unit arc. Knowing its origin means never mis-remembering it.
examTip.trap: **R and D are RECIPROCAL** — a large degree of curve means a **sharp** curve, a small one a flat curve. That inverse relation is easy to get backwards under time pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Degree of curve exists because it suits SETTING OUT** — a surveyor works in deflection angles per chord, not radii. And nearly every geometric element (e, widening, grade compensation) then depends on **R**.

questions.stem: What is the effect of using traffic signals at intersections?
options: reduce right angle collision as well as rear end collision
reduce rear end collision but may increase right angle collision
reduced right angle collision but may increase rear end collision
questions.solution:
**Reduce right-angle collisions but may increase rear-end collisions.**

**Why the trade-off exists:**

| Collision type | Effect of signals |
|---|---|
| **RIGHT-ANGLE (crossing)** | **REDUCED** — signals separate conflicting movements **in TIME**, so crossing streams no longer meet |
| **REAR-END** | **may INCREASE** — vehicles now **stop and start** where previously they flowed, and a driver who stops abruptly on amber is struck from behind |

> **The trade is deliberate and it is a good one**, because **right-angle collisions are far more severe than rear-end collisions.**

> A right-angle impact strikes the **side of a vehicle**, where there is little crush space and no structural protection; a rear-end impact is absorbed by both vehicles' crumple zones and is usually low-severity.

> **Signals therefore trade many MINOR collisions for few SEVERE ones** — a net safety gain even when the total number of collisions rises.

**The source lists both sides:**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| Improve overall safety | **May increase delay during the OFF-PEAK period** |
| Decrease average travel time through the intersection | **May increase certain accidents, such as REAR-END collisions** |
| Equalise the quality of service for all traffic streams | **Driver irritation if improperly configured** |
| Provide orderly movement; flexible to changes in flow | — |
| **Priority for emergency services** | — |
| **Reduce right-angle collisions** | — |

> **The off-peak delay point is important**: at low volumes a signal makes drivers wait for no reason, and **an unnecessary signal is a genuine disbenefit**, not merely a neutral one.

**The three ways of dealing with intersection conflict:**

| Method | Mechanism | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **CHANNELIZATION** | **Guides and reduces** conflicts with islands and markings | Lowest |
| **SIGNALS** | **Separate conflicts in TIME** | Moderate |
| **ROUNDABOUT** | **CONVERTS crossings into WEAVING** | Moderate |
| **GRADE SEPARATION** | **ELIMINATES crossing conflicts** | Highest |

> **A plain four-arm crossroads has 32 conflict points, of which 16 are CROSSINGS** — the most dangerous kind. **That number is why intersection treatment matters so much.**

**A ROUNDABOUT is the instructive alternative:**

> It **converts every crossing conflict into a weaving one** and requires **no one to stop** when gaps are available — so it avoids both the right-angle collisions and the stop-start rear-end risk.

> **Its limits are capacity and geometry**: the **weaving length must be at least 4 × the entry width**, with a **weaving angle of 15–40°**. **An undersized rotary performs worse than a signal**, because vehicles cannot complete the merge.

**Signal capacity**, for completeness:

> **Capacity = saturation flow × (effective green ÷ cycle time)**, with **effective green = green + amber − lost time.**

> **LOST TIME is 3–4 seconds per PHASE** and is pure overhead. **More phases therefore REDUCE capacity**, even though each phase individually looks safer.

> **Webster's optimum cycle: C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y)** — with **L in the numerator**, so cutting lost time shortens the cycle **and** raises capacity together. **Practical cycles are 40–120 seconds**; beyond that delay grows steeply and drivers begin to violate the signal.

**When signals are warranted at all**: traffic volume on both approaches, **pedestrian volume**, **accident record** (particularly a recurring right-angle pattern), and coordination with adjacent signals.

> **Signals are not always an improvement** — which is exactly what the off-peak delay and rear-end disbenefits reflect.

examTip.trick: Signals **separate conflicts in TIME**, which removes crossing (right-angle) conflicts — but they introduce **stopping and starting**, which creates rear-end risk. The trade is deliberate.
examTip.trap: The trade is **worth making because right-angle collisions are FAR more severe** — a side impact has no crush space. Signals trade many **minor** collisions for few **severe** ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **A four-arm crossroads has 32 conflict points, 16 of them CROSSINGS.** Channelization guides, **signals separate in time**, a roundabout converts, and grade separation **eliminates** — four answers at four costs.

questions.stem: What is the brake reaction time of a normal driver?
questions.solution:
**2.5 seconds** — the IRC design value.

**What the reaction time covers** — it is not a single act but a sequence, described by the **PIEV** theory:

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P — Perception** | The driver **sees** the object |
| **I — Intellection** | **Understands** what it is and what it means |
| **E — Emotion** | Decides on the response (and any emotional reaction) |
| **V — Volition** | **Acts** — moves the foot to the brake |

> **All four occur before the brakes begin to act at all**, and the vehicle travels its full speed throughout.

> **That is why 2.5 seconds is not merely "slow reflexes"** — it is a compound of several mental steps, and it is deliberately generous so as to cover ordinary drivers rather than alert ones.

**The distance it accounts for:**

> **SSD = v t + v²/(2 g f)**

| Component | Name |
|---|---|
| **v t** | **LAG (reaction) distance** |
| **v²/2gf** | **BRAKING distance** |

| Speed | Lag distance (2.5 s) | Braking distance (f = 0.35) |
|---|---|---|
| **50 km/h** | **34.7 m** | ~28 m |
| **80 km/h** | **55.6 m** | ~72 m |
| 100 km/h | 69.4 m | ~112 m |

> **At lower speeds the reaction distance DOMINATES**, and at higher speeds the braking term takes over — because **the lag distance grows with v while braking grows with v².**

> **That crossover explains why speed reduction is so effective in urban areas**: at 50 km/h more than half the stopping distance is consumed before the brakes even engage.

**The other design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reaction time (IRC)** | **2.5 s** |
| **Longitudinal friction f** | **0.35 – 0.40** |
| **On a gradient** | **f ± 0.01n** — **PLUS** upgrade, **MINUS** downgrade |
| **Driver's eye height** | **1.2 m** |
| **Object height (SSD)** | **0.15 m** |

> **A DOWNGRADE lengthens the required SSD substantially**, which matters greatly on hill roads where **steep descending gradients and sharp curves frequently coincide.**

**The sight distance family:**

| Type | Governs |
|---|---|
| **SSD** | **The absolute minimum on EVERY road** |
| **OSD** | Two-lane two-way roads — **about FIVE times SSD** |
| **Intermediate (ISD)** | **= 2 × SSD**, where full OSD is unattainable |
| **Headlight sight distance** | **VALLEY (sag) curves at night** |

> **SUMMIT curves are governed by SIGHT distance (a daytime problem); VALLEY curves by HEADLIGHT distance (a night-time one).** A sag curve looks unobstructed by day — its difficulty appears only after dark, when the beam (**1° upward from 0.75 m**) limits how far ahead the driver sees.

> **Getting that pairing backwards is a standard error**, and it matters because the two curves are designed by entirely different criteria.

**And the practical maintenance point:** sight distance is **obstructed on the INSIDE of a horizontal curve** by cut slopes, walls and vegetation. **The required set-back must be cleared and KEPT clear** — vegetation growing back into it is one of the commonest causes of degraded safety on an otherwise adequate road.

examTip.trick: **2.5 s covers the whole PIEV sequence** — Perception, Intellection, Emotion, Volition — not just reflexes. It is deliberately generous, covering ordinary drivers rather than alert ones.
examTip.trap: **At low speeds the REACTION distance dominates** (lag grows with v, braking with v²) — at 50 km/h more than half the stopping distance passes before the brakes engage. That is why urban speed reduction works so well.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a downgrade use f − 0.01n**, which lengthens SSD — critical where steep descents meet sharp curves. And **SUMMIT curves are a daytime SIGHT problem; VALLEY curves a night-time HEADLIGHT one.**

questions.stem: Paper is designated by which letter?
questions.solution:
**A** — as in A0, A1, A2, A3, A4.

> Paper is designated by the letters **A, B and C**, with the **A series** being the standard for drawings and documents.

**The A-series and its defining property:**

| Size | Dimensions (mm) |
|---|---|
| **A0** | **841 × 1189 — AREA EXACTLY 1 m²** |
| **A1** | 594 × 841 |
| **A2** | 420 × 594 |
| **A3** | 297 × 420 |
| **A4** | **210 × 297** |

> **A0 has an area of exactly 1 m²**, and **each successive size HALVES the longer dimension** — so A1 is half of A0, A2 half of A1, and so on.

**The elegant property that makes the system work:**

> **Every A-series sheet has the SAME ASPECT RATIO of 1 : √2.**

> **That is the only ratio for which halving the longer side preserves the proportions** — which is why an A4 page scales perfectly onto A3 with no cropping or blank margin.

> **The √2 ratio is what makes the whole series self-similar**, and it is why photocopier enlargement and reduction factors are 141% and 71% (that is, √2 and 1/√2).

**Why it matters for drawings:**

> **Lettering heights follow the same √2 progression: 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm.**

> **So a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its lettering exactly ONE standard size smaller and remains legible.** The two standards were designed to work together.

**The other paper series:**

| Series | Use |
|---|---|
| **A** | **Standard documents and drawings** |
| **B** | Intermediate sizes — posters, books |
| **C** | **Envelopes** — sized to hold the corresponding A sheet |

> **A C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat** — the C series exists precisely for that.

**The drawing conventions that accompany the sheet size:**

| Convention | Value |
|---|---|
| **Lettering styles** | **Vertical 90°** or **inclined 75°** — **only ONE per drawing** |
| **Aspect ratio of capitals** | **h : w = 7 : 5** |
| **Stroke thickness** | h/10 (type B) |
| **Line types** | Continuous **thick** = visible outline; **dashed** = hidden; **thin chain** = centre line |
| **Hatching** | Thin lines at **45°**, only on material the section plane **CUTS** |
| **Isometric axes** | **120°** apart; isometric scale ≈ **0.816** |

> **Ribs, webs, shafts, bolts and fasteners are NOT hatched** even when the section plane passes through them — hatching them would misrepresent the shape.

**And the convention that must never be omitted:**

> **Every drawing carries the PROJECTION SYMBOL in its title block** — because **first angle (top view BELOW) and third angle (top view ABOVE)** produce **mirror-image readings** of the same part.

> **A drawing read in the wrong system is a mirror image of the intended object**, which is why the symbol is mandatory rather than decorative.

**A note on scales**, since they appear alongside: the **drawing's dimension is stated FIRST**, so **x : 1 ENLARGES** and **1 : x REDUCES**. And **a GRAPHICAL bar scale should always be drawn**, because drawings are reproduced at altered sizes and a stated ratio then lies — while a drawn bar scale reduces with the drawing and stays correct.

examTip.trick: **A0 is exactly 1 m², and each size halves the longer dimension.** The **1 : √2 aspect ratio** is the only one for which halving preserves the proportions — which is what makes the series self-similar.
examTip.trap: **C is a real paper series too — for ENVELOPES**, sized to hold the corresponding A sheet. But drawings and documents use the **A** series.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lettering heights follow the SAME √2 progression (2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm)** — so a drawing reduced A1 → A2 keeps legible lettering exactly one size down. The two standards were designed together.

questions.stem: What is the expression for the sinking fund factor?
questions.solution:
**i/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** — note that the **whole denominator is bracketed.**

> **Options (a) and (c) contain the same characters with the brackets placed differently**, and that placement changes the value completely. **Reading the brackets is the whole question.**

**What the sinking fund factor does:**

> It converts a **required FUTURE amount F** into the **uniform annual deposit A** needed to accumulate it:

> **A = F × i/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]**

> where **i** is the interest rate and **n** the number of periods.

**Why the denominator has that form:**

> **[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/i** is the **uniform series compound amount factor** — the future value of a series of n annual deposits of 1, each accumulating at compound interest.

> **The sinking fund factor is simply its RECIPROCAL**, which is why the i moves to the numerator and the bracketed expression to the denominator.

> **Recognising the pair means only one of them needs remembering.**

**A sanity check that settles the brackets:**

> Take **n = 1** (a single deposit): the deposit must equal the required amount, so **A/F = 1.**

| Option | Value at n = 1, i = 0.1 |
|---|---|
| **(c) 0.1/[(1.1)¹ − 1] = 0.1/0.1** | **= 1** ✓ |
| (a) 0.1/(1.1)¹ − 1 = 0.0909 − 1 | = −0.909 ✗ |
| (b) 0.1/(1.1) + 1 | = 1.09 ✗ |
| (d) 0.1/[(1.1) + 1] | = 0.0476 ✗ |

> **Only option (c) gives 1 at n = 1**, as it must. **That single substitution settles the question without recalling the formula.**

**What a sinking fund IS:**

> A fund built up by **uniform annual deposits accumulating at compound interest**, so that the total at the end of an asset's life equals its **REPLACEMENT COST.**

> **It is for REPLACEMENT at end of life, not for maintenance during it** — that distinction is the most-tested point in the topic.

**The three depreciation methods:**

| Method | How it writes off value |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | An equal **AMOUNT** each year: **(C − S)/n** |
| **Declining balance** | A fixed **PERCENTAGE** each year — **faster early**, closest to how plant really loses value |
| **SINKING FUND** | Uniform deposits **accumulating at interest** |

> **Only the sinking fund method actually PROVIDES the money** rather than merely recording the loss of value on paper — which is why it appears in **valuation and lease agreements** rather than only in the accounts.

**The standard compound interest factors** worth holding as a set:

| Factor | Expression |
|---|---|
| Single payment compound amount | (1 + i)ⁿ |
| Single payment present worth | 1/(1 + i)ⁿ |
| **Uniform series compound amount** | **[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/i** |
| **SINKING FUND** | **i/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** |
| **Capital recovery** | **i(1 + i)ⁿ/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** |
| Uniform series present worth | [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/[i(1 + i)ⁿ] |

> **Each is the reciprocal of another**, so the set is far smaller than it looks — and **the bracketed [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] appears in four of the six.**

**The related valuation terms:** **scrap value** (dismantled materials, ~10% of cost), **salvage value** (still usable), **year's purchase = 100/rate of interest**, and **capitalised value = net annual income × YP.**

> **A lower interest rate gives a HIGHER year's purchase and a higher valuation** — the same discounting logic seen from the investor's side.

examTip.trick: **Substitute n = 1**: a single deposit must equal the required amount, so **A/F = 1**. Only option (c) gives **0.1/[1.1 − 1] = 1** ✓. One substitution, no recall.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (c) are the same characters with the brackets moved.** The whole denominator **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** must be bracketed — placement changes the value completely.
examTip.mnemonic: **The sinking fund factor is the RECIPROCAL of the uniform series compound amount factor** — so only one of the pair need be remembered. And **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1] appears in FOUR of the six standard factors.**

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines free float?
options: The total amount of time a task can be delayed without affecting the final project delivery date
The amount of time a task can be delayed without impacting other tasks in the path
questions.solution:
**The amount of time a task can be delayed without impacting other tasks in the path.**

> **Option (a) defines TOTAL float, not free float** — and it is the deliberate near-miss, because total float is the more familiar of the two.

**The two floats, precisely:**

| Float | Definition | Affects |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | Delay possible **without affecting the PROJECT completion date** | **= LST − EST** (or LFT − EFT) |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the NEXT (successor) activity** | **= EST(successor) − EFT(this activity)** |

> **Free float is the STRICTER condition**, because not delaying the immediate successor is a tighter requirement than not delaying the project as a whole.

> **Therefore FREE float ≤ TOTAL float, ALWAYS.** That inequality is a useful check on any computation.

**Why the distinction matters practically:**

| Using | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **FREE float** | **Nobody else is affected at all** — the delay is absorbed entirely within this activity |
| **TOTAL float** (beyond free float) | **The project date is safe, but SUCCESSOR activities are pushed later** — their own float is consumed |

> **Total float is SHARED along a chain of activities; free float belongs to one activity alone.**

> **That is the essential difference**: if one activity in a chain uses all the total float, the others in that chain have none left. **Free float can be used without depriving anyone.**

> **"Who owns the float" is therefore a genuine contractual question** — if a contractor consumes the float and the employer then causes a delay, the employer's delay becomes critical and compensable. **Modern contracts often address it explicitly.**

**The other floats:**

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Independent float** | Delay possible **without affecting EITHER neighbour** — the strictest of all |
| **Interfering float** | **Total − free** — the part whose use pushes successors |

> **Independent ≤ free ≤ total** is the complete ordering, each condition stricter than the last.

**How the floats are computed:**

> From the **forward and backward passes**:

| Pass | Rule |
|---|---|
| **FORWARD** (first to last) | **Take the MAXIMUM** — an activity cannot start until **all** predecessors finish |
| **BACKWARD** (last to first) | **Take the MINIMUM** — it must not delay the **earliest** successor |

> **Forward takes the maximum, backward the minimum** — and each has a clear reason, so it need not be memorised.

**And the identifying property of the critical path:**

> **A CRITICAL activity has ZERO TOTAL float** — which is precisely how the critical path is found.

> **Note it is zero TOTAL float, not zero free float.** An activity can have zero free float and still be non-critical.

**Where float is used:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESOURCE SMOOTHING** | Non-critical activities are **shifted within their float** to even the resource histogram — **without changing the completion date** |
| Prioritising management attention | The critical path first |
| Assessing a delay's significance | A delay within float costs nothing |
| Contractual claims | Whether a delay is excusable and compensable |

> **Smoothing consumes FLOAT, so it can only touch NON-CRITICAL activities** — a critical activity has none by definition.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) defines TOTAL float** — the more familiar of the two, and the deliberate near-miss. Free float is about **the next activity**, not the project date.
examTip.trick: **Free float is the STRICTER condition**, so **free ≤ total ALWAYS** — a useful check on any computation. The full ordering is **independent ≤ free ≤ total**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total float is SHARED along a chain; free float belongs to one activity alone.** Which is why **"who owns the float" is a real contractual question** — consuming it can make someone else's later delay critical.

questions.stem: What term denotes reduction of risk to a threshold level?
questions.solution:
**Mitigation.**

> **Risk mitigation involves taking actions to REDUCE the likelihood or impact of a risk to an acceptable level** — which is exactly what "reduction to a threshold level" describes.

**The four standard risk responses** for a threat:

| Response | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **AVOID** | **ELIMINATE** the risk by changing the plan or scope | Reroute away from an unstable slope |
| **TRANSFER** | Shift the **impact and ownership** to a third party | **Insurance**, bonds, fixed-price subcontract |
| **MITIGATE** | **REDUCE the probability or impact** to an acceptable level | Ground improvement; extra site investigation |
| **ACCEPT** | Absorb the consequence | **Contingency reserve** (active) or monitoring (passive) |

> **The one-line discriminator: mitigation REDUCES, avoidance ELIMINATES, transfer MOVES, acceptance ABSORBS.**

**Why the two wrong options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **ACCEPTANCE** | **Taking NO action** — the risk is absorbed, not reduced at all |
| **TRANSFER** | **MOVING** the impact elsewhere — the risk itself is unchanged |

> **Transfer is the more subtle of the two**: insurance does not stop the flood, it **pays for it**. The probability and the physical consequence are exactly what they were.

> **And the RESIDUAL risk always remains with the project** — an insurer who disputes the claim, or a subcontractor who becomes insolvent, hands the risk straight back.

**The key phrase "to a threshold level":**

> **Mitigation does not aim at zero risk** — it aims at a level the organisation is prepared to carry.

> **That is a realistic and important idea**: eliminating risk entirely is usually impossible and always expensive, so the objective is to bring it within **RISK APPETITE** — the amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept.

> **Beyond that threshold, further mitigation costs more than the risk it removes.**

**For a POSITIVE risk (an opportunity)** the four mirror responses are **exploit, share, enhance and accept.**

**The risk management process:**

| Step | Activity |
|---|---|
| **1. Identify** | Brainstorming, checklists, expert judgement, lessons learned |
| **2. Analyse — qualitative** | **Probability × Impact matrix**; rank and prioritise |
| **3. Analyse — quantitative** | Expected monetary value, sensitivity, **Monte Carlo** |
| **4. Plan responses** | Avoid / transfer / mitigate / accept |
| **5. Monitor and control** | Track the register; watch for new risks |

> **The risk register is a LIVING document.** One written at tender and never revisited has no value — and that is the commonest failure of risk management in practice.

**When mitigation is cheapest:**

> **Risks are cheapest to address EARLY**, in **feasibility and design**, where **the ability to influence is high and the cost of change is low.**

> **By the time a risk materialises in construction, the response options have narrowed to the expensive ones** — which is exactly why risk analysis belongs at feasibility, the phase that spends the least and decides the most.

**And the distinction worth carrying:** **RISK is where the probabilities are known or estimable; UNCERTAINTY is where they are not.**

> **Most large infrastructure decisions involve genuine uncertainty rather than measurable risk**, which is why judgement remains essential and why **sensitivity analysis — showing which assumption the decision turns on — is usually more valuable than a single probability-weighted number.**

examTip.trick: One line covers the family: **mitigation REDUCES, avoidance ELIMINATES, transfer MOVES, acceptance ABSORBS.** "Reduction to a threshold" matches only the first.
examTip.trap: **TRANSFER does not reduce risk** — insurance does not stop the flood, it pays for it. And the **residual risk stays with the project**: a failed insurer or insolvent subcontractor hands it back.
examTip.mnemonic: **"To a threshold level" matters — mitigation does not aim at ZERO risk**, but at the organisation's **risk appetite**. Beyond that point, further mitigation costs more than the risk it removes.

questions.stem: How many categories of NEA memberships are there?
questions.solution:
**Three categories.**

> The **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** has three membership categories:

| Category | Note |
|---|---|
| **GENERAL membership** | The standard category |
| **LIFE membership** | A one-time subscription |
| **FELLOW membership** | The senior category, by distinction |

**The distinction that underlies all questions in this area:**

> **The COUNCIL (NEC) REGULATES; the ASSOCIATION (NEA) REPRESENTS.**

| | **NEC** | **NEA** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Statutory REGULATOR** | **Voluntary professional ASSOCIATION** |
| Created by | **NEC Act 2055 (1998)** | Association, not statute |
| **Membership** | **REGISTRATION is a LEGAL REQUIREMENT to practise** | **VOLUNTARY** |
| Function | Register, license, set education standards, **discipline** | Represent members' interests, professional development, advocacy |
| Sanction | **Removal from the register ENDS the right to practise** | Loss of membership only |

> **Practising or signing engineering drawings without NEC registration is an OFFENCE under the Act.** NEA membership carries no such force.

**But the two are deliberately linked:**

> The Act gives the **NEA representation on the Council**:

| NEA presence on the NEC | Number |
|---|---|
| **President of the NEA, EX OFFICIO** | **1** |
| **Members ELECTED from the NEA** | **5** |
| **Total** | **6 of 21 seats** |

> **That is a substantial voice for the profession's own association within its regulator** — and it is a deliberate design, so that regulation is not imposed on the profession from outside it.

**The Council block worth learning as a unit:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total members** | **21** |
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's + **15 years**, **nominated by GoN** |
| **Vice-Chairman** | Bachelor's + **10 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Registrar (Member Secretary)** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| **Members nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **President of the NEA** | **Ex officio** |
| **Minimum for institutional affiliation** | **70%** |
| **Reconstitution after dissolution** | **3 months** |
| First Registrar | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |

> **These recall questions are the cheapest marks on the paper** for anyone who has read the Council's material once — and several appear in every sitting. **Learning the block is worth far more than the time it takes.**

**The Council's functions**: register engineers and maintain the register; **recognise** academic institutions and programmes; **prescribe** minimum standards for engineering education and for admission; prepare policy; **regulate professional conduct and take disciplinary action**; and issue the **license to practise.**

**And what it does NOT do**: open or run colleges, award degrees, fix fees or salaries, or **represent** engineers' interests — the last being the NEA's role.

examTip.trick: **General, Life and Fellow — three categories.** Pure recall, but it sits inside the Council/Association block that supplies several marks in every sitting.
examTip.trap: Keep the two bodies apart: **NEC REGULATES (registration compulsory, removal ends your career); NEA REPRESENTS (membership voluntary).** That one line answers most institutional questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **The NEA holds SIX of the NEC's 21 seats** — its President ex officio plus five elected members. A deliberate design, so the profession has a voice inside its own regulator.

questions.stem: What is the composition of quartzite?
questions.solution:
**Silicious** — quartzite is a **metamorphic rock composed primarily of quartz (silicon dioxide, SiO₂).**

**The chemical classification of rocks:**

| Class | Principal constituent | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **SILICIOUS** | **SILICA (SiO₂)** | **Quartzite, granite, sandstone** |
| **CALCAREOUS** | **Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)** | **Limestone, marble, dolomite** |
| **ARGILLACEOUS** | **CLAY (alumina)** | **Slate, shale, laterite** |

> **The names carry the chemistry: SILICA → silicious; CALCium → calcareous; argilla (Latin for clay) → argillaceous.** Knowing that makes the classification self-explanatory rather than a list to memorise.

**The engineering consequences of each class:**

| Class | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **SILICIOUS** | **HARD, durable, resistant to weathering — but ACIDIC** |
| **CALCAREOUS** | **Softer; ATTACKED BY ACID and by acid rain** — dissolves over time |
| **ARGILLACEOUS** | Often **laminated and weak**; may **soften or slake** when wet |

> **The calcareous vulnerability is real and visible**: limestone and marble buildings weather noticeably in polluted atmospheres, because **CaCO₃ reacts with acidic rainwater.** Silicious stone does not.

**Why the classification matters for AGGREGATE:**

> **STRIPPING** — the loss of adhesion between bitumen and aggregate in the presence of water — depends directly on this chemistry:

| Aggregate | Behaviour with bitumen |
|---|---|
| **SILICIOUS (acidic)** — quartzite, granite | **HYDROPHILIC — prefers water to bitumen → STRIPS readily** |
| **CALCAREOUS (basic)** — limestone, basalt | **Bonds well with bitumen → resists stripping** |

> **A hard, strong, durable silicious aggregate can still make a poor bituminous pavement**, because it sheds its binder when wet.

> **The remedy is an ANTI-STRIPPING AGENT (usually an amine) or HYDRATED LIME**, which is cheaper and works well. **This is a case where the strongest aggregate is not automatically the best one.**

**Quartzite specifically:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Origin** | **METAMORPHIC** — recrystallised sandstone |
| **Composition** | **Quartz (SiO₂)** |
| **Hardness** | **Very hard** — harder than turbine steel, which is why quartz sand erodes runners |
| Durability | Excellent |
| **Use** | Aggregate, road metal, building stone, railway ballast |

> **Quartz's hardness is why Himalayan sediment is so destructive to hydro turbines** — the suspended fraction is largely quartz, and a Pelton needle or Francis runner can lose its profile in a single monsoon without effective settling.

**The geological classification, for completeness:**

| Origin | Formation | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **IGNEOUS** | Cooled magma | Granite, basalt, trap |
| **SEDIMENTARY** | Deposited and consolidated | Sandstone, limestone, shale |
| **METAMORPHIC** | **Altered by heat and pressure** | **Quartzite (from sandstone), marble (from limestone), slate (from shale), gneiss (from granite)** |

> **Note how metamorphism preserves the chemistry while changing the structure**: sandstone (silicious) becomes quartzite (silicious); limestone (calcareous) becomes marble (calcareous); shale (argillaceous) becomes slate (argillaceous).

> **The parent rock's class is inherited by its metamorphic product**, which is a useful way to remember both lists at once.

examTip.trick: **The names carry the chemistry: SILICA → silicious, CALCium → calcareous, argilla (clay) → argillaceous.** Quartz is SiO₂, so quartzite is silicious.
examTip.trap: **A hard, durable SILICIOUS aggregate can still make a poor bituminous pavement** — it is **hydrophilic and STRIPS**. The strongest aggregate is not automatically the best.
examTip.mnemonic: **Metamorphism preserves the CHEMISTRY while changing the structure**: sandstone → quartzite (silicious), limestone → marble (calcareous), shale → slate (argillaceous). One rule, two lists.

questions.stem: Sealed quotations are used for projects up to:
questions.solution:
**Rs 2 million (20 lakhs).**

> **Sealed quotations are the procurement method for works up to about Rs 20 lakhs** — a simplified process for small contracts where full open tendering would cost more in time and administration than it saves.

**The procurement methods, by value:**

| Method | Typical threshold | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct purchase / user committee** | **Smallest works** | No competition required |
| **SEALED QUOTATION** | **Up to ~Rs 20 lakhs (2 million)** | **Limited competition; simplified documents** |
| **OPEN (national) bidding** | Above that | Full advertisement, full documents |
| **International bidding** | Large projects | Wider advertisement |

> **The principle behind the thresholds is PROPORTIONALITY**: the procurement effort should match the contract's value.

> **Full open tendering on a very small contract is uneconomic** — the cost of preparing documents, advertising, evaluating and administering can approach the contract sum itself.

> **But the simplified method also carries less competition and less transparency**, which is exactly why it is capped at a threshold rather than left to judgement.

**Why the thresholds matter professionally:**

> **SPLITTING a large work into several small packages to stay below a threshold is a serious procurement offence** — it defeats the competition the threshold exists to ensure.

> **That is one of the commonest audit findings in public works**, and an engineer who prepares such packages is party to it.

**The procurement principles the rules serve:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **COMPETITION** | Obtains the best price |
| **TRANSPARENCY** | Decisions are visible and reviewable |
| **Equal treatment** | All bidders on the same terms |
| **Value for money** | Not merely lowest price |
| Economy and efficiency | Proportionate effort |

**The contract types**, since they follow from procurement:

| Type | Risk borne by |
|---|---|
| **ITEM RATE (unit price)** | **Employer** carries **quantity** risk; contractor carries **rate** risk. **The commonest for civil works** |
| **LUMP SUM** | **Contractor** carries most risk; needs complete drawings |
| **Cost plus** | **Employer** carries almost all risk; for urgent or undefined work |
| Percentage rate | Contractor quotes above/below a schedule |

> **Item rate suits civil engineering because quantities genuinely cannot be known exactly in advance** — earthwork, foundations and rock excavation all depend on ground conditions discovered as the work proceeds.

**And the contractual instruments** that arise afterwards:

| Instrument | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION money** | **Security for DEFECTS** — commonly 5–10%, half released at completion and half after the **12-month defects liability period** |
| **LIQUIDATED DAMAGES** | A **pre-agreed estimate of the employer's loss from DELAY** — not a penalty |
| **Performance bond** | Security against contractor default |
| **VARIATION order** | A **WRITTEN instruction altering the scope** |
| **Contingency** | The employer's provision (**3–5%**) for unforeseen items |

> **Liquidated damages are a genuine PRE-ESTIMATE of loss, not a penalty** — a sum that is punitive rather than compensatory may be unenforceable, which is why the amount must be justifiable by reference to real anticipated loss.

> **And the single most valuable discipline on site is confirming instructions in WRITING**, because the dispute is almost never about whether the work was done, but about whether it was instructed.

examTip.trick: **20 lakhs = Rs 2 million.** The threshold reflects **PROPORTIONALITY** — full open tendering on a tiny contract costs more in administration than it saves.
examTip.trap: **SPLITTING a large work into small packages to stay below a threshold is a procurement OFFENCE** — it defeats the competition the threshold exists to ensure, and it is a common audit finding.
examTip.mnemonic: **ITEM RATE suits civil works because quantities genuinely cannot be known in advance** — earthwork and foundations depend on ground discovered as you go. And **liquidated damages are a pre-estimate of LOSS, not a penalty.**

questions.stem: How will the water table affect the effective stress if it rises above GL?
options: effective stress may increase or decrease
questions.solution:
**No effect** — the effective stress is **independent of the depth of water standing above the soil surface.**

**The proof.** At a point at depth z below the ground surface, with water standing to height h_w **above** ground level:

> **Total stress σ = γ_w h_w + γ_sat z** (the free water above contributes its own weight)
> **Pore pressure u = γ_w (h_w + z)**
>
> **σ′ = σ − u = γ_w h_w + γ_sat z − γ_w h_w − γ_w z = (γ_sat − γ_w) z = γ′ z**

> **The h_w terms CANCEL EXACTLY.** ✓

**The physical reading:**

> **Water above the ground surface presses DOWN on the soil AND pushes UP through the pore water by exactly the same amount.** It adds equally to σ and to u, so it contributes **nothing** to σ′.

> **Which is why a submerged riverbed or lakebed is no stronger for the water above it** — and why **raising a reservoir does not consolidate the soil beneath it.**

**The contrast that matters — water table moving WITHIN the soil:**

| Change | Effect on σ′ |
|---|---|
| **Water table RISES within the soil** (from depth to ground level) | **DECREASES** — γ replaced by γ′, roughly halving it |
| **Water table FALLS below ground level** | **INCREASES** |
| **Free water rises ABOVE ground level** | **NO CHANGE** ← |

> **The middle row is the practically important one: LOWERING the groundwater table INCREASES effective stress throughout and causes SETTLEMENT.**

> **That is the mechanism behind the subsidence of cities that over-pump their aquifers**, and behind the settlement of buildings adjacent to a deep excavation that is being dewatered.

> **Dewatering for construction settles the SURROUNDINGS, not just the site** — a genuine and frequently litigated consequence.

**Why σ′ = σ − u is the most important equation in soil mechanics:**

> **EVERYTHING that matters — strength, stiffness, volume change — is a function of EFFECTIVE stress alone.** Total stress on its own governs nothing.

| Property | Depends on |
|---|---|
| **Shear strength** | **τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′** |
| **Compressibility and settlement** | σ′ |
| **Stiffness** | σ′ |

> **TERZAGHI's principle of effective stress is the foundation of the whole subject**, and this question is a direct test of whether it is understood or merely recited.

**Two consequences of the same principle worth knowing:**

> **1. QUICK CONDITION.** Upward seepage reduces σ′; when it reaches zero the soil has **no shear strength at all** and behaves as a dense liquid. **The critical gradient i_c = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1.0.**

> **"Quick sand" is a CONDITION, not a type of soil** — any cohesionless soil becomes quick under a sufficient upward gradient.

> **2. CAPILLARY rise.** Above the water table the pore pressure is **NEGATIVE**, so **σ′ EXCEEDS σ** — which is the source of the **apparent cohesion** that lets moist sand stand in a vertical cut, and which **vanishes on saturation or complete drying.**

**And the undrained case:** for a saturated clay loaded undrained, **no volume change is possible**, so the added stress goes **entirely into pore pressure** and **σ′ is unchanged** — which is exactly why **φ_u = 0** and the undrained strength is independent of cell pressure.

examTip.trick: Write out **σ′ = σ − u** and watch the free-water terms cancel: water above ground adds **γ_w h_w to BOTH σ and u**, so it contributes nothing to σ′.
examTip.trap: This is a **different question** from the water table rising **WITHIN** the soil, which **decreases** σ′ (γ → γ′). Read where the water table is relative to the ground surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water ABOVE ground: no change. Water table rising WITHIN: σ′ falls. Water table LOWERED: σ′ rises — hence SETTLEMENT.** Dewatering settles the **surroundings**, not just the site.

questions.stem: If a simply supported beam carries a UDL across the entire span, then the shear force:
questions.solution:
**Changes linearly.**

**Why.** The governing relation is:

> **w = −dV/dx**

> **For a UNIFORM load, w is CONSTANT — so dV/dx is constant, and V varies LINEARLY.** That is calculus, not a rule to memorise.

**The shear force distribution:**

> **V(x) = wL/2 − wx**

| Position | Shear force |
|---|---|
| **At the supports** | **± wL/2 — MAXIMUM** |
| **At midspan** | **ZERO** |
| In between | Linear |

> **Shear is MAXIMUM at the SUPPORTS and ZERO at midspan** — which is exactly the reverse of the bending moment, and option (b) states that reverse.

**The complementary picture:**

| Quantity | Maximum at | Value | Shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR FORCE** | **The SUPPORTS** | **wL/2** | **LINEAR** |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **MIDSPAN** | **wL²/8** | **PARABOLIC** |

> **Option (a), "parabolic nature", describes the BENDING MOMENT diagram** — the right shape attached to the wrong quantity, and the most instructive of the distractors.

> **The moment is parabolic because it is the integral of a linear shear**, which is why the two shapes always differ by one order.

**The order relationship, which generalises:**

| Loading | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **Constant** (between loads) | **Linear** |
| **UDL** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** |
| Triangular load | Parabolic | Cubic |

> **Each integration raises the order by one** — load → shear → moment. **Knowing that, the shapes never need memorising.**

**Why option (c) is wrong:**

> **The shear force has a very definite maximum — wL/2 at each support.** It is zero only at midspan.

**The design consequence:**

> Since **shear peaks at the supports and moment at midspan**, the two design actions occur at **different sections**:

| Detailing | Follows from |
|---|---|
| **Stirrups CLOSELY spaced near the supports**, widely at midspan | Shear peaks at supports |
| **Main bars FULLY provided at midspan**, curtailed toward the ends | Moment peaks at midspan |

> **That is the entire logic of beam detailing in one sentence**, and it follows directly from the two diagrams.

**And the relations worth carrying:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Shear is the **SLOPE** of the moment diagram | — |
| **V = 0 marks a moment PEAK** | Here, at midspan ✓ |
| **Change in M = AREA of the SFD** | The fastest hand method |

> **Check: the area of the SFD from support to midspan is ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8** ✓ — exactly the midspan moment.

**A caution about where the maximum sits:** **V = 0 gives a STATIONARY value, not necessarily the greatest in the beam.**

> For a **CANTILEVER** the maximum moment is at the **fixed end**, where V is greatest rather than zero; for a **CONTINUOUS** beam it is often at an **interior support.** **Always check the ends and supports as well.**

examTip.trick: **w = −dV/dx**, so a **constant** load gives a **linear** shear. Each integration raises the order by one: **load → shear → moment** — constant → linear → parabolic.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), "parabolic", describes the BENDING MOMENT diagram**, and option (b) states the moment's location. Both are right facts attached to the wrong quantity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear peaks at the SUPPORTS, moment at MIDSPAN** — which is the whole logic of beam detailing: **stirrups bunched near the supports, main bars fullest at midspan.**

questions.stem: The component of paint that imparts colour to it is called:
questions.solution:
**The pigment.**

> **Pigments are granular SOLIDS incorporated in the paint to contribute COLOUR** — and also opacity, so the surface beneath is hidden.

**The components of paint:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **PIGMENT** | **COLOUR and OPACITY**; also contributes durability and corrosion resistance |
| **VEHICLE (BINDER)** | **The FILM-FORMING component** — binds the pigment and adheres it to the surface |
| **Solvent / thinner** | Adjusts **viscosity** for application; **evaporates** afterwards |
| **Drier** | Accelerates oxidation and hardening |
| **Extender / filler** | Bulk and body; reduces cost |

> The source makes the key point about the vehicle: **it is the ONLY component that MUST be present.** Other components are included optionally, depending on the properties wanted in the cured film.

> **A clear varnish is paint without pigment** — which demonstrates the point directly: the binder alone forms a film, while pigment alone would simply be a powder.

**Why "vehicle" is the tempting wrong answer:**

> **The name suggests it carries something** — and it does: it carries the pigment. **But carrying the colour is not the same as BEING the colour.**

> **The vehicle's job is adhesion and film formation**; the pigment's job is colour and opacity. **Option (c), "both", fails for the same reason** — only one component supplies the colour.

**Common pigments:**

| Pigment | Colour / purpose |
|---|---|
| **Titanium dioxide (TiO₂)** | **White — the commonest, with excellent opacity** |
| White lead | White — **now largely banned as toxic** |
| **Red lead** | **Anti-corrosive PRIMER for steel** |
| **Zinc chromate** | Anti-corrosive |
| Iron oxides | Red, yellow, brown |
| Carbon black | Black |

> **Red lead and zinc chromate are chosen for their CHEMISTRY, not their colour** — they passivate steel and inhibit rust. **A primer's pigment is functional; a finish coat's is decorative.**

**Why paint is applied at all** — the functions in order of importance:

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **PROTECTION** | From moisture, corrosion, weathering, decay — the primary purpose |
| **Decoration** | Appearance |
| **Hygiene** | A washable, non-absorbent surface |
| Light reflection | Interior brightness |
| Identification | Safety colour coding |

> **Protection is why paint exists**, and decoration is a by-product — which is worth remembering, because it explains why surface preparation matters far more than the paint itself.

**The painting system on steel:**

| Coat | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Surface preparation** | **The MOST important step** — remove rust, mill scale, grease |
| **PRIMER** | **Adheres to the metal and INHIBITS corrosion** |
| Undercoat | Builds thickness, provides an even base |
| Finish coat | Appearance and weather resistance |

> **Paint applied over loose rust or mill scale fails whatever its quality**, because the failure plane is beneath the paint rather than within it. **Surface preparation is worth more than a better paint.**

**And the distinction from related materials:** a **VARNISH** is a transparent film (binder without pigment); a **DISTEMPER** uses a water-based binder with chalk; **EMULSION paint** disperses the binder in water; and **ENAMEL** is a paint giving a hard, glossy film.

examTip.trick: **A clear VARNISH is paint without pigment** — which shows directly that the binder forms the film while the pigment supplies the colour. Carrying the colour is not being it.
examTip.trap: **The VEHICLE is the only component that MUST be present** — a genuinely important fact, but it answers a different question. It is the film-former, not the colourant.
examTip.mnemonic: **A primer's pigment is chosen for CHEMISTRY (red lead, zinc chromate inhibit rust), a finish coat's for colour.** And **surface preparation is worth more than a better paint** — paint over loose rust fails whatever its quality.

questions.stem: The bearing capacity depends upon:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — each genuinely affects the bearing capacity.

**How each enters:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SOIL TYPE** | Different soils have **varying strengths and densities** — c and φ are soil properties |
| **TYPE (and SIZE) of foundation** | **Affects the CONTACT AREA and load distribution** — shape factors and the width term |
| **WATER TABLE DEPTH** | **A higher water table increases pore pressure, REDUCING effective stress and bearing capacity** |

> **The source's own explanation lists all three with exactly these reasons**, which is what makes "all of the above" correct rather than a catch-all.

**Where each appears in the Terzaghi expression:**

> **q_u = c N_c s_c d_c i_c + q N_q s_q d_q i_q R_w1 + 0.5 γ B N_γ s_γ d_γ i_γ R_w2**

| Factor | Term |
|---|---|
| **Soil type** | **c and φ** (through N_c, N_q, N_γ) |
| **Foundation shape** | **s factors** — strip **1.0/0.5**, square **1.3/0.4**, circular **1.3/0.3** |
| **Foundation depth** | **q = γD_f** in the surcharge term, and the **d factors** |
| **Foundation width** | **B** in the third term |
| **Water table** | **R_w1 and R_w2** |

**The water table effect is the largest and most often underestimated:**

> **Submergence replaces the bulk unit weight γ with the SUBMERGED unit weight γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**, which is roughly **HALF**.

> **A high water table can therefore HALVE the bearing capacity of a SAND.** That is not a refinement — it is one of the biggest single corrections in foundation design.

> **The effect is much smaller in CLAY**, because for **φ = 0 the term N_γ = 0** and the width term vanishes entirely — so submergence affects only the surcharge term.

**The correction factors:**

| Factor | Applies to | Formula | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R_w1** | The **surcharge term** | **0.5[1 + Z_w1/D]** | **0.5 to 1.0** |
| **R_w2** | The **width term** | **0.5[1 + Z_w2/B]** | **0.5 to 1.0** |

> **R_w1 measures from GROUND LEVEL; R_w2 from the FOUNDATION BASE.** Getting the datum wrong swaps the two corrections.

**The shape factors are worth carrying:**

| Shape | Cohesion term | Width term |
|---|---|---|
| **Strip** | **1.0** | **0.5** |
| **Square** | **1.3** | **0.4** |
| **Circular** | **1.3** | **0.3** |

> **The two move in OPPOSITE directions**: cohesion **up** (the wedge is confined on all sides) and width **down** (the wedge is smaller relative to B). **That opposition is the point most often examined.**

**And two consequences worth knowing:**

> **For pure CLAY (φ = 0): N_γ = 0**, so the **width term vanishes** and **bearing capacity is INDEPENDENT of footing width.** Widening a footing on clay carries more total load but not more pressure.

> **For SAND (c = 0)**: the cohesion term vanishes, and capacity depends on **depth and width alone** — which is why footings on sand benefit from being deeper and wider.

**The final step:**

> **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F** with **F = 2.5 to 3**, applied to the **NET** value — then take the **LESSER** of that and the **settlement-limited** pressure.

> **SETTLEMENT usually governs, not bearing failure** — and it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement (limit about **1 in 300** angular distortion) that damages structures, not uniform settlement.

examTip.trick: Each factor appears explicitly in the Terzaghi expression: **soil type → c and φ; foundation type → shape and depth factors; water table → R_w1 and R_w2.** All three are genuine.
examTip.trap: **A high water table can HALVE a SAND's bearing capacity** (γ → γ′ ≈ γ/2) — one of the largest corrections in foundation design. **In CLAY it barely matters**, since N_γ = 0.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shape factors move OPPOSITE ways: cohesion UP (1.0→1.3), width DOWN (0.5→0.4→0.3).** And **SETTLEMENT usually governs, not bearing failure** — take the lesser of the two pressures.

questions.stem: In the long wall - short wall method, the length of the long wall is the sum of the centre line and:
questions.solution:
**b — the full width of one short wall.**

> The source states it directly: **the length of the long wall is typically the sum of the CENTRELINE length (the distance between the centres of the short walls) and the WIDTH (b) of ONE SHORT WALL at EACH END.**

> Adding **b/2 at each of the two ends** gives **b in total** ✓

**Why the correction is needed:**

> **The centre line length runs between the CENTRES of the short walls.** But the long wall physically extends **beyond those centres, to the outer face of each short wall.**

> **The projection at each end is HALF the short wall's width (b/2)**, and there are **two ends** — hence **2 × b/2 = b.**

> **Then, to avoid double-counting the corners, the SHORT wall is measured to its CENTRE LINE length MINUS b** — so the two corrections cancel and the total volume is correct.

**The two methods of taking out quantities:**

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **LONG WALL – SHORT WALL** | **Long wall measured OUT-TO-OUT; short wall measured IN-TO-IN** |
| **CENTRE LINE method** | **Total centre line length × the section**, with a deduction at each junction |

> **Both give the same answer** — they are alternative bookkeeping for the same volume.

**The CENTRE LINE method's rule:**

> **Deduct half the layer width for EACH JUNCTION** where walls meet:

| Junction type | Deduction |
|---|---|
| **T junction** | **b/2** |
| **Cross junction** | **b** (two × b/2) |

> **The centre line method is faster for a building with many rooms of the same wall thickness**, because one total length serves the whole layer.

> **The long wall–short wall method is clearer where wall thicknesses differ**, because each wall is measured on its own.

**Why the correction matters at all:**

> **The wall THICKENS toward the bottom** — footings are wider than the wall above them, in successive steps.

> **So the correction b changes with each layer**, and the calculation must be repeated for every step of the foundation. **A single blanket correction would be wrong.**

> **That is precisely why the method exists as a formal procedure rather than as arithmetic done by eye.**

**Where this sits in estimating:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / rough cost** | Feasibility; **administrative approval** | ±15–20% |
| Plinth area / cube rate | Approximate | — |
| **DETAILED** | **Item by item from drawings**; **technical sanction** | **±5%** |
| **REVISED** | When the sanctioned amount is exceeded by **more than 5%** | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY** | For **ADDITIONAL work** not originally included | — |

> **REVISED = same work costing more; SUPPLEMENTARY = additional work.** The discriminator is whether the **scope** changed or only the **cost**.

**And the measurement conventions that cause most disputes:**

| Item | Convention |
|---|---|
| **EARTHWORK** | **Mean area or PRISMOIDAL formula** — the two give different answers, and **prismoidal is more accurate** |
| Brickwork, concrete | Cubic metres, with **deduction rules for openings** above a stated size |
| Plastering | Square metres, with specific rules for jambs and soffits |
| Reinforcement | Weight, from the bar bending schedule |

> **An unstated convention is where money is lost** — the deduction rules for openings differ between items and between codes, and they must be agreed before measurement, not after.

examTip.trick: The long wall projects **b/2 beyond the centre at EACH of the two ends** — so the addition is **2 × b/2 = b**. And the short wall is correspondingly measured **minus b**, so the corrections cancel.
examTip.trap: **b/2 is the projection at ONE end**, not the total. The question asks for the whole addition to the centre line length, which covers both ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **The correction CHANGES with each footing step**, because the wall thickens downward — which is exactly why this is a formal procedure and not arithmetic done by eye.

questions.stem: The use of a draft tube in a reaction turbine helps to:
questions.solution:
**Convert the kinetic energy of water leaving the runner into pressure energy.**

> The source states it exactly: **the draft tube converts the KINETIC ENERGY of water leaving the turbine into PRESSURE ENERGY, ensuring efficient operation and preventing energy losses due to turbulence or eddies.**

**How it works:**

> The draft tube is a **gradually DIVERGING conduit** from the runner exit down to the tailrace.

| Step | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Area increases along the tube** | **Velocity DECREASES** (continuity: AV = constant) |
| **Velocity decreases** | **Pressure RISES** (Bernoulli) |
| **Pressure at the runner exit falls BELOW atmospheric** | **SUCTION is created** |

> **That suction is the whole point**: it lets the turbine be set **ABOVE the tailwater without losing the head between them.**

> **Without a draft tube, the head between the runner and the tailwater would simply be LOST** — the water would discharge freely to atmosphere and that potential energy would be wasted.

**The two benefits, stated together:**

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Recovers the EXIT KINETIC ENERGY** | Gradual expansion converts V²/2g into pressure |
| **Recovers the SETTING HEAD** | Suction allows the machine to sit above tailwater |

> **Together these can add several percent to the overall efficiency** — which is substantial for a machine already at 90%.

**The critical design constraint — CAVITATION:**

> **The suction that makes the draft tube valuable is also what makes cavitation possible.**

> **The lowest pressure in the whole machine is at the runner exit and in the upper draft tube** — and if it falls to the **VAPOUR PRESSURE**, vapour bubbles form, are carried to higher pressure, and **collapse implosively, pitting the runner and draft tube.**

> **THOMA's cavitation parameter σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s)/H** governs the turbine's permissible **height above tailwater (H_s)**, and **σ must exceed the critical value for that machine's specific speed.**

> **A high-specific-speed Kaplan may have to be set BELOW the tailwater** — in an excavated pit — to obtain sufficient σ. **Cavitation is therefore a CIVIL WORKS cost, not merely a mechanical one.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a real effect:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent air entering** | The draft tube must run **FULL of water**, and air admission is sometimes **deliberately provided** to cushion cavitation collapse — so this is not its purpose |
| **Increase flow rate** | The flow is set by the **guide vanes and the head**, not by the draft tube |
| **Prevent eddies** | **A genuine secondary benefit** — the source mentions it — but it follows from the gradual expansion rather than being the purpose |

> **Option (d) is the meaningful near-miss**: reducing eddies **is** part of what a well-shaped draft tube achieves. **But it is a consequence of the gradual expansion, not the reason for having one.**

**Why the expansion must be GRADUAL:**

> **A decelerating flow SEPARATES readily**, while an accelerating one does not. **The divergence angle is therefore kept small (commonly 5–8°)** to keep the flow attached.

> **Too rapid an expansion causes separation and eddies, destroying the pressure recovery** the tube exists to provide — which is the same principle that makes a **venturimeter's divergent cone gentler than its convergent one.**

**And the contrast with an IMPULSE turbine:**

> **A PELTON has NO draft tube.** Its runner operates at **atmospheric pressure in air**, discharging freely to the tailrace.

> **There is no exit pressure to recover, and no suction to create** — so **the head between a Pelton runner and the tailwater IS lost**, which is why a Pelton is set as close above the tailwater as flooding allows.

> **That single difference — does the pressure drop across the runner? — determines both the draft tube and the cavitation question.**

examTip.trick: The draft tube **diverges**, so velocity falls and pressure rises — recovering the exit kinetic energy **and** creating suction so the turbine can sit **above tailwater without losing that head**.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), preventing eddies, is a genuine secondary benefit** the source mentions — but it is a **consequence** of the gradual expansion, not the purpose. And air is sometimes **deliberately admitted** to cushion cavitation.
examTip.mnemonic: **The suction that makes a draft tube valuable is what makes CAVITATION possible.** Thoma's σ sets the permissible height above tailwater — and a **Pelton has no draft tube at all**, running at atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem: For 1st class bricks, the water absorption should not be more than:
questions.solution:
**15%** by weight, when immersed in cold water for 24 hours — with the typical range being **12–15% of the dry weight.**

**The brick class table, as the source gives it:**

| Class | **Water absorption (max)** | Range | **Crushing strength** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FIRST class** | **15%** | **12–15% of dry weight** | **≥ 10.5 N/mm²** |
| **Second class** | **20%** | 16–20% | **≥ 7 N/mm²** |
| **Third class** | **25%** | 25% | **≥ 3.5 N/mm²** |

> **Strength FALLS and absorption RISES together down the ladder** — because both measure the same underlying quality: **the degree of VITRIFICATION achieved in firing.**

> **A well-fired brick is dense; a dense brick is both strong and impermeable.** The two properties are not independent requirements but two views of the same thing.

**Why absorption matters:**

| Consequence of high absorption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weaker** | Porosity and strength are inversely related |
| **FROST damage** | Absorbed water freezes and expands, spalling the face |
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | More water carried in means more dissolved salts brought to the surface |
| **Poor bond with mortar** | A very absorbent brick sucks the water out of the mortar |
| Damp penetration | — |

> **The mortar point is the practical one on site**: a dry, highly absorbent brick **draws water from the mortar before it can hydrate**, leaving a weak, powdery joint.

> **That is why bricks are SOAKED before laying** — but **only until damp, never saturated.** A dripping brick cannot absorb any water and the mortar has nothing to key into.

**Note the range 12–15%, not merely the maximum:**

> **A first class brick is expected to absorb SOME water** — a completely impermeable brick would be over-fired, distorted and brittle.

> **Over-burnt bricks are hard but misshapen**, and they make poor masonry because they cannot be laid to line and their bond is poor. **The specification therefore brackets the property rather than simply capping it.**

**The other first class requirements:**

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Compressive strength** | **≥ 10.5 N/mm²** — tested with the **frog filled with 1:1 mortar** |
| **SOUND** | A **clear metallic RING** when two are struck together |
| **Scratch** | No impression from a fingernail |
| **Drop test** | Does not break when dropped flat from about **1 m** |
| **Fracture** | Uniform, compact, homogeneous |
| **Efflorescence** | **Nil to slight** |
| Shape and colour | Sharp edges, true right angles, uniform deep red |

> **The RING test is a genuine field test, not folklore**: a well-fired brick is dense and rings; an under-fired one is porous and gives a dull thud. **It costs nothing and anyone on site can do it.**

**And the compressive strength test detail** that makes the number meaningful:

> **The FROG is filled with 1:1 cement mortar and cured before testing.** Without that, the platen would bear only on the **narrow rim** around the frog, the stress would be wildly non-uniform, and the brick would fail early.

> **The procedure removes a specimen-shape artefact so the measured value belongs to the material** — the same principle that governs capping concrete cubes and defining a gauge length for steel.

examTip.trick: **Strength falls and absorption rises together down the ladder — 10.5/7/3.5 against 15/20/25%.** Both measure the same thing: how well the brick was **vitrified** in firing.
examTip.trap: A first class brick is expected to absorb **12–15%, not zero** — a completely impermeable brick would be **over-burnt, distorted and brittle**. The specification brackets the property rather than capping it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Soak bricks until DAMP, never saturated** — a dry brick steals water from the mortar, a dripping one gives it nothing to key into. And the **RING test** is a real field check that costs nothing.

questions.stem: The per capita demand of water is calculated in litres:
questions.solution:
**Per person per day** — the unit is **lpcd (litres per capita per day).**

**Typical values, as the source gives them:**

| Situation | Demand |
|---|---|
| **Rural areas** | **45 lpcd** |
| **Partially plumbed house** | **65 lpcd** |
| **Fully plumbed house** | **112 lpcd** |
| IS 1172 (full flushing systems) | **135 lpcd** |

> **The progression from 45 to 135 lpcd tracks the level of service**, not the level of need — a household with a tap in the yard uses a third of what one with internal plumbing uses.

> **That is worth noting for planning**: improving the service level **increases demand substantially**, and a scheme designed for standposts will be overwhelmed if house connections follow.

**Why the DAY is the natural unit:**

> **Water use follows a daily cycle** — people wake, wash, cook and bathe on a daily rhythm. **A day is the natural period over which consumption is roughly repeatable.**

> **A year is too coarse** to design anything with, and **an hour is too fine and too variable.** The day is where the pattern stabilises.

> **Everything else is derived from the daily figure** by applying peak factors.

**The peak factors, which COMPOUND:**

| Factor | Value |
|---|---|
| **Maximum DAILY demand** | **1.8 × average daily** |
| **Maximum HOURLY demand** | **1.5 × maximum daily** |
| **PEAK HOUR** | **≈ 2.7 × average** |

> **They multiply, not add** — which is why the peak hour is so far above the mean.

**And each component of the system is designed for a different one:**

| Component | Designed for |
|---|---|
| **Source and intake** | **Maximum DAILY** demand |
| **Treatment works** | **Maximum DAILY** demand |
| **Pumping and rising main** | Maximum daily (with a longer pumping day) |
| **DISTRIBUTION mains** | **PEAK HOURLY** demand (≈ 2.7 × average) |
| **Service reservoir** | **Balancing storage** from a mass curve |

> **The service reservoir is what allows the two to differ**: it **fills at night** when supply exceeds demand and **empties during the peak**, so the works upstream can be sized for the **daily** figure rather than the **hourly** one.

> **Without it, the treatment plant and every main would have to be sized for 2.7 × average** — nearly three times the capital cost, standing idle most of the day.

**What total demand comprises:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Domestic** | The lpcd figure |
| **Industrial and commercial** | Site specific |
| **Public / institutional** | Schools, hospitals, parks |
| **FIRE demand** | A short, very high draw — from **Kuichling's or Freeman's formula** |
| **LOSSES and wastage** | **Often 15–30%** — leakage and unaccounted-for water |

> **Losses are frequently the single largest "consumer" in an older system**, and **reducing leakage is usually far cheaper than developing new supply** — a point that applies directly in Nepali towns with ageing networks.

**And the design period** that the demand is projected over:

| Component | Period |
|---|---|
| **Dams and reservoirs** | **50 years** |
| **Distribution mains** | **30+ years** — buried, expensive to replace |
| Treatment works | 15–20 years, built in stages |
| **Pumps** | **10 years** — easily replaced |

> **Components hard to enlarge later get LONGER design periods** — which is why a buried main is sized generously and a pump is not.

examTip.trick: **The DAY is the natural unit** because water use follows a daily rhythm — a year is too coarse to design with, an hour too variable. Everything else is derived by **peak factors**.
examTip.trap: **Peak factors COMPOUND, not add**: 1.8 × 1.5 = **2.7 × average** for the peak hour. And different components are sized for different peaks — source and treatment for **daily**, mains for **hourly**.
examTip.mnemonic: **45 → 65 → 112 lpcd tracks the SERVICE LEVEL, not need** — house connections triple standpost demand. And **losses are often 15–30%**: fixing leaks usually beats developing new supply.

questions.stem: When a canal is taken as an example, what factor causes its water logging?
options: seepage of water from high land
questions.solution:
**Seepage through the canals** — which raises the water table in the adjacent land.

> The source states it exactly: **water logging in a canal can be caused by SEEPAGE THROUGH THE CANALS, which raises the water table in adjacent areas.**

> **The question specifies "when a CANAL is taken as an example"** — so the answer must be the mechanism **belonging to the canal itself**, not a general cause of waterlogging.

**Why the other options are wrong HERE:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Seepage from high land** | A genuine cause of waterlogging, but **not canal-related** |
| **Over and intensive irrigation** | A genuine cause — but it is the **FARMER's practice**, not the canal's |
| **Excessive rain** | A genuine cause — but **natural**, not attributable to the canal |

> **All four are real causes of waterlogging.** The question is which one the **canal** contributes — and that is seepage through its own bed and banks.

**Why canal seepage is so significant:**

> **An unlined canal loses a large fraction of its flow through the bed and banks** — commonly **30–50% of the water diverted** in an older earthen system.

> **That water does not disappear: it enters the ground and RAISES THE WATER TABLE** along the whole length of the canal.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **WATERLOGGING** | Water table rises into the root zone; **roots suffocate** |
| **SALINITY** | Capillary rise brings salts to the surface, where evaporation concentrates them |
| **Loss of command** | Water intended for the tail reach never arrives |
| Structural damage | Saturated embankments and foundations |

> **Waterlogging and salinity are the same problem seen at two stages** — and both originate in the rising water table.

**The sequence:**

| Step | Effect |
|---|---|
| **1** | Canal seepage raises the water table |
| **2** | Water table reaches the root zone → **WATERLOGGING** — roots suffocate for want of air |
| **3** | **CAPILLARY RISE** brings water to the surface, carrying dissolved salts |
| **4** | **EVAPORATION** removes the water and **CONCENTRATES the salts** → **SALINITY** |

> **The land is lost to salt, not to water** — and by then the damage is far harder to reverse than the waterlogging that caused it.

**Which makes CANAL LINING doubly valuable:**

| Benefit of lining | Note |
|---|---|
| **Saves water** | More command area from the same headworks |
| **PREVENTS WATERLOGGING** | The seepage that causes it is stopped at source |
| **Higher permissible velocity** | So a smaller section carries the same flow |
| **No weed growth** | Lower maintenance, better hydraulic performance |
| Lower roughness | **S ∝ n², so halving n lets the same discharge run on a third of the slope** |

> **Lining pays twice: the water saved AND the land saved.** That is why it is so often the cheapest single improvement available in an irrigation system — cheaper than developing new water, and cheaper than reclaiming salinised land afterwards.

**The remedies once waterlogging has occurred:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage** | **Lowers the WATER TABLE** — the only measure that addresses the cause |
| **Canal lining** | Stops further seepage |
| Reducing the full supply level | Less head driving the seepage |
| Vertical drainage (tubewells) | Pumping lowers the table and supplies irrigation water |

> **Surface drainage removes ponded water and does NOTHING to the water table** — so it cannot cure waterlogging. **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems and require SUBSURFACE drainage.**

> **And LEACHING WITHOUT DRAINAGE is worse than futile**: applying extra water to wash out salts **raises the water table further** and accelerates the salinisation it was meant to cure.

> **For a SODIC soil, apply GYPSUM FIRST, then leach** — leaching alone strips the calcium that holds the clay structure together and can make the soil permanently impermeable.

examTip.trap: **All four options are genuine causes of waterlogging** — but the question says **"when a CANAL is taken as an example"**, so the answer must be the mechanism belonging to the canal itself.
examTip.trick: An unlined canal can lose **30–50% of its flow** through bed and banks — and that water raises the water table along its whole length. **Lining pays twice: water saved AND land saved.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging and salinity are the same problem at two stages** — the table rises, capillary action lifts salts, evaporation concentrates them. **The land is lost to SALT, not to water.**

questions.stem: Provisions for live loads are made in which of the following IS codes?
questions.solution:
**IS 875 Part 2** — Imposed (live) loads.

> **"Live load" and "imposed load" are the same thing**, which the source notes explicitly — the codes use "imposed", everyday practice says "live".

**The IS 875 series (1987):**

| Part | Subject |
|---|---|
| **IS 875 Part 1** | **DEAD loads** — unit weights of building materials |
| **IS 875 Part 2** | **IMPOSED (LIVE) loads** ← |
| **IS 875 Part 3** | **WIND loads** |
| **IS 875 Part 4** | **SNOW loads** |
| **IS 875 Part 5** | **Special loads and load COMBINATIONS** |

> **The order runs 1 dead, 2 live, 3 wind, 4 snow, 5 combinations** — and it is worth learning as a sequence rather than as five separate facts.

**And IS 1893 is the separate seismic code:**

> **IS 1893 — Criteria for Earthquake Resistant Design of Structures.** It is **not part of the 875 series at all**, which is why option (c) is the odd one out on category.

> **The Nepali equivalent is NBC 105: Seismic Design of Buildings in Nepal (2020).**

**Typical imposed loads (IS 875 Part 2):**

| Occupancy | Load |
|---|---|
| **Residential** | **2 kN/m²** |
| **Office (general)** | **2.5 – 4 kN/m²** |
| **CLASSROOM** | **3 kN/m²** |
| **Assembly, with fixed seating** | 4 kN/m² |
| **Assembly, without fixed seating** | **5 kN/m²** |
| Storage | 5 – 10 kN/m² |
| **Roof (accessible)** | 1.5 kN/m² |
| Roof (inaccessible) | 0.75 kN/m² |

**The DEAD versus LIVE distinction:**

| | **DEAD** | **LIVE (imposed)** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Permanent and FIXED in position** | **Variable in magnitude or position** |
| Examples | Self weight, finishes, **permanent partitions**, fixed services | **PEOPLE**, movable furniture, stored goods |
| **Can be patterned?** | **NO — acts everywhere always** | **YES — positioned adversely** |
| Factor when adverse | **1.5** | 1.5 |
| **Factor when STABILISING** | **0.9** | Taken as **zero** |

> **PEOPLE are never a dead load** — that is the unambiguous case, whatever view is taken of fixed furniture.

**PATTERN LOADING is why live loads are treated differently:**

> Because live load can be **placed adversely**, a continuous beam must be checked under several arrangements:

| For maximum | Load pattern |
|---|---|
| **Span moment** | **ALTERNATE spans** loaded |
| **Support moment** | **Both spans ADJACENT** to that support loaded |

> **Analysing only the all-spans-loaded case UNDERESTIMATES both maxima** — a real error, and one that dead load never causes, since dead load cannot be patterned.

**The 0.9 dead load case** deserves emphasis because it is most often forgotten:

> Where dead load **RESISTS** — against **overturning, sliding or uplift** — it is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, because **relying on a load that might be smaller than estimated is unsafe.**

> **Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load conceals overturning and uplift failures entirely.** Cantilever canopies, light roofs under wind uplift, retaining walls and empty basements are all governed by this combination.

**And SEISMIC WEIGHT** is a related distinction: earthquake force is an **INERTIA** force, proportional to **MASS**.

> **Seismic weight = full DEAD load + 25–50% of the IMPOSED load** — only part of the live load is counted, because only part is likely to be present and it may not move rigidly with the structure.

> **Roof live load is usually excluded entirely.**
