examTip.trick: Learn the series as a sequence: **875 Part 1 dead, 2 LIVE, 3 wind, 4 snow, 5 combinations.** And **"live" and "imposed" are the same thing** — codes say imposed, practice says live.
examTip.trap: **IS 1893 is the SEISMIC code and not part of the 875 series at all** — the odd one out on category. Its Nepali equivalent is **NBC 105**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Live load can be PATTERNED, dead load cannot** — hence alternate spans for maximum span moment, adjacent spans for maximum support moment. And **0.9 DL when dead load STABILISES**, never 1.5.

questions.stem: The minimum depth of foundation, according to Rankine's formula, will be (given q = 180 kN/m², γ = 20 kN/m³ and φ = 30°):
questions.solution:
**1 metre.**

**Working.**

> **D_f = (q/γ) × [(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]²**
>
> **= (180/20) × [(1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°)]²**
> **= 9 × [(1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5)]²**
> **= 9 × (0.5/1.5)²**
> **= 9 × (1/3)²**
> **= 9 × 1/9 = 1.0 m** ✓

> **The arithmetic is deliberately clean**: sin 30° = 0.5 makes the bracket exactly **1/3**, its square exactly **1/9**, and 180/20 exactly **9** — so the nines cancel. **That cleanliness is a strong signal you have taken the intended route.**

**Recognising the bracket:**

> **(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = K_a**, the **RANKINE ACTIVE earth pressure coefficient** — which is why the formula carries Rankine's name.

> So the formula is really **D_f = (q/γ) K_a².**

> **For φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3 and K_p = 3** — a **ninefold** ratio, and values worth carrying since 30° is the commonest examination value.

**What the formula represents:**

> **The minimum depth at which the soil beneath the footing is NOT pushed out laterally** by the bearing pressure. Below that depth the surrounding soil provides enough confinement to resist the outward thrust.

> **It is a MINIMUM, not a design depth** — the actual founding depth is the **GREATEST** of several requirements.

**The other requirements that may govern:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Below the ZONE OF SEASONAL MOISTURE CHANGE** | Typically **1.5 m**, and much deeper in **expansive black cotton soil** |
| **Below the SCOUR depth** near a watercourse | **Lacey: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} × a location factor** (2.0 at a pier nose) |
| **Onto a stratum of adequate bearing capacity** | Usually the controlling requirement |
| Below frost depth | In cold regions |
| Below adjacent excavations and services | — |
| **Minimum practical depth** | **0.5 m** in any case |

> **Near a watercourse, SCOUR usually governs far more than bearing capacity does** — a pier founded above the scour level will be undermined in a flood however adequate its bearing pressure. **Scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.**

> **In expansive soil the seasonal moisture zone governs**, because a footing within it rises and falls with the swelling clay regardless of the soil's strength.

**Why depth increases bearing capacity anyway:**

> In **q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ**, the **surcharge term q = γD_f** grows directly with depth — so **deeper founding gives more confinement and therefore more capacity.**

> **That is a second, independent reason for founding deeper**, quite apart from the lateral-squeeze criterion this formula expresses.

**And the final design step:**

> **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F** with **F = 2.5 to 3**, applied to the **NET** value — then take the **LESSER** of that and the **settlement-limited** pressure.

> **SETTLEMENT usually governs, not bearing failure** — and it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement (limit about **1 in 300** angular distortion) that damages structures, not uniform settlement.

examTip.trick: **Recognise the bracket as K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ).** For φ = 30° it is exactly **1/3**, so K_a² = 1/9 — and 180/20 = 9 cancels it to give **1.0 m** with no calculator.
examTip.trap: This is a **MINIMUM, not a design depth** — the actual depth is the **greatest** of several requirements. Near a river, **SCOUR usually governs** far more than this criterion does.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ = 30° → K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3** — a ninefold ratio, the commonest examination value. And in **expansive soil the seasonal moisture zone governs** the depth, whatever the strength.

questions.stem: The recession limb of a hydrograph is independent of:
questions.solution:
**Storm characteristics.**

> The source states it directly: **the recession limb represents the DECREASE in streamflow AFTER a peak flow event. It is primarily influenced by BASIN characteristics — size, shape and drainage patterns. STORM characteristics such as rainfall intensity and duration mainly affect the RISING limb (peak flow).**

**The three parts of a hydrograph:**

| Part | Governed by |
|---|---|
| **RISING limb (concentration curve)** | **STORM characteristics** — intensity, duration, movement — **and** basin characteristics |
| **CREST (peak)** | Both |
| **RECESSION limb (falling limb)** | **BASIN characteristics ALONE** |

> **The rising limb reflects the storm; the recession limb reflects the basin.**

**Why the recession is independent of the storm:**

> **By the time the recession begins, the rain has STOPPED.** What remains is **water draining out of storage** — from the channel, from the soil, and from groundwater.

> **That drainage is governed entirely by the basin's own physical properties** — its geology, its soils, its slopes, its drainage network. **The storm that filled the storage no longer influences how it empties.**

> **A large storm and a small storm on the same basin produce recession limbs of the SAME SHAPE**, differing only in starting magnitude — which is exactly what "independent of storm characteristics" means.

**The recession equation:**

> **Q_t = Q₀ K_r^t**

> where **K_r** is the **recession constant — a property of the basin**, not of the storm.

> **Because K_r is a basin constant, the recession curve for a given catchment is REPRODUCIBLE**, and a **MASTER DEPLETION CURVE** can be constructed from several events and used for all of them.

> **That reproducibility is the practical value of the fact**: it allows base flow separation and low-flow forecasting on a catchment where the storms are never the same twice.

**The three recession components**, each with its own constant:

| Component | Drains from | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| **Channel storage** | The river channel itself | **Fastest** |
| **Interflow** | Shallow subsurface | Intermediate |
| **BASE FLOW (groundwater)** | The aquifer | **SLOWEST — sustains the river between storms** |

> **The base flow recession is what determines DRY SEASON flow** — and therefore what determines a run-of-river hydropower plant's **FIRM POWER.**

> **A basin with good groundwater storage sustains its flow through the dry months; one without it runs nearly dry** — which is why two catchments of the same area and rainfall can have very different firm power.

**The rising limb, for contrast:**

| Storm characteristic | Effect on the rising limb |
|---|---|
| **Higher intensity** | **Steeper rise, higher peak** |
| **Longer duration** | Broader hydrograph |
| **Storm moving DOWNSTREAM** | **Higher, sharper peak** — the runoff arrives together |
| Storm moving upstream | Lower, flatter peak |

> **The storm's DIRECTION of movement matters as well as its intensity**, which is a genuinely non-obvious effect and a good illustration of why the rising limb depends on the storm.

**And the connection to the unit hydrograph:**

> **Base flow must be SEPARATED before a unit hydrograph can be derived** — and the recession curve is what makes that separation possible, since the point at which the recession resumes its master curve marks the end of direct runoff.

> **TIME OF CONCENTRATION** governs the rising limb's duration: the design storm duration is taken **equal to t_c**, because that is when **the whole catchment contributes simultaneously** and the peak is greatest.

examTip.trick: **By the time the recession begins, the rain has STOPPED** — what remains is storage draining out, governed by the **basin's own properties**. The storm that filled the storage no longer affects how it empties.
examTip.trap: **The RISING limb reflects the STORM; the RECESSION limb reflects the BASIN.** The two halves of the hydrograph answer to different things, which is exactly what the question tests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q_t = Q₀K_r^t, with K_r a BASIN constant** — so the recession is reproducible and a **master depletion curve** can be built. And **base flow recession determines DRY SEASON flow, hence firm power.**

questions.stem: Given the carpet area of a floor is 100 m² and the circulation area is 50% of the plinth area, and the rate per sq. m of plinth area is Rs 40,000, what is the total estimate of the building?
questions.solution:
**Rs 80 lakhs.**

**Working.**

> Let **x** be the plinth area.
>
> **Circulation area = 50% of PLINTH area = 0.5x**
> **Plinth area = carpet area + circulation area**
> **x = 100 + 0.5x**
> **0.5x = 100**
> **x = 200 m²** (plinth area)
>
> **Estimated cost = plinth area × rate = 200 × 40 000 = Rs 8 000 000 = 80 lakhs** ✓

> **The self-referencing step is the whole difficulty**: the circulation area is defined as a percentage of the **PLINTH** area, which is itself the unknown — so x appears on both sides.

> **Reading it as 50% of the CARPET area would give plinth = 150 m² and a cost of 60 lakhs — which is option (d)**, and precisely the trap.

**The area definitions:**

| Area | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PLINTH area** | **The built-up area measured at floor level, to the OUTER face of the external walls** |
| **CARPET area** | The **usable floor area** — the area you could actually lay carpet on |
| **CIRCULATION area** | **Corridors, staircases, lobbies, verandahs** |
| Wall area | The area occupied by the walls themselves |

> **Plinth area = carpet area + circulation area + wall area**, though this question uses the simplified two-part relation.

> **The three are nested**: carpet ⊂ carpet + circulation ⊂ plinth. **Confusing which one a rate applies to is a common and expensive error.**

**Typical ratios:**

| Ratio | Value |
|---|---|
| **Carpet area** | **50 – 60% of plinth area** |
| Circulation area | 10 – 25% |
| Wall area | 10 – 15% |

> **Here the carpet area is 100/200 = 50% of the plinth** — at the lower end of the normal range, consistent with a building having generous circulation.

**The PLINTH AREA method of estimating:**

> **Cost = plinth area × plinth area rate**

> It is an **APPROXIMATE method**, used at the **preliminary stage** to obtain **administrative approval** before detailed drawings exist.

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH AREA / cube rate** | **Preliminary; administrative approval** | **±15–20%** |
| **DETAILED** | **Item by item from drawings; technical sanction** | **±5%** |
| **REVISED** | When the sanctioned amount is exceeded by **>5%** | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY** | For **ADDITIONAL work** not originally included | — |

> **The plinth area rate must come from a recently completed building of SIMILAR TYPE, SPECIFICATION and LOCALITY** — otherwise the method is worthless.

> **A rate from a different building type or a different market is not merely inaccurate; it is misleading**, because the method carries no internal check.

**And the distinction most often examined:**

> **REVISED estimate = the SAME work costing more. SUPPLEMENTARY estimate = ADDITIONAL work.**

> **The discriminator is whether the SCOPE changed or only the COST.**

**The analysis of rates**, for the detailed stage: materials + labour + plant + **overheads (~15%)** + **contractor's profit (~10%)**, with **contingencies of 3–5%** added to the **total estimate** — the last belonging to the **employer**, not the contractor.

examTip.trap: **Circulation is 50% of the PLINTH area, not the carpet area** — so x appears on both sides: x = 100 + 0.5x, giving **x = 200 m²**. Reading it as 50% of carpet gives 150 m² and **60 lakhs — option (d)**.
examTip.trick: **Sanity check the ratio**: carpet/plinth comes out at 100/200 = **50%**, at the low end of the normal 50–60% range. An answer implying 67% or 33% would signal a misread.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plinth area rate is a PRELIMINARY method (±15–20%)** for administrative approval — and the rate must come from a **similar building type, specification and locality**, or it is misleading rather than merely rough.

questions.stem: Given that the unsupported length of a column with both ends fixed is L, what will be the unsupported length of an equivalent column with one end fixed and the other end free?
questions.solution:
**L/4.**

**Working.** "Equivalent" means the two columns carry the **same critical load.**

> **P_cr = π²EI/(k L)²**, with **k = 0.5** for fixed–fixed and **k = 2** for fixed–free.

**Column 1 — both ends fixed, length L₁:**

> **P_cr1 = π²EI/(0.5 L₁)² = 4π²EI/L₁²**

**Column 2 — one end fixed, one free, length L₂:**

> **P_cr2 = π²EI/(2 L₂)² = π²EI/(4 L₂²)**

**Setting them equal:**

> **4π²EI/L₁² = π²EI/(4L₂²)**
> **4/L₁² = 1/(4L₂²)**
> **16 L₂² = L₁²**
> **L₂ = L₁/4** ✓

**The shortcut worth seeing:**

> **Equal capacity requires equal EFFECTIVE length.** So:
>
> **0.5 L₁ = 2 L₂**, giving **L₂ = L₁/4** ✓ — in one line.

> **That is the whole problem**: the effective lengths must match, and 0.5 versus 2 is a factor of four.

**The effective length table:**

| End conditions | **L_e** | Relative capacity |
|---|---|---|
| **Both FIXED** | **0.5 L** | **4 ×** |
| One fixed, one pinned | 0.707 L | 2 × |
| **Both PINNED** | **1.0 L** | **1 ×** |
| **One fixed, one FREE** | **2.0 L** | **1/4 ×** |

> **The full range spans a factor of SIXTEEN in buckling capacity** — from 4× down to ¼×.

> **And this question is exactly that factor of sixteen expressed as a length**: to match a fixed–fixed column, a cantilever column must be **four times shorter**, because **capacity goes as 1/L_e².**

**The practical meaning:**

> **A cantilever column of length L carries only a SIXTEENTH of what the same column fixed at both ends would carry.**

> **Which is why the free-end condition is the one to fear:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Column unbraced during construction** | The floor that would restrain it is not yet built |
| **Temporary props and shores** | Often free at the top |
| Scaffold standard with a missing tie | **The tie IS the restraint** |
| Cantilever pier or pole | Free by design |

> **Construction-stage stability failures very often come down to exactly this** — a column perfectly adequate in the finished structure, temporarily free at the top.

**Codes are more conservative than the theory:**

> **IS 456 and IS 800 give HIGHER effective lengths than the theoretical values** — **0.65 L rather than 0.5 L** for fixed–fixed, and **2.0 L or more** for a cantilever — because **a real "fixed" end always rotates a little.**

> **Never use the theoretical value in design.** Assuming a fixity the detail does not deliver is unconservative in the one direction where the penalty is a sudden collapse.

**And where Euler stops working:**

| Slenderness | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **λ < 12** (concrete) | **SHORT — fails by CRUSHING** |
| **Intermediate** | **INELASTIC buckling — Euler OVERESTIMATES** |
| **λ > ~100** (steel) | Euler's elastic formula applies |

> **RANKINE's formula — 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler — bridges both ends**, and is safer generally because **Euler alone is unsafe for intermediate slenderness**, which is where most real columns sit.

> **And r is always taken about the MINIMUM axis** — a column buckles the **weak** way.

examTip.trick: **Equal capacity means equal EFFECTIVE length**: set **0.5L₁ = 2L₂**, giving **L₂ = L₁/4** in one line. No need to write out P_cr at all.
examTip.trap: The factor is **4 in LENGTH but 16 in CAPACITY**, because P_cr ∝ 1/L_e². Confusing which factor the question asks for gives L/2 or L/8 — both offered.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cantilever column carries a SIXTEENTH of the same column fixed at both ends.** Which is why the free top is the condition to fear — and why **construction-stage failures so often come down to it.**

questions.stem: In the case of a simply supported I-section beam carrying a concentrated load at the mid span, what will be the length of the plastic hinge formed?
questions.solution:
**L/5** — as the closest available option.

**Working.** The length of the plastic hinge is:

> **L_p = L(1 − 1/S)**, where **S** is the **SHAPE FACTOR**.
>
> For an I-section, **S ≈ 1.2**:
> **L_p = L(1 − 1/1.2) = L(1 − 0.833) = 0.167 L = L/6**

> **L/6 is not among the options, and L/5 is the nearest** — which is what the source keys and explains: **"L(1 − 1/1.2) = L/6, so L/5 is the best one."**

> **Recognising that the exact answer is L/6 and selecting the closest offered value is the intended step** — a reminder that examination options are not always exact.

**Where the formula comes from:**

> The plastic hinge extends over the region where the moment exceeds the **YIELD moment M_y** — that is, where the section has begun to yield but is not yet fully plastic.

> For a **central point load**, the bending moment varies **linearly** from zero at the supports to **M_p** at midspan.

> **The moment reaches M_y at a distance where M/M_p = M_y/M_p = 1/S**, and by similar triangles the yielded length is **L(1 − 1/S)** ✓

> **The LINEAR moment variation is what makes the geometry so simple** — for a UDL the moment is parabolic and the hinge length works out differently.

**Why the shape factor controls it:**

| Shape factor | Hinge length **L(1 − 1/S)** |
|---|---|
| **I-section (1.12 – 1.15)** | **≈ L/8 to L/7** |
| **I-section (S = 1.2)** | **L/6** |
| **Rectangle (1.5)** | **L/3** |
| **Circle (1.7)** | 0.41 L |
| **Diamond (2.0)** | **L/2** |

> **A LOW shape factor gives a SHORT plastic hinge**, because there is little reserve between first yield and full plasticity — the section passes through the partly-plastic state over only a short length.

> **An I-section has the lowest shape factor of the common sections (≈1.12–1.15)** precisely because **almost all its material is already at the extreme fibres**, working hard in the elastic range. **There is little extra to be gained by going plastic.**

> **A DIAMOND has S = 2.0** because most of its material sits near the neutral axis doing nothing elastically — so plasticity mobilises a great deal of reserve, and the hinge is correspondingly long.

**Why the hinge length matters:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **ROTATION CAPACITY** | The plastic rotation is **concentrated in this length** |
| **Local buckling risk** | A **short** hinge means **high curvature** over a short length |
| Detailing | In concrete, confinement reinforcement is provided over the hinge length |

> **A short hinge concentrates the demand**, which is one reason **local buckling of the flange and web is checked so carefully in plastic design.**

**The validity condition for plastic analysis:**

> **Plastic analysis requires DUCTILITY** — the section must be able to **rotate at M_p without buckling locally.**

> **That is why IS 800 classifies sections as PLASTIC, compact, semi-compact and slender by their b/t ratios**, and why **plastic design requires a PLASTIC section.** A slender section buckles locally before the hinge can form, and the analysis becomes invalid.

> **It also explains why plastic methods apply to structural STEEL and not to concrete, cast iron or any brittle material.**

**The related plastic quantities:**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Plastic hinge** | A section fully yielded, **rotating at constant M_p** |
| **Number of hinges for collapse** | **D_s + 1** |
| **Shape factor S** | **M_p/M_y** |
| **Plastic modulus Z_p** | **S × Z_elastic** |
| **Load factor** | Collapse load ÷ working load = **S × factor of safety** |

examTip.trick: **L_p = L(1 − 1/S)**, and for an I-section with S = 1.2 that gives exactly **L/6**. Since L/6 is not offered, **L/5 is the nearest** — recognising that is the intended step.
examTip.trap: **A LOW shape factor gives a SHORT hinge.** An I-section has the lowest S (≈1.12–1.2) because its material is already at the extreme fibres — little reserve, so a short partly-plastic zone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangle 1.5 → L/3; DIAMOND 2.0 → L/2; I-section 1.2 → L/6.** And a **short hinge concentrates the rotation**, which is why local buckling is checked so carefully in plastic design.

questions.stem: If the EST = 5, LST = 7, and duration = 1, then what is TF?
questions.solution:
**Total float = 2.**

**Working.**

> **TF = LST − EST = 7 − 5 = 2** ✓

> **The duration is NOT needed** — and that is the point of including it. **It is a distractor within the data**, offered so that a candidate who half-remembers the formula might subtract it.

**Why duration does not appear:**

> **Total float can be computed two equivalent ways:**

> **TF = LST − EST** or **TF = LFT − EFT**

> Since **EFT = EST + D** and **LFT = LST + D**, the duration **appears in both terms and cancels**:

> **LFT − EFT = (LST + D) − (EST + D) = LST − EST** ✓

> **Both routes give 2**, and the duration drops out of each.

> **Check by the second route**: EFT = 5 + 1 = 6, LFT = 7 + 1 = 8, so TF = 8 − 6 = **2** ✓

**The four activity times:**

| Time | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **EST** — earliest start | Earliest the activity **can** start |
| **EFT** — earliest finish | **EST + D** |
| **LST** — latest start | Latest it can start **without delaying the project** |
| **LFT** — latest finish | **LST + D** |

**How they are computed:**

| Pass | Direction | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD** | First to last event | **Take the MAXIMUM** — an activity cannot start until **all** predecessors finish |
| **BACKWARD** | Last to first event | **Take the MINIMUM** — it must not delay the **earliest** successor |

> **Forward takes the maximum, backward the minimum** — and each has a clear reason, so it need not be memorised.

**The floats:**

| Float | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **LST − EST** — delay possible **without affecting PROJECT completion** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the NEXT activity** |
| **Independent float** | Without affecting **either** neighbour |
| Interfering float | **Total − free** |

> **Independent ≤ free ≤ total**, each condition stricter than the last.

> **FREE float ≤ TOTAL float always** — a useful check on any computation.

**The identifying property of the critical path:**

> **A CRITICAL activity has ZERO TOTAL FLOAT** — which is precisely how the critical path is found.

> **Here TF = 2, so this activity is NOT critical** — it has two units of slack, and could be delayed by two without affecting the project.

**Where float is used:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESOURCE SMOOTHING** | Non-critical activities are **shifted within their float** to even the resource histogram — **without changing the completion date** |
| Prioritising attention | Manage the critical path first |
| Assessing a delay | A delay within float costs nothing |
| **Contractual claims** | Whether a delay is **excusable and compensable** |

> **"Who owns the float" is a genuine contractual question**: if a contractor consumes it and the employer then causes a delay, the employer's delay becomes critical and compensable.

> **Total float is SHARED along a chain of activities; free float belongs to one activity alone** — which is exactly why the distinction matters commercially and not merely arithmetically.

examTip.trick: **TF = LST − EST = 7 − 5 = 2.** The **duration is not needed** — it cancels, since EFT = EST + D and LFT = LST + D. Check by the other route: 8 − 6 = 2 ✓.
examTip.trap: **The duration is a distractor WITHIN the data**, included so a half-remembered formula might subtract it. Recognising which given values are irrelevant is part of the question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM, backward the MINIMUM** — each for a clear reason. And a **CRITICAL activity has ZERO total float**, so TF = 2 means this one is not critical.

questions.stem: What is the specific gravity of a block if its weight in air is 60 N and the weight is 40 N when immersed in water?
questions.solution:
**3.**

**Working.**

> **Specific gravity = weight in air ÷ (weight in air − weight in water)**
>
> **= 60/(60 − 40) = 60/20 = 3** ✓

**Where the formula comes from — ARCHIMEDES' principle:**

> **The apparent loss of weight in water EQUALS the buoyant force, which equals the weight of the water displaced.**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Weight in air** | **60 N** = weight of the block |
| **Apparent loss** | **60 − 40 = 20 N** = **weight of an equal volume of water** |

> **Specific gravity is by definition the ratio of a body's weight to the weight of an equal volume of water:**
>
> **SG = 60/20 = 3** ✓

> **Knowing the derivation means the formula never has to be memorised** — it is Archimedes stated as a ratio.

**Checking the answer for sense:**

| Material | Specific gravity |
|---|---|
| **Cork** | ~0.25 |
| Water | **1.0** |
| **Concrete** | **2.4** |
| **Stone / rock** | **2.6 – 3.0** |
| Aluminium | 2.7 |
| **Steel** | **7.8** |
| **Mercury** | **13.6** |

> **SG = 3 is a dense rock or a heavy aggregate** — entirely plausible.

> **Options (c) and (d), being LESS THAN 1, would mean the block FLOATS** — but a floating block cannot have a positive apparent weight when "immersed", so they are physically inconsistent with the question. **Both can be discarded on sight.**

**Archimedes' principle and flotation:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **SG > 1** | **SINKS** — buoyancy less than weight |
| **SG = 1** | Neutrally buoyant |
| **SG < 1** | **FLOATS**, displacing its own weight of water |

> **A floating body displaces its OWN WEIGHT of fluid; a submerged body displaces its own VOLUME.** That distinction is the source of most errors in buoyancy problems.

**The stability of a floating body** — the related topic:

> **Stability depends on the METACENTRIC HEIGHT GM**, not merely on the centre of gravity:

| Condition | State |
|---|---|
| **M above G (GM positive)** | **STABLE** |
| M at G | Neutral |
| **M below G (GM negative)** | **UNSTABLE — it capsizes** |

> **GM = I/V − BG**, where I is the second moment of the waterplane area and V the displaced volume.

> **A body can float with its centre of gravity ABOVE its centre of buoyancy and still be stable**, provided the metacentre is higher still — which is why a ship is stable despite its high superstructure, and why the **waterplane's WIDTH (through I) matters so much.**

> **A wide, shallow vessel has a large I and is very stable; a narrow deep one is not** — the same reason a catamaran is hard to capsize.

**And the practical measurement:** this experiment — **weighing in air and in water** — is exactly how the **specific gravity of aggregate** is determined in the laboratory (IS 2386 Part 3), and the same principle gives the **water absorption** from the difference between saturated-surface-dry and oven-dry weights.

examTip.trick: **The apparent LOSS of weight equals the weight of water displaced** — so SG = weight in air ÷ loss = **60/20 = 3**. It is Archimedes stated as a ratio, not a formula to memorise.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) are BELOW 1, meaning the block would FLOAT** — inconsistent with having a positive weight when immersed. Both can be discarded on sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **A FLOATING body displaces its own WEIGHT; a SUBMERGED body displaces its own VOLUME.** And stability needs **M above G (GM positive)** — which is why waterplane width matters so much.

questions.stem: Which ministry passes the DRM strategy?
questions.solution:
**The Ministry of Home Affairs.**

> **Disaster Risk Management (DRM) in Nepal falls under the Ministry of Home Affairs**, which is the lead agency for disaster preparedness, response and coordination.

**Why Home Affairs rather than a dedicated ministry:**

> **Disaster response requires the coordination of MANY agencies at once** — police, armed police, army, local government, health services, and the district administration.

> **Home Affairs already commands the security forces and the district administration structure** (Chief District Officers), which is exactly the machinery a disaster response needs.

> **Option (c) names a "Ministry of Disaster Risk Management", which does not exist** — a plausible-sounding but fictitious body, and the trap in this question.

**The institutional structure under the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act 2074 (2017):**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management AUTHORITY (NDRRMA)** | The **executive agency**, under the Ministry of Home Affairs |
| **National Council** | Chaired by the **Prime Minister** — policy level |
| **Executive Committee** | Chaired by the **Home Minister** |
| Province and District committees | Regional coordination |
| Local level committees | Chaired by the mayor / chairperson |

> **The Act of 2074 marked a shift from RESPONSE to RISK REDUCTION** — from managing disasters after they occur to reducing the risk beforehand. **That shift is the substantive point worth knowing.**

**The DRM cycle:**

| Phase | Activities |
|---|---|
| **PREVENTION / MITIGATION** | Building codes, land use planning, structural measures |
| **PREPAREDNESS** | Early warning, drills, stockpiles, contingency plans |
| **RESPONSE** | Search and rescue, relief, emergency medical care |
| **RECOVERY / REHABILITATION** | Reconstruction — **"BUILD BACK BETTER"** |

> **The engineering contribution is concentrated in the FIRST phase**, and it is by far the most cost-effective.

> **Every rupee spent on prevention saves several spent on response** — which is the central argument of disaster risk reduction, and the reason building code enforcement matters more than relief capacity.

**Where engineering enters directly:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Building code enforcement** | **NBC 105** (seismic), **NBC 109 and 202** (masonry) |
| **Land use planning** | Keeping development off hazardous ground |
| **Retrofitting** | Existing vulnerable buildings, especially schools and hospitals |
| Structural mitigation | Embankments, slope stabilisation, check dams |
| **Lifeline protection** | Water, power, roads, hospitals must survive |

**The terminology that underlies all of it:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HAZARD** | The **potentially damaging EVENT** |
| **EXPOSURE** | **What lies in its path** |
| **VULNERABILITY** | **How badly the exposed elements would be affected** |
| **RISK** | **Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability** |

> **Engineering cannot reduce the HAZARD — an earthquake will happen regardless.** What engineering reduces is **VULNERABILITY**, by making structures able to withstand it; **planning reduces EXPOSURE**, by keeping development off hazardous ground.

> **That is the whole logic of disaster risk reduction**, and it explains why building codes and land use planning are complementary rather than alternative measures.

**Nepal's hazard profile**: **earthquake** (the whole country is seismically active), **LANDSLIDE** (the most frequent by number of events), **flood**, **GLOF** (glacial lake outburst flood), fire, drought and epidemic.

examTip.trap: **Option (c) names a "Ministry of Disaster Risk Management" that does not exist** — a plausible-sounding but fictitious body. Check whether an offered institution is real before choosing it.
examTip.trick: **Home Affairs already commands the security forces and the district administration (CDOs)** — exactly the machinery a multi-agency disaster response needs. That is why DRM sits there.
examTip.mnemonic: **RISK = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability.** Engineering cannot reduce the hazard — it reduces **VULNERABILITY**; planning reduces **EXPOSURE**. Prevention is worth several rupees of response.

questions.stem: Who appoints the chairman of the NEC?
questions.solution:
**The Government of Nepal.**

> The source gives the provision: **an engineer NOMINATED BY THE GOVERNMENT from amongst the engineers who have at least FIFTEEN YEARS' experience in the engineering profession after having obtained a Bachelor's Degree in a subject of engineering — Chairman.**

**The Council's composition (21 members) under the NEC Act 2055:**

| Position | Number | How appointed | Qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** | Bachelor's + **15 YEARS** |
| **Vice-Chairman** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| Members | 7 | Nominated by GoN — **one per province, at least three women** | Bachelor's + 7 years |
| **President of the NEA** | 1 | **EX OFFICIO** | — |
| Members | 5 | **ELECTED from the NEA** | — |
| Campus chief of an engineering campus | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| Representative, Institute of Engineering (TU) | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| Representative of universities teaching engineering | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Members** | **2** | **NOMINATED BY THE COUNCIL ITSELF** | Bachelor's + 7 years |
| **Member Secretary (Registrar)** | 1 | — | Bachelor's + **10 years** |

**The four appointment routes** — the discriminator in every question of this kind:

| Route | Who |
|---|---|
| **Nominated by the GOVERNMENT** | **Chairman**, VP, 7 provincial members, 3 academic representatives |
| **ELECTED from the NEA** | **5 members** |
| **EX OFFICIO** | The NEA President |
| **Nominated by the COUNCIL itself** | **2 members** |

> **The chairman is a government nomination**, not an election and not a judicial or presidential appointment.

**The four numbers most often asked:**

> **Chairman 15 years, Vice-Chairman 10 years, Registrar 10 years — and TWO members nominated by the Council itself.**

**The Council block worth learning as a unit:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total members** | **21** |
| **Members nominated by the Council** | **2** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **Minimum for institutional affiliation** | **70%** |
| **Reconstitution after dissolution** | **3 months** |
| **First Registrar** | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |
| **Code of conduct articles** | **8**, raised to **11** in 2079 |

> **These recall questions are the cheapest marks on the paper** for anyone who has read the Council's material once — and several appear in every sitting.

**The Council's functions:**

| Function |
|---|
| **Register engineers** and maintain the register |
| **Recognise (accredit)** engineering institutions and programmes |
| **Prescribe minimum standards** for engineering education and student admission |
| Prepare and implement **policy** for the profession |
| **Regulate professional conduct**; take disciplinary action |
| **Issue the license to practise** |

**And what it does NOT do:**

| Not a function | Who instead |
|---|---|
| **Open or run colleges** | Universities; Ministry of Education |
| Award degrees | Universities |
| Fix fees or salaries | The market |
| **Represent** engineers' interests | The **NEA** |

> **The standing distinction: the COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.** NEC registration is a **legal requirement** to practise and to sign engineering drawings; NEA membership is **voluntary**.

> **Practising or signing drawings without registration is an offence under the Act** — and **signing drawings one did not prepare or supervise is a disciplinary offence**, among the commonest real breaches of the code.

examTip.trick: Learn the **four appointment routes**: nominated by **GoN** (chairman, VP, provincial and academic members), **ELECTED from the NEA** (5), **EX OFFICIO** (NEA President), and nominated by the **Council itself** (2).
examTip.trap: The **President of Nepal and the Supreme Court have no role** in the Council's constitution — plausible-sounding state institutions offered where a government nomination applies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chairman 15 years, VP 10, Registrar 10; 2 nominated by the Council, 5 elected from the NEA.** Act **2055**, Regulations **2057**, **70%** for affiliation, **3 months** to reconstitute.

questions.stem: If the diameter of a rebar is D = 20 mm, for a U-bend, what is the value of anchorage length?
questions.solution:
**320 mm.**

**Working.**

> **For a U-bend, anchorage length = 16 D**
> **= 16 × 20 = 320 mm** ✓

**The anchorage values for standard hooks and bends (IS 456):**

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **U-bend (180° hook)** | **16 D** |
| **90° bend** | **8 D** |
| **45° bend** | 4 D |
| Each 45° of bend beyond | 4 D, up to a maximum of 16 D |

> **The progression is 4D per 45° of turn**, up to the 16D maximum at a full 180° U-bend — which makes the whole table one rule rather than four facts.

> **Option (b), 160 mm, is 8D — the 90° bend value**, and it is the natural wrong answer for anyone who remembers "8D" without remembering which bend it belongs to.

**What anchorage is FOR:**

> **A bar can only carry the force the calculation assumes if it is ANCHORED well enough to develop that force.**

> **Development length: L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd)** — the straight length needed to transfer the bar's full force into the concrete by bond.

> **A hook or bend provides an EQUIVALENT anchorage in a much shorter physical space**, which is why they exist: at a support there is simply not enough room for a full straight development length.

**Why the hook works:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bearing of the bend against the concrete inside it** | The bar cannot pull straight through a curve |
| **Additional bond along the bent length** | — |
| Mechanical interlock | — |

> **The bend's resistance comes mainly from BEARING, not bond** — which is why the concrete inside the bend must be sound and why **minimum bend radii** are specified. **Too tight a bend crushes the concrete inside it and splits the cover.**

**Minimum bend diameters (IS 2502):**

| Bar type | Minimum internal bend diameter |
|---|---|
| **Mild steel** | **2 D** for hooks |
| **Deformed (HYSD)** | **4 D** for bends, larger for hooks |

> **HYSD bars need larger bend radii** because they are stronger and less ductile — bending them too tightly can **crack the bar itself.**

**Where anchorage matters most:**

| Location | Note |
|---|---|
| **At simple supports** | Bars must be anchored **beyond the face** — a common detailing failure |
| **Curtailment points** | A bar must extend a development length beyond where it is no longer needed |
| **Laps** | **Lap length** for tension is typically L_d or greater |
| **Column–beam joints** | Especially critical in seismic design |

> **A bar that cannot develop its stress is not carrying the force the calculation assumed** — which is one of the commonest detailing failures in reinforced concrete, and it is invisible once the concrete is poured.

**The seismic dimension:**

> In seismic detailing, **anchorage into the joint must develop the bar's full YIELD strength**, because the design relies on the bar yielding rather than pulling out.

> **A pull-out failure is brittle and sudden; a yielding bar is ductile and gives warning.** The whole capacity-design philosophy depends on the anchorage being stronger than the bar.

**And the related seismic hook rule** worth carrying: **ties must have 135° HOOKS with adequate extension**, because a **90° hook OPENS OUT the moment the cover spalls** — which is exactly when the tie is needed.

examTip.trick: **4D per 45° of turn, to a maximum of 16D** — so a 90° bend gives **8D** and a 180° U-bend gives **16D**. One rule generates the whole table.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), 160 mm, is 8D — the 90° BEND value.** Remembering "8D" without remembering which bend it belongs to is exactly the error being tested.
examTip.mnemonic: **A bend anchors mainly by BEARING, not bond** — which is why **minimum bend radii** matter: too tight a bend crushes the concrete inside and splits the cover. HYSD bars need larger radii still.

questions.stem: The area of a triangular section is 66.72 m² and the wetted perimeter of the section is 24.03 m. Calculate the value of Manning's rugosity, if the bed slope of the channel is 1:500 and the discharge through the channel is 117.6 cusec.
questions.solution:
**n = 0.05.**

**Working.** Rearranging Manning's equation for n:

> **Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**, so **n = (1/Q) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **R = A/P = 66.72/24.03 = 2.777 m**
>
> **n = (1/117.6) × 66.72 × (66.72/24.03)^{2/3} × (1/500)^{1/2}**
> **= (1/117.6) × 66.72 × (2.777)^{2/3} × 0.04472**
> **= (1/117.6) × 66.72 × 1.9834 × 0.04472**
> **= 0.05** ✓

> **Compute R first** — it appears inside a fractional power, and getting it right early prevents compounding an error through the rest.

**A note on the units:**

> The discharge is given as **117.6 "cusec"**, but the source's working uses **117.6 directly with SI area and slope** — so it is being treated as **m³/s** in the calculation. **Following the source's own arithmetic gives the keyed answer.**

> **This is worth flagging because Manning's equation is UNIT-SENSITIVE**: it is **empirical and dimensionally inhomogeneous**, the **1/n carrying hidden units**. **The SI form applies only in SI**; in foot-pound units the coefficient becomes **1.486/n.**

> **Mixing units in Manning's equation is a real and easy error**, and the reason to be careful whenever a problem quotes cusecs.

**What the answer means:**

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth concrete** | **0.012** |
| Ordinary concrete lining | 0.014 |
| Brickwork | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean** | **0.022** |
| Earth, weedy or winding | **0.030** |
| **Natural stream, clean** | **0.030** |
| **Stony, irregular stream** | **0.040 – 0.070** |

> **n = 0.05 describes a rough natural channel** — stony, irregular, perhaps with vegetation. **A triangular section with that roughness is consistent with a natural gully or an unmaintained drain**, which is a useful sanity check on the answer.

**Why n matters so much:**

> **S ∝ n² at constant V and R** — so **doubling the roughness QUADRUPLES the slope required** for the same velocity.

> **The whole practical range is only about 0.012 to 0.07 — a factor of six.** But since the effect is quadratic, **that becomes a factor of 36 in slope**, which is why estimating n well matters enormously in natural channel work.

> **And it is why canal LINING pays so handsomely**: halving n from 0.025 to 0.014 lets the same discharge run on about **a third of the slope**, or the same slope carry far more.

**Estimating n in practice:**

> **It is the least certain input in open channel hydraulics.** It is judged from **photographs of gauged channels**, from **Cowan's method** (a base value adjusted for irregularity, obstruction, vegetation and meandering), or **back-calculated from a measured flood.**

> **A back-calculated n from a gauged event is by far the most reliable**, which is why gauging stations are so valuable.

**The most efficient section**, for context:

| Shape | Most efficient proportions | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **b = 2y** | **y/2** |
| **Trapezoidal** | **Half-hexagon**, side slope 1:√3 | **y/2** |
| **TRIANGULAR** | **Side slopes at 45°** (a right angle at the invert) | **y/(2√2)** |
| **Any shape** | **SEMICIRCLE** | **y/2** |

> **A triangular section is hydraulically poor** compared with a trapezoid of the same area, because its wetted perimeter is longer for the area enclosed — which is one reason trapezoidal drains are preferred.

examTip.trick: Rearrange first: **n = (1/Q) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**, and **compute R = A/P = 2.777 m before anything else** — it sits inside a fractional power, so an early error compounds.
examTip.trap: **Manning's equation is UNIT-SENSITIVE** — the 1/n carries hidden units and the SI form applies only in SI (1.486/n in foot-pound). A problem quoting **cusecs** is exactly where mixing units bites.
examTip.mnemonic: **n = 0.05 is a rough natural channel** — stony and irregular. And **S ∝ n²**, so the modest 0.012–0.07 range becomes a **36-fold** range in required slope. That is the case for lining.

questions.stem: Calculate the second moment of area of a hollow circular section with external and internal diameter 20 cm and 10 cm respectively.
questions.solution:
**7,363 cm⁴.**

**Working.**

> **I = (π/64)(D⁴ − d⁴)**
>
> **= (π/64)(20⁴ − 10⁴)**
> **= (π/64)(160 000 − 10 000)**
> **= (π/64)(150 000)**
> **= 0.049087 × 150 000**
> **= 7 363.1 cm⁴** ✓

> **Note the fourth powers: 20⁴ = 160 000, not 20² × 2.** The dominance of D⁴ is what makes the outer diameter so much more important than the inner.

**The revealing arithmetic:**

> **The hole is HALF the outer diameter, yet it removes only 10 000 of 160 000 — that is, 1/16 of the second moment.**

> Meanwhile it removes **1/4 of the AREA** (since area goes as D²).

> **A quarter of the material removed for a sixteenth of the stiffness lost** — which is the entire argument for hollow sections, visible directly in these numbers.

**Why that works:**

> **Material near the neutral axis contributes almost nothing to bending resistance**, because its stress **σ = My/I** is nearly zero. **Removing it costs little strength and saves a great deal of weight.**

> **The same logic produces the I-section**, which places material in **flanges far from the neutral axis** and keeps only a thin **web** to carry the shear.

**Option (b), 3,681 cm⁴, is exactly HALF the answer** — the value obtained from **π/32** instead of **π/64**, which is the **POLAR** moment constant. **Confusing I and J is the trap.**

**The circle's properties:**

| Quantity | In terms of D | In terms of R |
|---|---|---|
| **I (second moment)** | **πD⁴/64** | **πR⁴/4** |
| **J (polar)** | **πD⁴/32** | **πR⁴/2** |
| **Section modulus Z** | **πD³/32** | πR³/4 |

> **J = 2I** in every form — the **perpendicular axis theorem (J = I_xx + I_yy)** applied to a shape whose two principal second moments are equal.

> **Which value to use where: I for BENDING (σ = My/I), J for TORSION (τ = Tr/J), and the MINIMUM I for BUCKLING.**

**A quick check on the answer:**

> The solid 20 cm circle alone gives **π(20)⁴/64 = 7 854 cm⁴.** Subtracting the small 10 cm core (491 cm⁴) leaves **7 363** ✓

> **The hollow section retains 94% of the solid one's second moment** while weighing 25% less — a very favourable exchange, and worth stating because it makes the result memorable.

**And for a COLUMN the advantage is greater still:**

> Buckling depends on the **radius of gyration r = √(I/A)**. **A tube has a large r for its area in EVERY direction**, so it has no weak axis.

> Here: **A = π(20² − 10²)/4 = 235.6 cm²**, so **r = √(7363/235.6) = 5.59 cm** — against **5.0 cm** for a solid circle of the same outer diameter.

> **A solid bar of the same AREA (D = 17.3 cm) would have r = 4.33 cm** — substantially worse. **That is why a tube is the natural shape for a strut.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) is exactly HALF the answer** — the result of using **π/32 (the POLAR constant)** instead of **π/64**. Confusing **I** and **J** is the trap, and **J = 2I** for a circle.
examTip.trick: Watch the fourth powers: **20⁴ = 160 000**. The hole is **half** the diameter yet removes only **1/16 of I** while removing **1/4 of the AREA** — the whole argument for hollow sections in one calculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **I for BENDING, J for TORSION, MINIMUM I for BUCKLING.** And a tube has a large **radius of gyration in every direction** — no weak axis, which is why it is the natural strut.

questions.stem: The sequent depths in a hydraulic jump occurring in a horizontal rectangular channel are 0.25 m and 1.25 m. The energy lost in this jump is:
questions.solution:
**0.8 m.**

**Working.**

> **ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**
>
> **= (1.25 − 0.25)³/(4 × 0.25 × 1.25)**
> **= (1.0)³/(1.25)**
> **= 1/1.25**
> **= 0.8 m** ✓

> **The arithmetic is deliberately clean** — the depth difference is exactly 1.0 m, so the cube is 1.0 and only the denominator needs computing.

**Checking the physics of the answer:**

> **The energy loss (0.8 m) is more than THREE TIMES the initial depth (0.25 m)** — an enormous dissipation.

> That is entirely consistent with the depth ratio: **y₂/y₁ = 1.25/0.25 = 5**, which from the sequent depth relation corresponds to:

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1] = 5**
> **11 = √(1 + 8Fr₁²)**, so **Fr₁² = 15**, **Fr₁ = 3.87**

| Fr₁ | Jump type | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 – 1.7 | Undular | < 5% |
| 1.7 – 2.5 | Weak | 5 – 15% |
| **2.5 – 4.5** | **OSCILLATING — AVOID** | **15 – 45%** |
| 4.5 – 9.0 | **STEADY — best for a stilling basin** | 45 – 70% |
| > 9.0 | Strong | 70 – 85% |

> **Fr₁ = 3.87 puts this jump in the OSCILLATING range** — effective at dissipating energy, but **the unstable jet oscillates between bed and surface and throws WAVES far downstream**, eroding banks and damaging structures.

> **A stilling basin designed to operate in this range performs badly however well it is built** — which is why the range is avoided, and why **baffle blocks** are used to force stabilisation where the Froude number cannot be raised out of it.

**Why the jump is analysed by MOMENTUM, not energy:**

> **The energy loss is large and UNKNOWN in advance** — it is what we are trying to find, so it cannot also be an input.

> **But the EXTERNAL FORCES are small**: the jump is short, so bed friction over its length is negligible. **That makes the momentum balance exact.**

> **Specific force M = Aȳ + Q²/(gA) is the SAME on both sides**, and equating it gives the conjugate depth relation.

> **Applying Bernoulli across a hydraulic jump is therefore a serious error** — and the distinction between **CONJUGATE depths (same specific FORCE, across a jump)** and **ALTERNATE depths (same specific ENERGY, smooth transition)** exists precisely to prevent it.

**The jump relations, as a set:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Sequent (conjugate) depths** | **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]** |
| **ENERGY LOSS** | **ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)** |
| **Length** | **≈ 5 to 7 × y₂** (commonly 6y₂) — **empirical** |
| Height | y₂ − y₁ |

> **The length is purely empirical** — no theory predicts it, which is why it is quoted as a range.

**And the design risk that governs a stilling basin:**

| Tailwater | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Too LOW** | **The jump SWEEPS OUT downstream** — high-velocity flow escapes onto erodible bed and **undermines the apron** |
| Correct | Forms within the basin |
| **Too HIGH** | **DROWNED** — poor dissipation; the fast jet dives along the bed |

> **Sweep-out is what destroys spillway aprons**, and it typically occurs **not at the design flood but at an INTERMEDIATE discharge**, where the tailwater rating curve and the required conjugate depth diverge most.

> **The basin must therefore be checked across the FULL RANGE of operating discharges**, not merely at the maximum.

examTip.trick: **ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂)** — and here the difference is exactly **1.0 m**, so the cube is 1 and only the denominator (4 × 0.25 × 1.25 = 1.25) needs computing.
examTip.trap: **Check the Froude number the depths imply**: y₂/y₁ = 5 gives **Fr₁ = 3.87 — the OSCILLATING range**, which throws waves far downstream. A basin designed there performs badly however well built.
examTip.mnemonic: **A jump is a MOMENTUM problem, not an energy one** — its loss is large and unknown, but its forces are small. And the **TAILWATER must actually supply y₂**, or the jump **sweeps out** and undermines the apron.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not among the common types of mat foundation?
questions.solution:
**"Double flat plate thickened"** — which is not a recognised type of mat foundation.

> The source states it directly: **mat foundations can include various types such as flat plate type, box structures, and mats on piles. However, "double flat plate thickened" is NOT commonly recognised as a distinct type of mat foundation.**

**The recognised types of mat (raft) foundation:**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **FLAT PLATE** | A **uniform thickness slab** over the whole area — the simplest |
| **Flat plate THICKENED under columns** | Extra depth locally, where **punching shear** is critical |
| **BEAM AND SLAB (waffle)** | Slab **stiffened by beams** in two directions — efficient for large column spacing |
| **BOX STRUCTURE (cellular)** | **Basement walls and slabs act together as a rigid box** — very stiff |
| **MATS ON PILES** | The raft is **supported on piles** — for very poor soil or high water table |

> **Note that "flat plate THICKENED under columns" is a genuine type**, which is what makes option (d) a well-constructed distractor: it borrows the real words and rearranges them into something that does not exist.

**The BOX (cellular) raft** deserves emphasis because it is the stiffest:

> **The basement walls, base slab and ground floor slab act together as a hollow box**, giving **enormous rigidity** for its weight.

> **That rigidity is what makes it valuable**: it **distributes column loads uniformly** and **virtually eliminates differential settlement**, because the whole structure moves as one.

> **It also provides usable basement space and, being hollow, reduces the net load on the soil** — which connects directly to the **floating (compensated) foundation** idea.

**When a raft is used at all:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **Footings would cover MORE THAN ABOUT HALF the plan area** | The classic criterion |
| **Low soil bearing capacity** | Spreading the load over the whole area |
| **DIFFERENTIAL settlement must be controlled** | The raft ties columns together |
| Basement required | The raft doubles as the basement floor |
| Highly variable soil | Bridges over soft pockets |

**The raft's essential virtue:**

> **A raft does not necessarily reduce TOTAL settlement — it makes settlement UNIFORM.**

> **By tying all the columns together, it converts DIFFERENTIAL settlement into uniform settlement** — and it is **differential** settlement that damages buildings, not uniform.

> **A building that settles 100 mm uniformly is undamaged; one that settles 25 mm at one column and 50 mm at the next may crack severely.** The limit is about **1 in 300 angular distortion.**

**The two design approaches:**

| Method | Assumption |
|---|---|
| **RIGID (conventional)** | The raft is **infinitely stiff**; soil pressure varies **LINEARLY** |
| **FLEXIBLE (Winkler)** | The soil is a **bed of independent SPRINGS** with modulus **k** |

> **The Winkler model's weakness is that the springs are INDEPENDENT** — it cannot represent the fact that loading one point also depresses the soil around it.

> **For a thick raft on soft soil the RIGID method remains safer**, precisely because it does not depend on **k** — a parameter that is measured on a small plate and must be **size-corrected** (× 0.3/B for clay), with a tenfold error if that correction is skipped.

**And the FLOATING (compensated) raft**, the most elegant case:

> **If the structure's weight equals the weight of soil excavated, the soil experiences NO NET STRESS CHANGE — and therefore theoretically ZERO settlement.**

> **It is Archimedes applied to soil**, and it is the solution where deep soft clay offers nothing firm to found on. **Its risks are base heave during excavation, settlement of the surroundings from dewatering, and UPLIFT of the empty basement** — for which the resisting dead load is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, never up.

examTip.trap: **"Flat plate THICKENED under columns" IS a real type** — option (d) borrows those words and rearranges them into something that does not exist. Recognising the genuine type is what exposes the fake.
examTip.trick: Read the **NOT**. Three options are recognised raft types; only the fourth is a plausible-sounding invention.
examTip.mnemonic: **A raft does not reduce TOTAL settlement — it makes it UNIFORM**, converting the differential settlement that damages buildings into the uniform kind that does not. Limit: **1 in 300 angular distortion.**

questions.stem: Le-Chatelier's device is used for determining the:
questions.solution:
**Soundness** — by measuring the **expansion** of cement specimens.

> The source states both halves of the pair: **Le-Chatelier's device determines the SOUNDNESS of cement by measuring the expansion of cement specimens. VICAT's plunger determines the CONSISTENCY test of cement.**

**The apparatus for each cement test** — this is a straight four-way match:

| Test | Apparatus |
|---|---|
| **Consistency and SETTING TIME** | **VICAT** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **LE CHATELIER** (or the autoclave) |
| **Fineness** | **Blaine air permeability**, or the 90 μm sieve |
| **Compressive strength** | **Compression testing machine** on 70.6 mm mortar cubes |
| Tensile strength | Briquette test (rarely used now) |

> **VICAT and LE CHATELIER are the pair that gets swapped**, and both appear as options here. **Vicat for setting; Le Chatelier for soundness.**

**What UNSOUNDNESS is, and why it is the most dangerous defect:**

> Unsoundness is caused by **excess FREE LIME (CaO) or MAGNESIA (MgO)** in the cement — compounds that **hydrate very slowly and EXPAND as they do.**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Timing** | **The expansion appears MONTHS after construction** |
| **Effect** | **Cracks concrete that was perfectly sound when placed** |
| **Remedy** | **NONE — by then nothing can be done** |

> **That delay is what makes unsoundness uniquely dangerous.** Every other cement defect shows itself during construction, when it can still be corrected; **unsoundness is invisible until the structure is finished and occupied.**

> **Which is precisely why the test exists** — it is an accelerated check for a slow-acting fault.

**The limits:**

| Test | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Le Chatelier** | **≤ 10 mm** expansion |
| **Autoclave** | **≤ 0.8%** |

> **The Le Chatelier test detects free LIME; the AUTOCLAVE test detects both lime and MAGNESIA**, because magnesia hydrates so slowly that only high-pressure steam accelerates it enough to show up.

> **That is why both tests exist** — they are not alternatives but complements, catching different causes of the same defect.

**How the Le Chatelier test works:**

> A **split brass mould with two indicator arms** is filled with cement paste of standard consistency and immersed in water. **The distance between the arm tips is measured, the specimen is boiled, and the distance is measured again.**

> **The increase in separation, magnified by the long arms, is the expansion.**

> **Boiling accelerates the hydration of free lime**, compressing months of slow reaction into a few hours — which is what makes an accelerated test possible at all.

**The other cement requirements:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Initial setting time** | **NOT LESS THAN 30 minutes** |
| **Final setting time** | **NOT MORE THAN 600 minutes** |
| **Fineness (Blaine)** | **≥ 225 m²/kg** |
| **Compressive strength (OPC 33)** | **16 / 22 / 33 MPa at 3 / 7 / 28 days** |
| Specific gravity | 3.15 |

> **The two setting limits run in OPPOSITE directions** — a **minimum** on the initial set (time to place) and a **maximum** on the final set (time to proceed). That asymmetry is the most-tested point in the topic.

**And the compound that controls setting:**

> **C₃A hydrates almost instantly and would cause a FLASH SET.** **Gypsum (2–3%) is interground with the clinker purely to retard it** — that is the entire reason gypsum is in cement.

> **C₃S gives EARLY strength (to 7 days), C₂S the LATER strength (beyond 28 days)** — and **low heat cement reduces C₃A and C₃S while raising C₂S**, which is why it is slower in every respect and used for mass concrete.

examTip.trap: **VICAT and LE CHATELIER are the pair that gets swapped**, and both are represented here. **Vicat = consistency and SETTING; Le Chatelier = SOUNDNESS.**
examTip.trick: **Unsoundness appears MONTHS after construction** — free lime hydrating slowly and expanding. Boiling the specimen compresses that into hours, which is what makes an accelerated test possible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Le Chatelier detects free LIME; the AUTOCLAVE detects lime AND MAGNESIA** — magnesia hydrates so slowly that only high-pressure steam reveals it. The two tests are complements, not alternatives.

questions.stem: A power generating station has a plant capacity of 200 MW and maximum power demand is 150 MW. If the average power generation is 110 MW, then find the load factor and capacity factor respectively.
questions.solution:
**0.73 and 0.55.**

**Working.**

> **LOAD FACTOR = average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND = 110/150 = 0.73** ✓
> **CAPACITY FACTOR = average load ÷ PLANT CAPACITY = 110/200 = 0.55** ✓

> **Option (a) is the same two numbers in the REVERSE order** — which is exactly the trap. **Read the order in which the question asks for them.**

**The discriminator is the DENOMINATOR:**

| Factor | Definition | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD FACTOR** | Average load ÷ **MAXIMUM DEMAND** | **150 MW** |
| **CAPACITY (plant load) FACTOR** | Average load ÷ **INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **200 MW** |

> **Both share the same numerator (average load).** Only the denominator distinguishes them — and since **installed capacity ≥ maximum demand always**, the **capacity factor is ALWAYS ≤ the load factor.**

> **That inequality is a free check on the answer**: 0.55 < 0.73 ✓. **Option (a), giving load factor 0.55 and capacity factor 0.73, violates it and is impossible.**

**What each tells you:**

| Factor | Measures |
|---|---|
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **How STEADY the DEMAND is** — how close the peak is to the average |
| **CAPACITY FACTOR** | **How fully the PLANT is used** |

> **Load factor is about the CONSUMERS; capacity factor is about the PLANT.** That is the clearest way to keep them apart.

**The reserve margin**, which this question implicitly illustrates:

> **Capacity 200 MW against a maximum demand of 150 MW** leaves a **50 MW (33%) reserve** — capacity held for maintenance outages, unexpected failures and demand growth.

> **That reserve is why the capacity factor can never equal the load factor** in a properly planned system, and why a capacity factor near 1 would actually be alarming rather than efficient.

**Typical values:**

| System | Load factor | Capacity factor |
|---|---|---|
| **Domestic supply** | **Low (~20–30%)** | — |
| **Continuous-process industry** | **High (~70–90%)** | — |
| **Base load thermal** | — | **60 – 80%** |
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | — | **~40 – 60%** |
| **Peaking plant** | — | **10 – 20%** |

> **A low capacity factor is not necessarily bad** — a **peaking plant is MEANT to run rarely**, and its value lies in being **available** at the daily peak, not in the energy it produces.

> **Judging a peaking or standby plant by its capacity factor misunderstands its purpose entirely.**

**Why load factor matters commercially:**

> **A high load factor allows cheaper generation** — plant runs continuously at its efficient point instead of cycling, and capacity is not built merely to stand idle.

> **A low load factor requires expensive peaking capacity used for a few hours a day**, and someone must pay for that idle plant.

> **That is why industrial tariffs REWARD a high load factor**, and why **time-of-day tariffs** exist — they are attempts to make the consumer's incentive match the system's cost.

**The rest of the family:**

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Demand factor** | Maximum demand ÷ **connected load** |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Σ individual maxima ÷ system maximum — ALWAYS > 1** |
| **Coincidence factor** | Its **reciprocal — always ≤ 1** |
| Plant use factor | Energy ÷ (capacity × hours **in service**) |

> **Diversity is what makes electricity supply economically possible** — peaks do not coincide, so the whole network can be built smaller than the sum of its consumers' demands.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the same two numbers REVERSED.** Read the order the question asks for — load factor first, capacity factor second.
examTip.trick: **Capacity factor ≤ load factor ALWAYS**, since installed capacity ≥ maximum demand. That inequality is a free check: 0.55 < 0.73 ✓, while option (a) violates it and is impossible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load factor is about the CONSUMERS (how steady the demand); capacity factor is about the PLANT (how fully used).** Same numerator, different denominator — and a low capacity factor is fine for a **peaking** plant.

questions.stem: Bearing stress is 180 kN/m², unit weight = 20 kN/m³, internal angle of friction = 30 degrees. According to Rankine's theory, what is the minimum depth of foundation?
questions.solution:
**1 metre** — the same calculation as Q61, with the same data.

**Working.**

> **D_f = (q/γ) × [(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]²**
> **= (180/20) × [(1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°)]²**
> **= 9 × (0.5/1.5)² = 9 × (1/3)² = 9 × 1/9 = 1.0 m** ✓

> **Note that this paper asks the same question twice** — as Q61 and again here — with identical data and only the wording changed. **The answer is naturally the same.**

> **That repetition is worth noticing in the examination itself**: recognising a question already answered saves the whole working, and it is a reminder to read each question rather than assume it is new.

**The bracket is K_a:**

> **(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = K_a**, the **RANKINE ACTIVE earth pressure coefficient** — which is why the formula bears Rankine's name.

> **For φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3 and K_p = 3** — a **ninefold** ratio, and the commonest values in examination questions.

> **The arithmetic is clean precisely because sin 30° = 0.5**, which is why 30° is chosen so often.

**What the formula gives, and what it does not:**

> **It is the minimum depth at which the soil beneath the footing is not squeezed out laterally** by the bearing pressure.

> **It is a MINIMUM criterion, not a design depth.** The actual founding depth is the **GREATEST** of:

| Requirement | Typical governing case |
|---|---|
| **Rankine minimum** | This calculation |
| **Below the seasonal moisture zone** | **1.5 m**, deeper in **expansive clay** |
| **Below SCOUR depth** | **Near any watercourse — usually the governing one** |
| **Onto adequate bearing stratum** | The usual practical control |
| Below frost depth, adjacent excavations, services | — |
| **Minimum practical** | **0.5 m** |

> **Near a river, SCOUR governs far more often than this criterion does** — and **scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.**

> **Lacey: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a location factor — **2.0 at a bridge pier nose, 2.75 at a severe bend.**

**Why depth helps bearing capacity independently:**

> In **q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ**, the surcharge term **q = γD_f** grows directly with depth — so deeper founding gives **more confinement and more capacity**, quite apart from the lateral-squeeze criterion.

**And the design sequence that follows:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Compute **q_u** with shape, depth, inclination and **water table (R_w)** factors |
| **2** | **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F**, with **F = 2.5 to 3**, on the **NET** value |
| **3** | Compute the **settlement-limited** pressure |
| **4** | **Take the LESSER of the two** |

> **SETTLEMENT usually governs, not bearing failure** — a soil can safely carry the pressure and still settle more than the structure tolerates.

> **And it is DIFFERENTIAL settlement that damages structures** (limit about **1 in 300** angular distortion), not uniform settlement. **A building that settles 100 mm uniformly is undamaged.**

**One caution on the water table**, since it is the largest single correction: **a high water table can HALVE a sand's bearing capacity**, because γ is replaced by **γ′ ≈ γ/2.** In clay it barely matters, since **N_γ = 0 for φ = 0.**

examTip.trick: **This paper asks the same question twice** — Q61 and Q77, identical data, different wording. Recognising a repeat saves the entire working, and it rewards reading each question rather than assuming it is new.
examTip.trap: It is a **MINIMUM criterion, not a design depth.** The actual depth is the **greatest** of several requirements — and near a watercourse **SCOUR usually governs.**
examTip.mnemonic: **φ = 30° → K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3**, and sin 30° = 0.5 makes the arithmetic clean — which is why 30° appears in so many questions. **9 × 1/9 = 1 m.**

questions.stem: Given a Gumbel's distribution with μ = 0 and β = 1, find the probability that X is less than or equal to 2.
questions.solution:
**0.864** — the closest option to the computed value of **0.873**.

**Working.** The Gumbel cumulative distribution function:

> **F(x) = exp[−exp(−(x − μ)/β)]**
>
> **F(2) = exp[−exp(−(2 − 0)/1)]**
> **= exp[−exp(−2)]**
> **= exp[−0.1353]**
> **= 0.873**

> **The nearest offered value is 0.864**, which the source keys ✓

> **The DOUBLE exponential is the whole structure of the formula** — an exponential inside an exponential, which is why the distribution is also called the **double exponential distribution.**

**Immediate checks that eliminate two options:**

> **A cumulative probability must lie between 0 and 1.** **Option (c), 1.124, exceeds 1 and is impossible** — it can be discarded on sight.

> **And since x = 2 is well above the mode (μ = 0), the probability should be HIGH** — comfortably above 0.5. **Option (b), 0.564, is too close to the median to be right for a value two scale-units above the mode.**

> **Those two checks leave only (a) and (d)**, and the computation settles between them.

**What the Gumbel distribution is FOR:**

> It is the **EXTREME VALUE TYPE I** distribution — the limiting distribution of the **MAXIMUM of a large sample.**

> **That is precisely why it dominates flood frequency analysis**: the annual maximum flood is, by definition, the largest of many daily flows, and Gumbel is the distribution such maxima tend toward.

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLOOD frequency analysis** | The classic use |
| **Maximum rainfall** | Design storms |
| **Extreme WIND speeds** | Basic wind speed maps |
| Maximum temperatures, wave heights | — |

**Reading the result hydrologically:**

> **F(x) = P(X ≤ x)** is the **non-exceedance** probability, so:

> **Exceedance probability = 1 − F = 1 − 0.873 = 0.127**
> **Return period T = 1/(1 − F) = 1/0.127 ≈ 7.9 years**

> **So a value of 2 in these units corresponds to roughly an 8-year event** — a useful way of making the abstract number concrete.

**The frequency-factor form used in practice:**

> **x_T = x̄ + K σ**, where **K** is the **frequency factor** depending on the return period and the sample size.

> **For Gumbel, K = −(√6/π)[0.5772 + ln(ln(T/(T−1)))]** — and the **0.5772 is EULER's constant**, which appears because the Gumbel distribution's mean sits that far above its mode.

**The wider context — hydrologic risk:**

> **Annual exceedance probability = 1/T**, and the risk over an **n-year design life** is:

> **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ**

| Design | 50-year life |
|---|---|
| **T = 100** | **40%** |
| T = 500 | 10% |
| T = 1000 | 5% |

> **A structure designed for the 100-year flood with a 50-year life has a 40% chance of being exceeded at least once** — closer to a coin toss than to a rarity.

> **When n = T the risk is always about 63%**, and to hold the risk at 10% over n years requires **T ≈ 10n.**

> **Which is why a large dam abandons return periods entirely** and is designed for the **PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD** — derived from the Probable Maximum Precipitation, not from statistics, because **no annual probability of failure is acceptable.**

**The other distributions used in flood frequency:** **Log-Pearson Type III** (the US federal standard), **log-normal**, and **GEV (Generalised Extreme Value)**, of which Gumbel is a special case.

examTip.trick: **F(x) = exp[−exp(−(x−μ)/β)]** — a **double exponential**. Work outward: exp(−2) = 0.1353, then exp(−0.1353) = **0.873**, nearest to the offered 0.864.
examTip.trap: **A cumulative probability cannot exceed 1**, so option (c) is impossible on sight. And since x = 2 is well above the mode, the answer must be **well above 0.5** — which rules out (b).
examTip.mnemonic: **Gumbel is the distribution of MAXIMA**, which is why it dominates flood frequency. Here **F = 0.873 → return period ≈ 8 years.** And **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ**: a 100-year design over 50 years carries **40%** risk.

questions.stem: The maximum spacing of contraction joints in unreinforced concrete slabs for a slab thickness of 20 cm is:
questions.solution:
**4.5 m.**

> **In PCC (plain cement concrete), the maximum spacing for a contraction joint is 4.5 m** — and it stays at **4.5 m for every PCC slab thickness.**

**The joint spacing table:**

| Slab type | Thickness (m) | **Expansion joint** | **Contraction joint** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RCC** | 0.25 | 51 m | **17 m** |
| | 0.20 | 45 m | **14 m** |
| | 0.15 | 36 m | **13 m** |
| | 0.10 | 30 m | **7.5 m** |
| **PCC** | **0.20 and above** | **36 m** | **4.5 m** |
| | 0.15 | 27 m | **4.5 m** |
| | 0.10 | 27 m | **4.5 m** |

> **Note the striking difference: RCC allows 13–17 m between contraction joints, PCC only 4.5 m.**

> **The reason is the reinforcement.** In an RCC slab the steel **holds the shrinkage cracks tightly closed and distributes them**, so a long slab can be tolerated with fine, harmless cracks between joints.

> **PCC has nothing to hold a crack closed**, so the joints must be close enough that cracking is confined to them.

> **That is the whole logic of the table**, and it explains why the PCC value does not vary with thickness while the RCC values do.

**Why contraction joints exist at all:**

> **Concrete WILL crack as it shrinks — that is unavoidable.** A contraction joint does not prevent cracking; **it decides WHERE the crack forms.**

> By **sawing a groove to about a QUARTER of the slab depth**, a **plane of weakness** is created, and the crack forms there — **straight, sealed and maintainable** — instead of wandering randomly across the slab.

> **The timing of the saw cut is critical**: too early and the concrete ravels at the cut; too late and the slab has already cracked somewhere of its own choosing.

**The joints in a rigid pavement:**

| Joint | Direction | Purpose | Bars |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION** | Transverse | Allow **shrinkage**; **control where cracks form** | **Dowels** |
| **EXPANSION** | Transverse | Allow **thermal expansion**; compressible filler | **Dowels** (one end capped) |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | Parallel to traffic | Control **warping** cracking | **TIE BARS** |
| Construction | Either | End of a day's work | As appropriate |

> **TIE bars TIE slabs together (deformed, longitudinal); DOWEL bars carry LOAD across (smooth, greased, transverse).** One sentence covers every question on the pair.

> **Using a deformed bar as a dowel LOCKS the joint** — the slab can no longer move, and it cracks elsewhere. **A real and damaging construction error.**

**Why WARPING drives the spacing:**

> A **temperature GRADIENT through the slab depth** makes the top expand more than the bottom by day and less by night — so the slab **curls**, and the restrained curling generates stress.

> **The longer the slab, the greater the warping stress** — which is the structural reason behind a maximum length, quite apart from shrinkage.

> **Warping stresses often EXCEED the traffic stresses in a concrete pavement**, and the critical design case is the **worst load position combined with the worst warping condition.**

**And Westergaard's three load positions:** **interior, EDGE (usually most critical for load stress), and CORNER (critical when warping combines).**

> **The corner is the slab's weakest point**, supported on only two sides — which is exactly why **dowels at transverse joints matter**, letting the adjacent slab share the load rather than leaving the corner alone.

examTip.trick: **PCC contraction joints are 4.5 m at EVERY thickness**, while RCC allows 13–17 m — because **reinforcement holds shrinkage cracks closed and distributes them.** PCC has nothing to do that.
examTip.trap: The other options are plausible **EXPANSION** joint spacings (27–45 m). Read which joint is asked for — expansion and contraction spacings differ by a factor of about eight.
examTip.mnemonic: **A contraction joint does not prevent cracking — it decides WHERE.** Saw to a quarter depth, and time the cut carefully. **WARPING stresses often exceed traffic stresses**, which is why slab length is capped.

questions.stem: If 40 ml of sewage is diluted to 240 ml of mixture, what is the TON value?
questions.solution:
**6.**

**Working.**

> **TON = final volume ÷ initial (sample) volume**
> **= 240/40 = 6** ✓

> **Option (a), 1/6, is the ratio INVERTED** — and option (d), 1/5, inverts the wrong pair as well. **Getting the direction of the ratio right is the whole question.**

**Why the ratio runs that way:**

> **TON is a DILUTION RATIO** — it expresses **how many volumes of the diluted mixture one volume of sample became.**

> **A stronger odour requires MORE dilution before it becomes undetectable, so a HIGHER TON means a STRONGER odour.**

> **That is the sense check**: if the ratio were inverted, a strong sample would score a small number, which would be perverse. **A number below 1 could never be right**, since dilution always increases the volume.

**The formula in its fuller form:**

> **TON = (volume of sample + volume of odour-free dilution water) ÷ volume of sample**

> Here: **40 ml sample + 200 ml dilution water = 240 ml total**, so **TON = 240/40 = 6** ✓ — the same result by either route.

**What TON measures:**

> The **THRESHOLD ODOUR NUMBER** — the **dilution ratio at which the odour becomes just barely detectable.**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Acceptable** | **1 TON** |
| **Cause for rejection** | **3 TON** |

> **A TON of 6 is well above the rejection threshold**, which is entirely expected for sewage — the test is being applied here to a wastewater sample rather than a drinking water one.

**The essential caveat about the test:**

> **The detector is the HUMAN NOSE.** There is no instrument that measures odour objectively, which makes this **one of the few genuinely subjective parameters in water quality.**

> **A PANEL of testers is used** to reduce individual variation, and testers must be free of colds and must not have smoked or eaten recently.

> **The apparatus is called an OSMOSCOPE or OLFACTOMETER**, but it only presents the dilutions — the judgement remains human.

**Sources of taste and odour:**

| Source | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Dissolved gases** | **H₂S (rotten eggs)**, CO₂ |
| **ALGAE** | The commonest cause of seasonal complaints |
| Organic decay | Vegetation, sewage |
| Inorganic salts | Iron, manganese |
| **Industrial discharges** | **Phenols in particular** |

> **The phenol–chlorine reaction is worth knowing**: **chlorophenols are detectable at parts per BILLION**, so a trace industrial discharge upstream can make a whole supply undrinkable without exceeding any other parameter.

**Treatment, matched to the cause:**

| Method | Removes |
|---|---|
| **AERATION** | **Dissolved GASES** — H₂S, CO₂; also oxidises iron and manganese |
| **ACTIVATED CARBON** | **Adsorbs ORGANIC** taste and odour compounds |
| Ozonation | Oxidises the compounds |
| **Algae control** | Copper sulphate — treats the commonest cause |

> **Aeration for gases, activated carbon for organics** — neither works on the other's problem, so matching the method to the cause is what makes treatment effective.

**And why an aesthetic parameter carries a standard at all:**
