> **People who dislike the taste or smell of treated water turn to UNTREATED sources.** An unpalatable safe supply can therefore be **less protective of health than a palatable one**, because it is not used.

> **That is a genuinely important point in a rural water supply context**, and it is why taste and odour are regulated rather than dismissed as cosmetic.

examTip.trick: **TON = final volume ÷ sample volume = 240/40 = 6.** A **stronger odour needs MORE dilution**, so a higher TON means a stronger odour — which fixes the direction of the ratio.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (d) invert the ratio.** A TON below 1 is impossible, since dilution always increases the volume — that check alone eliminates both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Acceptable 1 TON, reject at 3.** The detector is the **HUMAN NOSE** — the only truly subjective water quality parameter. And **aeration for gases, activated carbon for organics**.

questions.stem: Seasoning of timber below the fibre saturation point causes the timber to:
questions.solution:
**Shrink and strengthen** — both happen together, and for the same reason.

**The FIBRE SATURATION POINT is the threshold that explains everything:**

> **At about 30% moisture content, the cell CAVITIES are empty but the cell WALLS are still saturated.**

| Moisture content | What is happening |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE 30%** | Water sits **FREE in the cavities**. **NO shrinkage, NO strength change** |
| **BELOW 30%** | Water leaves the **cell WALLS**. **SHRINKAGE and STRENGTH INCREASE together** |

> **One threshold, both behaviours** — which is what makes the fibre saturation point worth knowing rather than memorising two separate facts.

**Why removing wall water does both:**

> **The cell wall is a composite of cellulose fibres in a lignin matrix, and water sits BETWEEN the fibres, pushing them apart.**

> **Removing it lets the fibres draw closer**, which **contracts the wall (shrinkage)** and **increases the bonding between fibres (strength).**

> **Free water in the cavities touches nothing structural**, which is exactly why drying from 60% to 35% changes neither dimension nor strength.

**Target moisture contents:**

| Use | Moisture content |
|---|---|
| **Interior joinery, heated building** | **10 – 14%** |
| **Structural timber** | **15 – 18%** |
| Exterior work | 15 – 20% |

> **Timber equilibrates with the humidity around it**, so the target depends on where the timber will live — and **timber seasoned for one environment will move if installed in another.**

**Shrinkage is ANISOTROPIC**, which explains the seasoning defects:

| Direction | Shrinkage |
|---|---|
| **TANGENTIAL** (along the growth rings) | **Greatest — about 2× radial** |
| **RADIAL** (across the rings) | Moderate |
| **LONGITUDINAL** (along the grain) | **Almost NIL** |

> **Because tangential shrinkage is twice radial, boards CUP AWAY FROM THE HEART** as they dry.

> **That single ratio is why QUARTER-SAWN timber (rings roughly perpendicular to the face) is more stable and more valuable than plain-sawn** — its faces shrink in the radial direction, which moves least.

**The seasoning defects:**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Bow, cup, twist, spring** | **Anisotropic or uneven shrinkage** |
| **Checks and splits** | Surface drying faster than the interior |
| **Honeycombing** | **Internal** splitting from over-rapid drying |
| **CASE HARDENING** | Outside sets while the inside is wet — **locked-in stresses** |
| Collapse | Cell walls crushed by rapid drying |

> **CASE HARDENING is the insidious one**: the timber looks perfect until it is **sawn**, at which point the locked-in stresses release and it **distorts violently.**

**And why seasoning is essential rather than optional:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dimensional stability** | Shrinkage happens **before** the timber is fixed, not after |
| **Increased strength** | This question |
| **DECAY resistance** | **Fungi need moisture above about 20%** |
| Takes preservatives and finishes | Paint will not penetrate wet timber |
| Lighter to handle | — |

> **Unseasoned timber shrinks IN PLACE** — opening joints, loosening fasteners, distorting frames and cracking finishes. **All of that is avoided simply by drying it first.**

examTip.trick: **One threshold explains both**: above 30% water sits free in the **cavities** (nothing happens); below it water leaves the cell **WALLS**, so the timber **shrinks AND strengthens together**.
examTip.trap: Drying from 60% to 35% changes **neither** dimension nor strength — the useful drying is entirely below the fibre saturation point. That is why 30% is the number to carry.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tangential shrinkage is TWICE radial, so boards CUP away from the heart** — which is why quarter-sawn timber is more stable and costs more. And **CASE HARDENING** hides until the timber is sawn.

questions.stem: In levelling, the rise and fall method is preferred over the height of instrument method because:
options: It provides an arithmetic check on the intermediate sights as well
It does not require a backsight
It eliminates curvature and refraction errors
questions.solution:
**Because it provides an arithmetic check on the INTERMEDIATE sights as well.**

**The two methods and their checks:**

| Method | Arithmetic check | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** | **Only the backsights and foresights** |
| **RISE AND FALL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** | **Everything, INCLUDING the intermediate sights** |

> **The rise-and-fall check has THREE parts, not two** — and it is that third leg (**ΣRise − ΣFall**) which catches an error in an intermediate sight.

> **In the height-of-instrument method an intermediate sight error passes completely undetected**, because intermediate sights never enter the check at all. **The computation balances perfectly while carrying a wrong reduced level.**

> **That is a genuinely serious defect**, since most of the readings on a detail survey are intermediate sights.

**Why the trade-off exists:**

| | **Height of instrument** | **Rise and fall** |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | **FASTER** — one instrument height serves many intermediate sights | Slower — every consecutive pair must be differenced |
| **Check** | **Incomplete** | **COMPLETE** |
| Suits | **Many intermediate sights** — profile and contour work | **Precise work, few intermediate sights** |

> **So option (a) is the reverse of the truth**: the height-of-instrument method is the **quicker** one, and that speed is exactly what it trades for the weaker check.

> **The choice is between speed and verification**, and it is made according to whether accuracy or coverage matters more on that particular job.

**Why option (d) is wrong, and instructively so:**

> **Curvature and refraction are eliminated by BALANCING THE SIGHTS** — setting the instrument **midway** between the staff stations — **not by the booking method.**

> **The booking method is arithmetic; the error elimination is field procedure.** They are independent, and no way of writing the numbers down can remove a field error.

**Balancing the sights** removes three errors at once, because each is **proportional to the sighting distance** and a level reading is a **difference**:

| Error | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| **CURVATURE** | **+0.0785 d²** m (d in km) |
| **REFRACTION** | **−0.0112 d²** m — about **1/7 of curvature, opposite sign** |
| **COLLIMATION** | Proportional to distance |

> **Combined curvature and refraction correction = −0.0673 d²** metres.

> **Equal backsight and foresight distances make the error identical in both readings, so it cancels in the difference.** It is the single most effective precaution in levelling and costs nothing.

**What balancing does NOT remove:** staff not vertical (use a bubble, or **wave the staff and take the minimum**), staff graduation errors, **settlement** of the instrument or change point, an off-centre bubble, and parallax.

**And RECIPROCAL LEVELLING** is the technique for when balancing is impossible:

> **Across a river or ravine the instrument cannot be set midway.** Readings are taken **from each bank in turn and AVERAGED** — the errors being equal and opposite in the two positions, they cancel in the mean.

**The permissible closing errors:**

| Class | Error |
|---|---|
| **Rough** | **±0.100 √D** |
| **Ordinary** | **±0.025 √D** |
| **Accurate** | **±0.012 √D** |
| **Precise** | **±0.006 √D** |

> **The √D reflects RANDOM error accumulation** — four times the distance gives only twice the error. **A SYSTEMATIC error would accumulate LINEARLY**, which is why systematic errors must be eliminated by procedure rather than averaged away.

examTip.trick: The rise-and-fall check has **THREE parts (ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL)**, and that third leg is what catches an **intermediate sight** error. The HI check has only two.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the REVERSE of the truth** — the height-of-instrument method is the **faster** one, and that speed is exactly what it trades away for the weaker check.
examTip.mnemonic: **Curvature and refraction are killed by BALANCING THE SIGHTS, not by the booking method** — field procedure, not arithmetic. Combined correction **−0.0673 d²** m; refraction is **1/7 of curvature and opposite**.

questions.stem: In a consolidated undrained (CU) triaxial test with pore pressure measurement, the parameters obtained are:
options: c′ and φ′, the effective stress parameters
questions.solution:
**c′ and φ′ — the effective stress parameters.**

**Why measuring pore pressure is what makes the difference:**

> **In an undrained test the pore pressure changes during shearing**, so the total and effective stresses diverge.

> **Measuring u lets you compute σ′ = σ − u at every stage** — and plotting the **EFFECTIVE stress** Mohr circles gives the **effective stress envelope**, hence **c′ and φ′.**

> **Without pore pressure measurement the same test gives only TOTAL stress parameters**, which are far less useful because **strength and volume change depend on σ′ alone.**

**The three triaxial tests:**

| Test | Consolidation | Shearing | Gives | Models |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (unconsolidated undrained)** | **No** | **Undrained** | **c_u, φ_u = 0** for saturated clay | **SHORT-term** loading |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | **Yes** | **Undrained** | **c′, φ′** if u is measured | **The most versatile** |
| **CD (consolidated drained)** | **Yes** | **Drained** | **c′, φ′** directly | **LONG-term** |

> **Option (a) describes the UU test** — the φ_u = 0 result belongs to an **unconsolidated** undrained test on saturated clay, not to a CU test with pore pressure measurement.

**Why CU is the workhorse:**

> **It gives effective stress parameters FAR FASTER than a CD test.**

> **A drained test on clay can take WEEKS**, because the shearing rate must be slow enough for pore pressures to dissipate completely throughout the specimen. **A CU test shears quickly and measures the pore pressure instead.**

> **Same parameters, a fraction of the time** — which is why CU with pore pressure measurement is the standard laboratory test for effective stress parameters.

**Why φ_u = 0 for a saturated clay tested undrained:**

> **No volume change is possible**, so any increase in cell pressure goes **entirely into pore pressure**, leaving **σ′ unchanged.** Since strength depends on σ′, the strength is unchanged too.

> **Every total-stress Mohr circle therefore has the SAME diameter**, and their common tangent is **horizontal — φ_u = 0.**

> **That is a property of the TEST, not of the clay.** The same soil has a genuine **φ′ of 20–30°** in effective stress terms.

**Which parameters to use, and when:**

| Condition | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **Short term** (end of construction) | **c_u, φ_u = 0** — total stress analysis |
| **Long term** | **c′, φ′** — effective stress analysis |

**And which is critical depends on the problem:**

> **EMBANKMENT (loading): the SHORT term is worse** — the clay consolidates afterwards and gains strength.

> **CUTTING (unloading): the LONG term is worse** — pore pressures rise back to equilibrium and the clay softens.

> **Getting that pairing backwards is a genuine design error**, and it is among the most frequently examined points in soil mechanics.

**Why the triaxial test is preferred to the direct shear box:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drainage is CONTROLLED** | The box cannot control it |
| **Pore pressure can be MEASURED** | Giving effective stresses |
| **The failure plane is NOT predetermined** | The specimen fails on its **weakest** plane |
| Stress state known throughout | — |

> **The direct shear box FORCES failure on a horizontal plane** whether or not that is the weakest — which can **overstate the strength of an anisotropic soil.**

**The relation used to extract the parameters:** **sin φ′ = (σ′₁ − σ′₃)/(σ′₁ + σ′₃)** for c′ = 0 — which is simply Mohr's circle geometry, **radius ÷ distance to centre.**

examTip.trick: **Measuring u is what converts total stresses into effective ones** — σ′ = σ − u at every stage. Without it the same test gives only total stress parameters.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) describes the UU test.** The **φ_u = 0** result belongs to an **unconsolidated** undrained test on saturated clay — a property of the TEST, not of the clay, which has a real φ′ of 20–30°.
examTip.mnemonic: **CU is the workhorse because a CD test on clay takes WEEKS** — the shearing must be slow enough for pore pressures to dissipate. Same parameters, a fraction of the time.

questions.stem: A fluid is distinguished from a solid by the fact that a fluid:
options: Deforms continuously under any shear stress
questions.solution:
**It deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small.**

**The defining distinction:**

| | **SOLID** | **FLUID** |
|---|---|---|
| Shear stress proportional to | **The AMOUNT of deformation: τ = Gγ** | **The RATE of deformation: τ = μ(dγ/dt)** |
| Under a small sustained shear | **Deforms a finite amount and STOPS** | **Keeps deforming — FLOWS indefinitely** |
| At rest | **Can sustain shear** | **CANNOT sustain any shear at all** |

> **A solid reaches an equilibrium deformation; a fluid never does.** That single difference is the whole definition, and everything else about fluid mechanics follows from it.

> **"However small" is the essential phrase**: there is no threshold shear below which a fluid behaves as a solid. **Any shear, no matter how tiny, produces continuous motion.**

**The immediate consequence:**

> **A fluid at rest can support NO shear stress.** Therefore **the only stress in a static fluid is NORMAL (pressure)** — which is exactly why **hydrostatic pressure acts equally in all directions** (Pascal's law), and why a free surface at rest must be **horizontal.**

> **The whole of hydrostatics rests on this definition.**

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **"Cannot be compressed"** | **Liquids are nearly incompressible, but GASES are highly compressible — and both are fluids.** Compressibility does not distinguish fluids from solids |
| **"Has no weight"** | Plainly false — fluids have density and weight; that is why hydrostatic pressure increases with depth |
| **"Always has a free surface"** | **A GAS fills its container completely and has NO free surface**, and a liquid in a full closed pipe has none either |

> **Option (c) is the most instructive error**: a free surface is a property of a **LIQUID in an open container**, not of fluids generally. **"Fluid" covers both liquids AND gases**, and the definition must apply to both.

**Newton's law of viscosity:**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

> where **du/dy is the velocity gradient — which IS the rate of angular deformation.**

| Fluid type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ ∝ du/dy** — μ constant. **Water, air, most oils** |
| **Non-Newtonian** | μ varies with the shear rate |
| **Bingham plastic** | **Needs a YIELD stress before flowing at all** — e.g. **fresh concrete, drilling mud, toothpaste** |

> **A Bingham plastic is the interesting borderline case**: below its yield stress it behaves as a solid, and only above it does it flow.

> **Fresh concrete is exactly that** — it holds its shape in a slump cone until the shear from its own weight exceeds the yield value, which is precisely what the **slump test** measures.

**And how viscosity behaves with temperature** — the two phases move opposite ways:

| Fluid | Viscosity with rising temperature |
|---|---|
| **LIQUIDS** | **DECREASES** — thermal agitation overcomes **cohesion** |
| **GASES** | **INCREASES** — more **molecular momentum exchange** |

> **The opposite behaviour reflects opposite mechanisms**: a liquid's viscosity comes from cohesion between molecules, which heat weakens; a gas's comes from momentum transfer between layers, which heat intensifies.

> **Which is why hot oil flows freely while hot air is more viscous than cold** — counter-intuitive until the mechanism is known.

examTip.trick: **A solid resists the AMOUNT of shear strain (τ = Gγ); a fluid resists only its RATE (τ = μ dγ/dt).** A solid stops deforming; a fluid never does — and **"however small" means there is no threshold.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the instructive error**: a free surface belongs to a **LIQUID in an open container**. "Fluid" covers **gases too**, and a gas fills its container with no free surface at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **A fluid at rest can support NO shear — so the only stress is pressure**, acting equally in all directions. The whole of hydrostatics follows from this one definition.

questions.stem: In a pipe flowing full, the ratio of mean velocity to maximum velocity for laminar flow is:
questions.solution:
**0.5 — the mean velocity is exactly HALF the maximum.**

**Why.** In laminar flow through a circular pipe the velocity profile is **PARABOLIC** (Hagen–Poiseuille):

> **u(r) = u_max [1 − (r/R)²]**

> Integrating over the cross-section gives:
>
> **V_mean = u_max/2** exactly ✓

> **The result is EXACT, not approximate** — it follows directly from integrating a paraboloid, whose mean ordinate is half its peak.

**The contrast with turbulent flow:**

| Flow | Velocity profile | V_mean/u_max |
|---|---|---|
| **LAMINAR** | **PARABOLIC** | **0.50 — exactly** |
| **TURBULENT** | **Much FLATTER (roughly 1/7 power law)** | **≈ 0.82** |

> **Option (d), 0.82, is the TURBULENT value** — offered here because the two are always examined together.

**Why turbulent flow gives a flatter profile:**

> **Turbulent MIXING transports momentum across the pipe**, evening out the velocity. Fast fluid from the centre is continually exchanged with slow fluid near the wall.

> **The result is a nearly uniform core with a steep gradient confined to a thin layer at the wall** — which is exactly why the mean is so close to the maximum.

> **In laminar flow there is no such mixing**: each layer slides over the next, and the velocity falls smoothly and parabolically from centre to wall.

**The other laminar flow results, all from the same solution:**

| Quantity | Laminar value |
|---|---|
| **V_mean/u_max** | **0.5** |
| **Friction factor** | **f = 64/Re** — **ROUGHNESS IS IRRELEVANT** |
| **Head loss** | **h_f ∝ V** (LINEAR in velocity) |
| Shear stress | Varies **linearly** from zero at the axis to maximum at the wall |

> **The linear head loss is the striking one**: in laminar flow **h_f ∝ V**, while in turbulent flow **h_f ∝ V²**. **Doubling the flow doubles the loss in laminar flow but quadruples it in turbulent.**

> **And roughness plays NO part in laminar flow at all** — the flow slides over the irregularities without disturbance, which is why the Moody diagram's laminar region is a single line regardless of e/D.

**The transition:**

| Flow | Pipe Reynolds number |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR** | **Re < 2000** |
| Transitional | 2000 – 4000 |
| **TURBULENT** | **Re > 4000** |

> **Re = VD/ν**, and for water **ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s** — worth memorising, since it appears in every calculation.

> **In practice almost all civil engineering pipe flow is TURBULENT**: a 100 mm pipe carrying water at even 0.1 m/s gives Re = 10 000. **Laminar flow in water supply is essentially never encountered** — it belongs to groundwater seepage, oil pipelines and laboratory viscometry.

**Where laminar flow DOES matter in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Seepage through soil** | **Darcy's law is valid only for laminar flow** |
| Capillary and film flows | — |
| **Sedimentation (Stokes' law)** | **v_s = gd²(G−1)/18ν** assumes laminar settling |
| Viscometry | Measuring viscosity |

> **Darcy's law v = ki holds only while the seepage is laminar** — which it is in sand and finer soils, but **not in coarse gravel or rockfill**, where the relation becomes non-linear. **That is a real limitation, not a technicality.**

**And the velocity measurement point** that follows from the profile: **the MEAN velocity in a turbulent pipe occurs at about 0.75 R from the axis**, and in an **open channel at 0.6 × depth** — which is what makes single-point river gauging practical.

examTip.trick: **Laminar flow is PARABOLIC, and a paraboloid's mean ordinate is exactly half its peak** — so V_mean/u_max = **0.5 exactly**, not an approximation.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), 0.82, is the TURBULENT value** — the profile is far flatter because turbulent mixing evens out the velocity. The two are always examined together.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laminar: f = 64/Re, h_f ∝ V, roughness IRRELEVANT. Turbulent: h_f ∝ V².** And **Darcy's law holds only while seepage is laminar** — it fails in coarse gravel and rockfill.

questions.stem: In a beam of rectangular cross-section subjected to transverse loading, the shear stress distribution across the depth is:
options: Linear, maximum at the extreme fibres
Parabolic, maximum at the neutral axis
Linear, zero at the neutral axis
questions.solution:
**Parabolic, with the maximum at the NEUTRAL AXIS.**

**The relation:**

> **τ = V A ȳ /(I b)**

> For a rectangle, evaluating the first moment **Aȳ** at depth y gives a **quadratic in y**, so the distribution is **PARABOLIC**:

| Position | Shear stress |
|---|---|
| **Extreme fibres (top and bottom)** | **ZERO** |
| **NEUTRAL AXIS** | **MAXIMUM** |

> **τ_max = 1.5 × (V/A) for a rectangle** — that is, **50% higher than the average shear stress.**

**Why the shear is ZERO at the extreme fibres:**

> **The top and bottom surfaces are FREE** — no shear can be applied to them.

> By the **complementary shear stress theorem**, the vertical shear at a point equals the horizontal shear there. **Since the horizontal shear must vanish at a free surface, so must the vertical shear.**

> **That is not a mathematical accident but a boundary condition**, and it is worth knowing because it fixes the shape of the distribution immediately.

**The essential contrast with BENDING:**

| Action | Distribution | MAXIMUM at | ZERO at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BENDING (σ = My/I)** | **LINEAR** | **EXTREME FIBRES** | **NEUTRAL AXIS** |
| **TRANSVERSE SHEAR (τ = VAȳ/Ib)** | **PARABOLIC** | **NEUTRAL AXIS** | **EXTREME FIBRES** |
| **TORSION (τ = Tr/J)** | **LINEAR** | **OUTER SURFACE** | **CENTRE** |

> **Bending and transverse shear are exact opposites** — each is zero where the other is maximum. **Options (b) and (d) describe the bending and torsion patterns respectively**, which is what makes them well-constructed distractors.

**The design consequence:**

> **The two actions peak at DIFFERENT POINTS in the section**, so a beam is not usually critical for both at once.

| Location | Critical for |
|---|---|
| **Extreme fibres, at midspan** | **BENDING** |
| **Neutral axis, near the supports** | **SHEAR** |

> **That separation is why bending and shear are checked as separate criteria** rather than combined — except at points where both are significant, such as a **short deep beam** or the web of a plate girder.

**For an I-SECTION the distribution is far from parabolic:**

> **The WEB carries about 90–95% of the shear**, and the flanges almost none — because **b (the width) in τ = VAȳ/Ib is small in the web and large in the flange.**

> **That is why steel design permits the approximation τ = V/(web area)**, ignoring the flanges entirely. **The I-section separates the two jobs: flanges for bending, web for shear.**

> **It also explains why WEB BUCKLING and WEB CRIPPLING are the shear-related failures of a steel beam** — the web is doing all the work.

**Why shear deflection is usually neglected:**

> **For a slender beam, shear deflection is a small fraction of bending deflection** — bending goes as **L³** while shear goes as **L**, so the ratio falls rapidly as the span grows.

> **For a DEEP or SHORT beam (span/depth less than about 4) shear deflection becomes significant**, and such members must be treated as **deep beams**, where plane sections no longer remain plane and ordinary beam theory fails.

**And in reinforced concrete the picture changes entirely:**

> **Concrete cracks in DIAGONAL TENSION long before the shear stress becomes critical**, because shear produces **principal tension at about 45°** and concrete's tensile strength is only **10–15%** of its compressive.

> **So "shear reinforcement" is really diagonal-tension reinforcement**, and **stirrups are vertical precisely to cross those 45° cracks.**

examTip.trick: **Shear must be ZERO at the free top and bottom surfaces** — a boundary condition, via the complementary shear theorem. That fixes the parabolic shape with its peak at the neutral axis.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) describe BENDING and TORSION.** Bending is linear with the maximum at the extreme fibres; transverse shear is the exact opposite. Each is zero where the other peaks.
examTip.mnemonic: **τ_max = 1.5 V/A for a rectangle.** In an **I-SECTION the WEB carries 90–95% of the shear**, which is why steel design uses τ = V/(web area) — flanges for bending, web for shear.

questions.stem: Müller-Breslau's principle states that the influence line for any force quantity in a structure is given by:
options: The bending moment diagram under a unit load at midspan
The shear force diagram for the full design load
The deflected shape obtained by releasing the corresponding restraint and imposing a unit displacement
The envelope of maximum moments from all load cases
questions.solution:
**The deflected shape obtained by releasing the corresponding restraint and imposing a unit displacement in its direction.**

**What the principle says:**

> **To obtain the influence line for any force quantity — a reaction, a shear, a moment — REMOVE the restraint corresponding to that quantity and give the structure a UNIT DISPLACEMENT in its direction. The resulting DEFLECTED SHAPE IS the influence line.**

| Quantity wanted | Release | Impose |
|---|---|---|
| **REACTION at a support** | Remove the support | **Unit vertical displacement** |
| **SHEAR at a section** | Insert a **shear release** (a sliding device) | **Unit relative vertical displacement** |
| **MOMENT at a section** | Insert a **HINGE** | **Unit relative ROTATION** |

> **The releases mirror the quantities**: a moment is released by a hinge, a shear by a sliding connection, a reaction by removing the support.

**Why it matters so much:**

> **For a DETERMINATE structure the influence line is made of STRAIGHT LINES and can be found by statics** — the principle merely confirms what direct calculation gives.

> **For an INDETERMINATE structure the influence line is a CURVE and CANNOT be obtained by statics at all.** Müller-Breslau is then the only practical route, and it gives the **SHAPE immediately** without any analysis.

> **That is the principle's real value**: it converts an intractable analytical problem into a qualitative sketch that anyone can draw.

**Its most useful application — PATTERN LOADING:**

> **The deflected shape shows AT A GLANCE which spans should be loaded to maximise a given effect.**

> **Load every region where the influence line is POSITIVE (for a maximum positive effect), and leave the negative regions unloaded.**

| For maximum | Load |
|---|---|
| **Span moment** in a continuous beam | **ALTERNATE spans** |
| **Support moment** | **Both spans ADJACENT** to that support |

> **Those two rules are not arbitrary — they are read directly off the Müller-Breslau deflected shapes**, and knowing that makes them impossible to forget or confuse.

> **Analysing only the all-spans-loaded case UNDERESTIMATES both maxima**, which is exactly the error the principle prevents.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **Bending moment diagram under a unit load** | A **BMD — fixed load, varying section.** An influence line is the reverse |
| Shear force diagram for the design load | Again a **diagram, not an influence line** |
| **Envelope of maximum moments** | A genuine and useful thing — but it is the **RESULT of applying influence lines**, not the influence line itself |

> **Option (d) is the meaningful near-miss**: a moment **envelope** is what you build **using** influence lines and pattern loading. **It is the output, not the tool.**

**The distinction that underlies all of this:**

| | **Bending moment diagram** | **INFLUENCE LINE** |
|---|---|---|
| The **section** | **Varies** — every point on the beam | **FIXED — one chosen section** |
| The **load** | **FIXED** in position | **MOVES** across the structure |
| Horizontal axis | Position along the **beam** | **Position of the LOAD** |
| Answers | "How is this loading resisted?" | **"Where should the load go to make this worst?"** |

> **One quantity, ONE fixed section, MOVING load** — that is the definition, and the two can share a triangular shape on a simple span while answering completely different questions.

**Using an influence line — two rules cover everything:**

| Load | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at its position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |

> And the placement rules follow: **point load → maximum ordinate; UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.**

> **Because a SHEAR influence line changes sign at the section, loading both sides partly CANCELS** — so maximum shear needs **one side loaded only.**

examTip.trick: **The release MIRRORS the quantity**: a hinge releases a **moment**, a sliding device releases a **shear**, removing a support releases a **reaction**. Then the deflected shape **is** the influence line.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), the moment envelope, is the OUTPUT of applying influence lines**, not the influence line itself. A genuine and useful thing offered in the wrong role.
examTip.mnemonic: **The principle's real value is for INDETERMINATE structures**, where the influence line is a curve statics cannot find. And it gives pattern loading directly: **alternate spans for span moment, adjacent spans for support moment.**

questions.stem: In a water distribution system, a water hammer arrestor or surge protection is required mainly because:
options: The pipe material expands in hot weather
Water is compressible enough that rapid valve closure generates a large pressure wave
The pump motor overheats at high flow
Air accumulates at high points in the main
questions.solution:
**Because water is compressible enough that rapid valve closure generates a large pressure wave.**

**The mechanism:**

> When a valve closes rapidly, the **moving water column must decelerate** — and because both the **water and the pipe wall are slightly ELASTIC**, that deceleration propagates as a **PRESSURE WAVE** travelling back up the pipe.

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρ c ΔV**

| Term | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **ρ** | 1000 kg/m³ |
| **c** — wave speed | **~1000 m/s** in a rigid pipe, less in a flexible one |
| **ΔV** | The velocity destroyed |

> **For ΔV = 2 m/s: Δp = 1000 × 1000 × 2 = 2 × 10⁶ Pa = 2 MPa — about 200 metres of head.**

> **That is many times the normal working pressure**, from a velocity change that seems trivial. **It is why water hammer bursts pipes.**

**The essential point about compressibility:**

> **In a TRULY incompressible fluid in a perfectly rigid pipe, closing a valve instantly would generate INFINITE pressure.**

> **The finite wave speed — and therefore the finite pressure rise — exists ONLY because the water and the pipe are slightly elastic.**

> **So compressibility is not a complication in water hammer; it is the reason water hammer is survivable at all.** That is a genuinely illuminating way to see it, and it is why option (b) is not merely correct but explanatory.

**The timing criterion:**

> **The wave's round trip takes 2L/c**, where L is the pipe length.

| Closure time | Result |
|---|---|
| **FASTER than 2L/c** | **FULL Joukowsky pressure**, however fast it actually is |
| **SLOWER than 2L/c** | **GREATLY REDUCED** surge |

> **"Sudden" has a precise meaning**: it is not "quick" but "faster than the wave can return". **Below that threshold, closing faster changes nothing — the pressure is already at its maximum.**

> **Above it, every extra second of closure time reduces the surge substantially**, which is why slow-closing valves are so effective and so cheap a remedy.

**The protective measures:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **SLOW-closing valves** | The simplest and cheapest — extend closure beyond 2L/c |
| **SURGE TANK / standpipe** | **REFLECTS the wave at a free surface**, so only the pipe **below** it feels the full surge |
| **Air vessel (accumulator)** | A cushion of compressed air absorbs the surge |
| **Pressure relief valve** | Opens to discharge the excess |
| Flywheel on the pump | Extends the run-down time on power failure |

> **A surge tank does not absorb the wave — it REFLECTS it**, which is why its **POSITION matters so much**: as close as possible to the point being protected.

**The case that is often worse than valve closure:**

> **PUMP TRIP on power failure.** The pump stops abruptly, the water column decelerates, and the pressure **first FALLS sharply** — potentially to **vapour pressure**, causing **COLUMN SEPARATION.**

> **When the separated column rejoins, the impact generates a far higher pressure than the original transient** — and that rejoining shock has burst many mains.

> **The negative transient is therefore often more dangerous than the positive one**, which is counter-intuitive and is why **air valves and vacuum breakers** are provided at high points.

> **Note that option (d) — air at high points — is a REAL problem** requiring air valves, but it is a **separate issue** from water hammer, even though the same fittings often address both.

**And the hydropower parallel:** the **GOVERNOR is the origin of water hammer in a penstock** — a load rejection makes it close the gates, and **Δp = ρcΔV** follows. **The governor timing, the surge tank and the penstock wall thickness are therefore designed together**, against the **2L/c** criterion.

examTip.trick: **Δp = ρcΔV** — for a 2 m/s velocity change that is about **200 m of head**, many times the working pressure. And with c ≈ 1000 m/s, even a small ΔV produces an enormous surge.
examTip.trap: **"Sudden" means FASTER THAN 2L/c**, not merely quick. Below that threshold closing faster changes nothing; above it, every extra second helps substantially.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compressibility is why water hammer is SURVIVABLE** — in a truly incompressible fluid the pressure would be infinite. And **PUMP TRIP is often worse than valve closure**, because column separation's rejoining shock exceeds the original.

questions.stem: In the activated sludge process, the purpose of returning sludge from the secondary clarifier to the aeration tank is to:
options: Maintain the required concentration of active micro-organisms in the aeration tank
questions.solution:
**To maintain the required concentration of active micro-organisms in the aeration tank.**

**Why return is essential:**

> **The activated sludge process works by holding a large population of micro-organisms in contact with the wastewater.** Those organisms consume the dissolved organic matter that settling cannot remove.

> **But the wastewater passes through the aeration tank in only 4–8 hours** — far too short for a microbial population to grow from nothing.

> **Returning settled sludge REINOCULATES the tank continuously**, maintaining the biomass concentration (**MLSS**) at the design level.

> **Without return, the organisms would be washed out with the effluent and the process would fail within hours.**

**The key decoupling this achieves:**

| Time | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HRT — Hydraulic Retention Time** | How long the **WATER** stays — **4 to 8 hours** |
| **SRT — Sludge Retention Time (sludge age)** | How long the **ORGANISMS** stay — **5 to 15 days** |

> **Sludge return DECOUPLES the two**: the water passes through quickly while the biomass is retained for days.

> **That decoupling is the whole invention.** It lets a compact tank hold a microbial population that would otherwise need a vessel many times larger — which is why activated sludge treats a city's sewage in a fraction of the area a lagoon would need.

**Why SLUDGE AGE is the master control parameter:**

| Sludge age | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO SHORT** | **Organisms washed out faster than they grow** — the process fails |
| **Moderate (5–15 days)** | Good BOD removal, good settling |
| **LONGER (>10–15 days)** | **NITRIFICATION** occurs — the slow-growing nitrifiers are retained |
| Too long | Over-oxidised, poorly settling sludge |

> **NITRIFICATION requires a long sludge age** because nitrifying bacteria grow much more slowly than the ordinary heterotrophs. **If the sludge age is too short they are washed out before they can multiply**, and ammonia passes straight through.

> **That is why sludge age, not detention time, is what an operator adjusts to control the process** — it is set by controlling the **rate of WASTING** excess sludge.

**The two sludge streams:**

| Stream | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **RAS — Return Activated Sludge** | **Maintains the MLSS** in the aeration tank |
| **WAS — Waste Activated Sludge** | **Removed to control the SLUDGE AGE** — the surplus growth |

> **Both come from the secondary clarifier's underflow**, and the split between them is the operator's principal control.

> **The organisms GROW, so a surplus must be removed continuously** — otherwise the MLSS would rise without limit.

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **MLSS** | **1500 – 4000 mg/l** |
| **HRT** | **4 – 8 hours** |
| **Sludge age (SRT)** | **5 – 15 days** |
| **F/M ratio** | **0.2 – 0.5** kg BOD per kg MLSS per day |
| Return sludge ratio | 25 – 100% of inflow |
| **BOD removal** | **85 – 95%** |

> **The F/M (food to micro-organism) ratio is the other key control**: too high and the organisms are overfed and settle poorly; too low and they starve.

**The characteristic operational problem:**

> **BULKING SLUDGE** — filamentous organisms proliferate, the sludge will not settle in the clarifier, and **solids carry over into the effluent.**

> **A plant that cannot settle its sludge cannot return it either**, so bulking attacks the process at both ends. Causes include **low DO, low F/M, nutrient deficiency and septic influent.**

**And the contrast with a TRICKLING FILTER**, the other classic secondary process:

| | **Activated sludge** | **Trickling filter** |
|---|---|---|
| Biomass | **SUSPENDED** — held by aeration and return | **ATTACHED** to media — no return needed for biomass |
| Land | **Compact** | Larger |
| Power | **High — aeration** | **Low — gravity** |
| Operation | **Skilled** | **Simple and robust** |

> **For Nepali conditions the trickling filter's low power demand and operational simplicity are real advantages**, which is why the choice is not simply about efficiency.

examTip.trick: **Return DECOUPLES the water's residence time (HRT, 4–8 hours) from the organisms' (SRT, 5–15 days).** That decoupling is the whole invention — it lets a compact tank hold a large biomass.
examTip.trap: Without return, **the organisms would wash out with the effluent within hours** — they cannot grow from nothing in a 6-hour pass. The process would fail, not merely underperform.
examTip.mnemonic: **SLUDGE AGE is the master control**, set by the **WASTING** rate — and **NITRIFICATION needs a LONG sludge age**, because nitrifiers grow slowly and are washed out otherwise.

questions.stem: A manhole in a sewerage system is provided mainly to:
options: Increase the flow velocity in the sewer
Act as a settling chamber for solids
Give access for inspection, cleaning and maintenance
questions.solution:
**To give access for inspection, cleaning and maintenance.**

**Where manholes are required:**

| Location | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Every CHANGE OF DIRECTION** | A sewer cannot be rodded round a bend |
| **Every CHANGE OF GRADIENT** | — |
| **Every CHANGE OF DIAMETER** | — |
| **Every JUNCTION** of sewers | — |
| **At regular intervals on straight runs** | So every length can be reached |

> **A sewer is buried and unreachable except at manholes** — so every point in the system must lie within rodding distance of one.

**Typical spacing on straight runs:**

| Sewer size | Manhole spacing |
|---|---|
| **Up to 0.3 m** | **45 m** |
| 0.3 – 0.6 m | 75 m |
| 0.6 – 0.9 m | 90 m |
| **Above 0.9 m** | **150 m or more** |

> **The spacing grows with size because a large sewer can be entered and worked in**, while a small one can only be rodded from the ends — and **rodding length is the limiting factor.**

**The secondary functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | Perforated covers let sewer gases escape |
| Junction chamber | Joining sewers safely |
| Change of level | A **drop manhole** where the incoming sewer is much higher |
| Flow measurement point | — |

> **Option (c) names ventilation, which is genuine but incomplete** — it is one function among several, and access is the primary one. **A question offering a real-but-partial answer alongside the fuller one wants the fuller one.**

**Why option (b) is not merely wrong but harmful:**

> **A manhole must NOT act as a settling chamber.** Solids settling in a manhole are exactly what causes blockages.

> **The manhole is built with a BENCHING and a CHANNEL** — a smooth half-round invert continuing the sewer's shape, with the surrounding floor sloped steeply toward it.

> **The benching exists precisely to prevent settlement**, keeping the flow concentrated and its velocity maintained through the chamber.

> **A manhole with a flat floor and no benching silts up and becomes the blockage it was built to prevent.**

**And option (a) is wrong for a related reason:**

> **A manhole does not increase velocity** — at best it maintains it. **Any widening of the flow path REDUCES velocity**, which is why the benching is shaped to avoid exactly that.

**The DROP MANHOLE** deserves mention:

> Where a branch sewer enters much higher than the main, **the flow is brought down through a vertical drop pipe rather than allowed to cascade into the chamber.**

> **Cascading water erodes the benching, splashes, and releases H₂S** — accelerating **crown corrosion.** The drop pipe contains it.

**Which connects to the wider corrosion problem:**

> **H₂S released from septic sewage is oxidised by bacteria on the moist crown to SULPHURIC ACID**, destroying concrete sewers from the top down within decades.

| Defence | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | Lets the gas escape rather than accumulate |
| **Maintaining SELF-CLEANSING velocity** | Prevents the sewage going septic in the first place |
| Protective lining | Where the risk is high |

> **Turbulence RELEASES H₂S from solution** — which is why drops, falls and rough junctions are hot spots for crown corrosion, and why the benching's smoothness matters for durability as well as for flow.

**And the velocity limits** that the whole system is designed around: **minimum 0.6–0.75 m/s AT MINIMUM FLOW** (self-cleansing) and **maximum 3.0 m/s** (erosion).

> **The self-cleansing check at MINIMUM flow is what makes sewer design harder than water main design** — the gradient must scour the pipe on day one, when only a few connections exist.

examTip.trick: **A sewer is buried and unreachable except at manholes** — so they go at every change of direction, gradient, diameter and junction, plus regular intervals. **Rodding length sets the spacing.**
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the reverse of the truth** — a manhole must NOT settle solids. It is built with **BENCHING and a channel** precisely to keep the flow moving and prevent deposition.
examTip.mnemonic: **Turbulence RELEASES H₂S** — which is why a **DROP MANHOLE** contains the fall in a pipe rather than letting it cascade, and why smooth benching matters for durability as well as flow.

questions.stem: A canal escape is provided in an irrigation system mainly to:
options: Raise the water level for an offtake
Carry the canal across a natural drain
Lower the canal bed where the ground falls steeply
Dispose of surplus water from the canal
questions.solution:
**To dispose of surplus water out of the canal.**

**Why the surplus arises:**

> A canal is fed at its head, but **demand downstream can collapse suddenly and without warning:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAINFALL in the command** | **Irrigation demand vanishes; every outlet closes at once** |
| Sudden closure of outlets | Downstream demand stops |
| Breach or blockage downstream | Flow cannot continue |
| Excess supply at the head | Regulation error, or a flood |
| Emptying for maintenance | Deliberate |

> **The water already in the canal has nowhere to go.** Without an escape the level rises, and **the banks overtop or breach** — flooding the surrounding land and destroying a length of embankment.

> **An escape is the canal's SAFETY VALVE**, and it is what makes a canal operable at all.

**The types:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weir / surplus escape** | An **automatic side weir at bank level** — spills whenever the level rises |
| **SCOURING (sluice) escape** | **Gated, at bed level — ALSO FLUSHES accumulated silt** |
| Tail escape | At the canal's end, keeping the tail reach in supply |

> **A scouring escape does two jobs at once** — relieving surplus water and flushing silt — which is why it is placed at low points where silt accumulates.

**The distinction from the other canal structures**, which is what the distractors test:

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **ESCAPE** | **Dispose of SURPLUS water OUT of the canal** |
| **CROSS REGULATOR** | **RAISE the water level** so an offtake can draw |
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | Control flow **INTO the distributary** |
| **FALL** | Take the **BED down a step** where the ground falls faster than the canal |
| **CROSS-DRAINAGE works** | **Carry the canal past a natural drain** |
| **OUTLET / module** | Deliver water from a minor to a watercourse |

> **Each distractor names a real structure with a completely different function** — so this tests whether the family is understood as a set.

**The cross regulator and head regulator work as a PAIR:**

> Built together at every major offtake — **the cross regulator provides the head; the head regulator controls how much is taken.**

**And the four cross-drainage works**, named by **which one goes over:**

| Structure | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **Canal OVER drain**; drain flows free |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | Canal over drain; **drain under PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Drain OVER canal**; canal free |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | Drain over canal; **canal under PRESSURE** |

> **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top. Add "syphon" when what is underneath runs under pressure.** One rule generates all four.

**And the alignment decision** that determines how many of these structures are needed:

| Alignment | Cross-drainage works |
|---|---|
| **WATERSHED (RIDGE)** | **NONE — streams flow away on BOTH sides; commands land on both sides** |
| **SIDE SLOPE** | **None — runs WITH the drainage** |
| **CONTOUR** | **MANY — crosses every natural drain**; commands one side only |

> **The ridge alignment is preferred wherever topography allows** — it eliminates cross-drainage works entirely, which is the largest single saving available in canal design.

> **Its cost is a LONG LEAD** from the headworks up to the ridge, commanding nothing along the way.

examTip.trick: An escape is a **SAFETY VALVE**. Demand can vanish in an hour — **rain in the command closes every outlet at once** — and the water already in the canal must go somewhere or the banks breach.
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a real structure with a different job**: cross regulator (raise level), cross-drainage (cross a drain), fall (lower the bed). The family must be known as a set.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SCOURING escape does two jobs — relieves surplus water AND flushes silt.** And for crossings: **"aqueduct" means the CANAL is on top; add "syphon" when what is underneath is pressurised.**

questions.stem: A guide bank at a bridge or barrage is provided primarily to:
options: Increase the discharge capacity of the river
Reduce the sediment load carried by the river
Confine the river to the designed waterway and prevent outflanking of the structure
questions.solution:
**To confine the river to the designed waterway and prevent OUTFLANKING of the structure.**

**What outflanking means, and why it is the danger:**

> **A river in flood does not stay in its channel.** On an alluvial plain it can shift its course by hundreds of metres in a single season.

> **OUTFLANKING is when the river simply goes AROUND the end of a structure** — leaving the bridge or barrage standing in dry ground while the river flows past it through newly eroded land.

> **The structure is then useless without having failed structurally at all**, and the approach embankments are destroyed. **That is the specific failure guide banks exist to prevent.**

**How they work:**

> **A pair of GUIDE BANKS (Bell's bunds)** — one on each side — **funnel the river into the designed waterway** and hold it there.

| Feature | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Curved head (upstream)** | **Turns the approaching flow smoothly into the waterway** |
| Straight shank | Confines the flow through the structure |
| **Curved tail (downstream)** | Guides the flow back out without eroding the bank |
| **LAUNCHING APRON** at the toe | **Armours the developing scour hole** |

> **The upstream curve is the critical part** — a sharp entry would create severe local scour and eddying at the head, which is exactly where guide banks fail when they fail.

**The LAUNCHING APRON** deserves emphasis because its principle is unusual:

> **Loose stone is laid horizontally at the toe. As the river SCOURS a hole beside it, the stone at the edge FALLS (launches) into the hole, progressively armouring the newly exposed slope.**

> **It is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in a controlled way** — the apron consumes itself to protect the bank.

> **The stone quantity is calculated to cover the anticipated scour slope (usually 2:1) down to the deepest expected scour level.**

**And that scour depth comes from Lacey:**

> **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a **location factor:**

| Location | Factor |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | 1.25 |
| **Bridge PIER NOSE** | **2.0** |
| **Severe bend / guide bank head** | **2.75** |

> **The guide bank head experiences the most severe scour of any point** — which is why it carries the heaviest protection.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **Increase discharge capacity** | Guide banks **CONFINE** the flow — if anything they concentrate it, they do not increase the river's capacity |
| **Reduce sediment load** | A **silt excluder or settling basin** does that; guide banks do not |
| **Raise the upstream level** | That is a **WEIR or BARRAGE** — the structure the guide banks protect, not the guide banks themselves |

> **Option (d) is the meaningful near-miss**: it describes the very structure the guide banks accompany. **The guide bank protects the barrage; it does not do the barrage's job.**

**The other river training works:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **GROYNE / SPUR** | Projects **from the bank into the river**; **deflects the current away and induces silting** in its lee |
| **Marginal bund** | Embankment along the bank confining floodwater |
| **Revetment / pitching** | Armours the bank face directly |
| Cut-off | Shortens an excessive meander |

> **A REPELLING groyne points UPSTREAM** — counter-intuitive, but an upstream-pointing spur throws the current off the bank while a downstream-pointing one **attracts** it.

**And why rivers migrate at all:**

> **A meander erodes its OUTER bank (where velocity and depth are greatest) and deposits on the INNER bank.** The **helical secondary current** drives it: surface water moves outward, bed water inward.

> **The meander therefore migrates laterally AND downstream over time** — taking land and threatening any structure in its path.

> **That same helical current is why a river INTAKE belongs on the OUTSIDE of a bend** — the bed load is swept to the inside, leaving cleaner water at the outer bank. **One free siting decision that removes more sediment than any structure downstream.**

examTip.trick: **OUTFLANKING is the specific failure**: the river goes **around** the structure, leaving it in dry ground. The bridge has not failed structurally — it has simply been abandoned by the river.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) describes the BARRAGE itself** — the structure the guide banks protect. A guide bank protects the barrage; it does not do the barrage's job.
examTip.mnemonic: **A LAUNCHING APRON is designed to be DESTROYED** — its stone falls into the scour hole as it forms. Size it from **Lacey's R = 1.35(q²/f)⅓ × a location factor**, and the **guide bank head takes 2.75**, the worst of all.

questions.stem: In hydropower planning, the flow duration curve is used mainly to:
options: Determine the maximum flood for spillway design
Establish the design discharge and estimate the annual energy
Find the sediment concentration of the river
Fix the height of the dam
questions.solution:
**To establish the design discharge and estimate the annual energy.**

**What a flow duration curve shows:**

> The **percentage of time a given discharge is equalled or exceeded** — a complete summary of the river's flow regime in one curve.

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Q10** | A **high** flow, available only 10% of the time |
| **Q40** | The typical **DESIGN DISCHARGE** for a run-of-river plant |
| **Q95** | **FIRM / dependable** flow — available almost always |
| Q100 | The absolute minimum |

> **A HIGHER percentage means a LOWER flow**, because it is exceeded a greater proportion of the time. **Reading the curve backwards is the standard error in this topic.**

**The two things it is used for:**

> **1. DESIGN DISCHARGE.** The plant is normally sized at about **Q40** — a choice that is **ECONOMIC, not hydrological.**

| Design at | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Q90 (firm flow)** | Plant runs at full capacity almost always — but it is **SMALL and SPILLS most of the monsoon** |
| **Q40** | Full output ~40% of the time, part load the rest — **MAXIMISES annual ENERGY per rupee invested** |
| **Q10** | A huge, expensive machine **idle most of the year** |

> **2. ANNUAL ENERGY.** **The AREA under the curve UP TO the design discharge is the water the plant can actually use**; everything above it is **spilled.**

> **That single picture explains the whole trade-off**: raising the design flow captures more area but costs more machine, and **the added area shrinks as you move up the curve** — which is why an optimum exists.

**Why the other options belong to different analyses:**

| Option | Correct tool |
|---|---|
| **Maximum flood for spillway design** | **FLOOD FREQUENCY analysis** (Gumbel, Log-Pearson) or the **PMF** — the flow duration curve says nothing about extremes |
| **Sediment concentration** | **Sediment rating curve and sampling** |
| **Height of the dam** | Topography, storage requirement and **reservoir capacity curve** |

> **Option (a) is the most instructive error**: a flow duration curve is about **how often ordinary flows occur**, not about the **magnitude of rare extremes.**

> **A curve built from daily flows contains no reliable information about a 1000-year flood** — which requires **extreme value statistics** on annual maxima, an entirely different analysis on an entirely different data set.

**FIRM POWER**, the other quantity read from the curve:

> **Firm (dependable) power is taken at Q95** — the power the plant can be relied on to deliver almost always.

> **It is limited by the DRY SEASON flow**, and it commands a **much higher price than secondary power** because a utility can plan around it.

> **Two plants with the same annual energy can have very different value** if one delivers reliably through the dry season and the other only in the monsoon.

**The Nepali context that makes this decisive:**

> **About 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months**, while **demand peaks in the dry winter evening.**

| Solution | Addresses |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE reservoir** | **The SEASONAL mismatch** — the only measure that does |
| **Pondage (PROR)** | The **DAILY** peak |
| **Pumped storage** | Time-shifting **within a day** |
| Cross-border trade | Export monsoon surplus, import in the dry season |

> **Only STORAGE moves monsoon water into January.** Pondage and pumped storage shift energy within a day and cannot touch the seasonal problem.

**And the power equation the curve feeds:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**, with **η ≈ 0.85–0.90.**

> **Q comes from the flow duration curve — at Q40 for design discharge, Q95 for firm power. H comes from the topography.**

examTip.trick: **The AREA under the curve up to the design discharge is the usable water; everything above is SPILLED.** That picture explains why an optimum exists around **Q40** — the added area shrinks as you go higher.
examTip.trap: **A flow duration curve says NOTHING about extreme floods** — it describes how often ordinary flows occur. Spillway design needs **flood frequency analysis or the PMF**, a different analysis on different data.
examTip.mnemonic: **A HIGHER percentage means a LOWER flow** — Q95 is small and dependable, Q10 large and rare. And the design choice is **ECONOMIC**: design at Q90 and you spill the monsoon; at Q10 the machine idles.

questions.stem: In an earth dam, the primary purpose of a chimney drain or internal filter is to:
options: Increase the dam's weight for stability
Reduce the cost of the impervious core
Intercept seepage and prevent piping by carrying it safely to the downstream toe
questions.solution:
**To intercept seepage and prevent piping by carrying it safely to the downstream toe.**

**The problem it solves:**

> **An earth dam is permeable by nature — seepage through it is inevitable and expected.** The dam is not designed to be watertight; it is designed to **control** the seepage.

| Uncontrolled seepage causes | Note |
|---|---|
| **PIPING** | Soil particles washed out, forming a channel |
| **Sloughing of the downstream face** | Seepage emerging on the slope saturates and destabilises it |
| High pore pressures | Reducing effective stress and shear strength |
| Loss of water | Usually minor by comparison |

> **PIPING is the leading cause of earth dam failure**, and the internal drainage system is the principal defence against it.

**How a chimney drain works:**

> A **vertical or steeply inclined layer of graded filter material** placed just downstream of the core, connected to a **horizontal blanket drain** leading to the **toe drain.**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **INTERCEPTS seepage** before it reaches the downstream shell | — |
| **LOWERS the phreatic surface** within the dam | Keeping the downstream shell **dry and stable** |
| **Carries the seepage safely out** at the toe | Where it can be measured |
| **Prevents particle migration** | The filter retains the soil while passing the water |

> **Lowering the phreatic line is the structural benefit**: a dry downstream shell has full strength and no seepage forces, which improves slope stability substantially.

**The FILTER CRITERIA that make it work:**

> **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4 to 5** — the **RETENTION** criterion (fine enough to hold the soil back)
> **D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4 to 5** — the **PERMEABILITY** criterion (coarse enough to drain freely)

> **The two pull in OPPOSITE directions, and both must be satisfied simultaneously.**

| If the filter is | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO FINE** | **Clogs — pore pressure builds behind it**, defeating the purpose |
| **TOO COARSE** | **The soil washes through — PIPING**, the very failure it was built to prevent |

> **That opposition is why a filter is DESIGNED rather than simply specified as "gravel"**, and why graded multi-layer filters are used where the soil is very fine.

**Why piping is so dangerous:**

> **It is SELF-ACCELERATING.** Once erosion begins:

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1** | Soil is washed out, forming a channel |
| **2** | The channel **SHORTENS the seepage path** |
| **3** | A shorter path means a **HIGHER gradient** |
| **4** | Which **erodes faster** — working backwards toward the reservoir |

> **The process gives very little warning before breach**, which is why the factor of safety on the exit gradient is **4 to 5** rather than the 1.5–3 used for most geotechnical checks.

> **The critical gradient i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.0** for most soils.

**The zoned earth dam:**

| Zone | Function |
|---|---|
| **Impervious CORE** | Reduces seepage |
| **FILTERS / transition zones** | **Prevent particle migration between core and shell** |
| **CHIMNEY and BLANKET drains** | **Intercept and carry seepage out** |
| **Shells (pervious)** | Provide **stability** — the structural bulk |
| Riprap | Protects the upstream face from **wave action** |

> **The core provides watertightness, the shells provide stability, and the filters and drains manage what gets through.** Each zone has one job.

**And the other earth dam failure modes**, for context:

| Failure | Cause |
|---|---|
| **OVERTOPPING** | **Inadequate spillway capacity — the commonest cause of embankment dam failure** |
| **PIPING / internal erosion** | Inadequate filters |
| **Slope instability** | Especially on **RAPID DRAWDOWN** of the upstream face |
| Foundation failure | Weak or permeable foundation |

> **RAPID DRAWDOWN is the critical case for the UPSTREAM slope**: the reservoir falls quickly, the pore pressures inside the embankment cannot dissipate as fast, and **the slope is left saturated with no water pressure supporting it.**

> **The upstream slope is therefore checked for drawdown, and the downstream slope for steady seepage** — two different critical conditions on the same dam.

examTip.trick: **An earth dam is not designed to be watertight — it is designed to CONTROL seepage.** The drain intercepts it, lowers the phreatic line, and carries it out safely where it can be measured.
examTip.trap: **The two filter criteria pull OPPOSITE ways**: too fine and it **clogs**, building pore pressure; too coarse and the soil **washes through** — the very piping it was built to prevent.
examTip.mnemonic: **PIPING is self-accelerating and gives almost no warning** — hence a factor of safety of **4–5** on exit gradient. And check the **upstream slope for RAPID DRAWDOWN, the downstream for steady seepage.**

questions.stem: An anchor block on a penstock is provided mainly to:
options: Support the penstock's self weight along straight lengths
Reduce friction losses in the penstock
Allow thermal expansion of the pipe
Resist the unbalanced thrust at bends and changes of section
questions.solution:
**To resist the unbalanced thrust at bends and changes of section.**

**Why a bend generates thrust:**

> **Water flowing round a bend has its MOMENTUM changed in direction** — and by Newton's second law that requires a **force.**

> **The pipe exerts that force on the water, and the water exerts an equal and opposite force on the pipe.** There is also an **unbalanced pressure force**, since the pressure acts on the projected areas of the bend.

> **Both effects push the bend outward**, and on a high-head penstock the resultant is **enormous** — easily hundreds of tonnes.

| Contribution | Source |
|---|---|
| **Momentum change** | **ρQ(V₁ − V₂)** vectorially |
| **PRESSURE force** | **pA on each face**, unbalanced at a bend |

> **The pressure term dominates on a penstock**, because the head is large and the velocity modest.

**What the anchor block does:**

> A **large mass of concrete that GRIPS the pipe firmly and transfers the thrust into the ground** by its own weight and by bearing against the soil or rock.

> **The pipe is fixed rigidly at the anchor** — it cannot move there at all, which is precisely the point.

**Where anchor blocks are required:**

| Location | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Every horizontal or vertical BEND** | Unbalanced thrust |
| **Every change of DIAMETER** | Unbalanced pressure force |
| **At valves and blank ends** | The full pA force |
| **At intervals on steep straight runs** | To resist the **downhill component of self weight** |

> **The last row is why option (a) is not absurd** — anchor blocks do carry the axial component of weight on a slope. **But the primary purpose, and the reason they exist at bends, is the thrust.**

**The companion element — EXPANSION JOINTS:**

> **Between every pair of anchor blocks there must be an EXPANSION JOINT.**

> **The pipe is rigidly fixed at each anchor, so it CANNOT expand or contract there.** Without a joint between them, **thermal movement would generate very large axial stresses** — potentially buckling or splitting the pipe.

> **So option (c) names a real requirement that belongs to a DIFFERENT component**: the expansion joint allows movement, while the anchor block **prevents** it. **They are complementary opposites, and both are needed.**

**And SADDLE (support) piers** are the third element:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **ANCHOR BLOCK** | **Fixes the pipe; resists THRUST** |
| **EXPANSION JOINT** | **ALLOWS thermal movement** between anchors |
| **SADDLE / support pier** | **Carries the pipe's WEIGHT between anchors, allowing it to slide** |

> **Saddles support; anchors fix; joints release.** Three components, three distinct jobs — and confusing them is the commonest error in penstock questions.

> **Option (a) actually describes the SADDLE's job** — supporting self weight along straight lengths.

**The penstock design checks:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **Wall thickness** | **t = pD/(2σ)** — from the **HOOP stress**, plus a corrosion allowance |
| **WATER HAMMER** | **Δp = ρcΔV** — often **governs the thickness**, not the static head |
| **Economic diameter** | Balances capital cost against **50 years of lost generation** |
| Anchor blocks and expansion joints | This question |
| Buckling under external pressure | For a pipe that may be emptied |

> **Hoop stress governs because it is TWICE the longitudinal stress** — which is why a pressurised pipe **splits along its length** rather than tearing across.

> **And water hammer often governs the wall thickness**, which is why the **governor closure timing, the surge tank and the penstock are designed together** against the **2L/c** criterion.

**The economic diameter** is worth noting because the sensitivity is extreme:

> **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵** — a **10% larger pipe cuts the head loss by nearly 40%**, and that saving is **generation never produced**, recurring for the plant's entire life.

> **Design velocities are typically 3–6 m/s**, set by minimising the sum of capital cost and the capitalised value of lost energy.

examTip.trick: **A bend changes the water's MOMENTUM and leaves an unbalanced PRESSURE force** — both push outward, and on a high-head penstock the resultant is hundreds of tonnes. The **pressure term dominates**.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) names a real requirement belonging to the EXPANSION JOINT** — which allows movement, while the anchor block **prevents** it. And **option (a) describes the SADDLE's job.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Saddles SUPPORT, anchors FIX, joints RELEASE** — three components, three jobs. And **water hammer often governs the wall thickness**, not the static head.

questions.stem: A transition curve is provided between a straight and a circular curve mainly because:
options: It reduces the total length of the road
It allows the radial acceleration and the superelevation to be introduced gradually
It increases the design speed of the road
questions.solution:
**Because it allows the radial acceleration and the superelevation to be introduced gradually.**

**The problem without a transition:**

> **On a straight, the radius is infinite and the radial acceleration is ZERO. On a circular curve of radius R, the radial acceleration is V²/R.**

> **Joining them directly means that acceleration appears INSTANTANEOUSLY** — a step change at the tangent point.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The driver must JERK the steering wheel** | Uncomfortable and unsafe |
| **The superelevation must appear abruptly** | Physically impossible to build |
| Sudden lateral force on the vehicle | Passenger discomfort, load shift |
| The vehicle wanders while the driver corrects | Effective lane width reduced |

> **A transition curve spreads that change over a length**, so the radial acceleration builds up gradually and the superelevation can be applied progressively along it.

**Why a SPIRAL (clothoid) is the shape used:**

> **Its RADIUS DECREASES UNIFORMLY WITH LENGTH: R × L = constant.**

> **That is exactly what a driver naturally produces by turning the steering wheel at a STEADY RATE** — so the spiral matches the path a vehicle takes anyway.

> **The curve fits the driver rather than requiring the driver to fit the curve**, which is why it is used in preference to any other shape.

**The four functions of a transition curve:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Introduce the radial acceleration GRADUALLY** | Comfort and safety |
| **Apply the SUPERELEVATION progressively** | Physically necessary |
| **Introduce the EXTRA WIDENING gradually** | Same reason |
| Improve appearance | The alignment flows |

> **All three geometric provisions — superelevation, extra widening and curvature — are introduced along the transition**, which is why its length must satisfy all of them.

**The length is the GREATEST of three criteria:**

| Criterion | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Rate of change of RADIAL ACCELERATION** | **L = 0.0215 V³/(C R)**, with **C = 80/(75 + V)** |
| **Rate of applying SUPERELEVATION** | **1 in 150 for hills**, 1 in 100–200 generally |
| **IRC empirical** | **L = 2.7 V²/R** (plain/rolling), **L = V²/R** (hilly) |

> **Taking the greatest ensures every requirement is met** — a length adequate for comfort may be too short to apply the superelevation at an acceptable rate, or vice versa.

**The superelevation itself:**

> **e = V²/(225 R)**, where **225 = 127 ÷ 0.75²** — because superelevation is designed for **75% of the design speed**, so that **slow vehicles are not made to slide inward** on a steeply banked curve.

| Terrain | e_max |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** | **7%** |
| **Hilly, not snow bound** | **10%** |
| **SNOW BOUND** | **7%** |

> **Snow-bound roads are capped at 7% even in the hills**, because a steeply banked icy road makes a **stationary or slow vehicle slide inward off the carriageway.**

**And the EXTRA WIDENING** introduced along the same transition:

> **W_e = n l²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)**

| Component | Cause |
|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL — nl²/2R** | **Off-tracking** — the rigid wheelbase makes rear wheels cut the corner |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL — V/(9.5√R)** | Drivers keep further from the edge and from each other |

> **Mechanical widening is pure GEOMETRY (no speed appears); psychological widening is BEHAVIOURAL (speed does).** The presence or absence of V tells them apart.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| Reduces total length | A transition **LENGTHENS** the alignment slightly |
| Increases design speed | **Design speed is set by road class and terrain**, not by the curve type |
| Reduces earthwork | If anything the reverse |

> **Option (c) inverts the causation**: the design speed determines the transition length, not the other way round.

**And the companion provision on hill roads — GRADE COMPENSATION:**

> **(30 + R)/R percent, maximum 75/R**, not applied below 4% gradient.

> **A vehicle on a curve already faces curve resistance from tyre scrub**; adding a steep gradient makes the total excessive. **Failing to compensate is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends.**

examTip.trick: **A spiral's radius decreases UNIFORMLY with length (RL = constant)** — exactly the path a driver produces by turning the wheel at a steady rate. **The curve fits the driver, not the reverse.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) inverts the causation** — design speed is set by road class and terrain, and it **determines** the transition length. The transition does not raise the speed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Superelevation, extra widening AND curvature are all introduced along the transition** — so its length is the **GREATEST of three criteria**. And **e = V²/225R**, with 225 = 127 ÷ 0.75².

questions.stem: The stripping value test on aggregate measures:
options: The percentage of fines produced under impact
The resistance of the aggregate to abrasion
The shape of the aggregate particles
The tendency of bitumen to separate from the aggregate in the presence of water
questions.solution:
**The tendency of bitumen to separate from the aggregate in the presence of water.**

**What stripping is:**

> **The LOSS OF ADHESION between the bituminous binder and the aggregate surface, caused by water displacing the binder from the stone.**

> **Water is more strongly attracted to most mineral surfaces than bitumen is** — so given access, it works its way between them and the binder peels off.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The mix loses COHESION** | The binder no longer holds the aggregate |
| **RAVELLING** | Aggregate is shed from the surface |
| **POTHOLES** | The failure progresses rapidly once water enters |
| Loss of strength | The whole layer degrades |

> **Stripping is a MOISTURE-INDUCED failure, and it is why water in a bituminous pavement is so destructive.**

**The test and its criterion:**

> Coated aggregate is **immersed in water**, and the **percentage of the surface that remains COATED** is assessed.

> **Retention must exceed 95%** — that is, **less than 5% stripping.**

> **Note this is the ONE aggregate test where a HIGH number is wanted**, because it measures what is **kept**, not what is **lost**. Every other test — crushing, impact, abrasion, soundness, absorption, flakiness — measures **damage**, so **lower is better.**

**What determines susceptibility — the aggregate's CHEMISTRY:**

| Aggregate | Chemistry | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **SILICIOUS (acidic)** — quartzite, granite | **Hydrophilic — "water-loving"** | **STRIPS readily** |
| **CALCAREOUS / basic** — limestone, basalt | **Hydrophobic relative to water** | **Bonds well with bitumen** |

> **A hard, strong, durable silicious aggregate can still make a poor bituminous pavement** — it passes every strength test and then sheds its binder when wet.

> **That is the instructive point: the strongest aggregate is not automatically the best one**, and strength tests alone cannot reveal it.

**The remedies:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **HYDRATED LIME** (1–2% of the aggregate) | **Cheap and highly effective** — the usual first choice |
| **Anti-stripping agent (amine)** | Added to the binder |
| **Choosing a basic aggregate** | Where available |
| **Keeping the mix DRY and well compacted** | Low voids exclude water |
| Adequate drainage | Prevents water reaching the layer |

> **Hydrated lime works by altering the aggregate surface chemistry** so the bitumen bonds to it in preference to water — and it is far cheaper than a proprietary amine.

**The full family of aggregate tests:**

| Test | Measures | Limit (wearing course) |
|---|---|---|
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradual** load | **30%** |
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** (toughness) | **30%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | **Abrasion, impact and grinding combined** | **30 – 40%** |
| **Soundness** | Weathering resistance | 12% / 18% |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | **< 2%** |
| **Flakiness / elongation** | **SHAPE** | **15% / 30% combined** |
| **STRIPPING value** | **Binder ADHESION** | **Retention > 95%** |
| Polished stone value | Skid resistance retained | — |

> **Each distractor in this question names a different real test** — impact (fines under shock), abrasion (wear), flakiness (shape). **This is a four-way match, not a guess.**

**Why moisture is the underlying enemy:**

> **The bitumen moisture limit is 0.2%** because bitumen is handled at about **150 °C** — water flashes to steam, the boiler froths over, and the binder cannot bond to a wet aggregate.

> **And the mix's own air voids are held at 3–5%** partly to keep it **impermeable**: above 5% the mix admits water and air, which both **oxidise the binder and enable stripping.**

> **So the void target, the moisture limit and the stripping test are all aspects of the same concern** — keeping water away from the binder–aggregate interface.

examTip.trick: **This is the ONE aggregate test where a HIGH number is wanted** — retention above **95%**, because it measures what is **kept**. Every other test measures **damage**, so lower is better.
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a different real test** — impact (fines under shock), abrasion (wear), flakiness (shape). A four-way match, not a guess.
examTip.mnemonic: **SILICIOUS aggregates (quartzite, granite) are HYDROPHILIC and strip readily** — so the strongest stone is not automatically the best. **Hydrated lime (1–2%)** is the cheap and effective cure.

questions.stem: In traffic engineering, the passenger car unit (PCU) is used to:
options: Measure the average speed of vehicles
Calculate the fuel consumption of a vehicle fleet
Determine the axle load for pavement design
Express a mixed traffic stream in terms of an equivalent number of cars
questions.solution:
**To express a mixed traffic stream in terms of an equivalent number of cars.**

**Why the conversion is needed:**

> **A traffic stream contains vehicles of very different sizes, speeds and manoeuvring characteristics** — cars, buses, trucks, motorcycles, cycles, rickshaws and animal-drawn carts.

> **They cannot simply be added together**, because a bus occupies far more road space and interferes with far more other vehicles than a motorcycle does.

> **The PCU converts them all to a common unit**, so that capacity and volume can be expressed as a single number.

**Typical PCU values (IRC):**

| Vehicle | PCU |
|---|---|
| **Passenger car, light van** | **1.0** |
| **Motorcycle / scooter** | **0.5** |
| **Bicycle** | **0.2** |
| **Bus or truck** | **3.0** |
| **Tractor-trailer** | **4.5** |
| Cycle rickshaw | 1.5 |
| **Animal-drawn cart** | **6 – 8** |
