> **The animal-drawn cart's very high value is instructive**: it is not large, but it is **SLOW**, and a slow vehicle in a mixed stream causes far more disruption than its size suggests.

> **PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size** — which is why speed differential matters as much as physical dimensions.

**What PCU is used for:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPACITY analysis** | Road capacity is quoted in **PCU/hour** |
| **Level of service** | Volume-to-capacity ratio |
| **Intersection design** | Saturation flow in **PCU/hour of green** |
| Geometric design | Number of lanes required |

> **Capacity of a two-lane two-way road is about 2000–3000 PCU/hour**; a single lane about **1500–1800 PCU/hour** under ideal conditions.

**The critical distinction — PCU is NOT for pavement design:**

> **Option (c) names the other traffic conversion, and the two must never be confused.**

| Purpose | Unit | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| **CAPACITY and geometric design** | **PCU** | **Road SPACE and interference** |
| **PAVEMENT design** | **msa — million standard axles** | **AXLE LOAD, via the FOURTH POWER LAW** |

> **A motorcycle has a PCU of 0.5 but does essentially ZERO pavement damage**; a loaded truck has a PCU of 3 but does **thousands of times** a car's damage.

> **The two measures diverge enormously**, because they answer different questions: **how much ROOM does it take** versus **how much DAMAGE does it do.**

**The fourth power law**, which governs the pavement side:

> **Damage ∝ (axle load)⁴**

| Axle load | Damage relative to a standard axle |
|---|---|
| **Standard (8160 kg)** | **1** |
| 1.5 × standard | ~5 |
| **2 × standard (overloaded)** | **16** |

> **One truck at twice the legal axle load does sixteen times the damage of a legal one — and more than a thousand cars.**

> **That is why AXLE LOAD CONTROL matters far more than traffic volume for pavement life**, and why overloading is the single greatest cause of premature pavement failure in Nepal.

**Design traffic for a pavement (IRC 37):**

> **N = [365 A ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1)/r] × VDF × LDF**

> where **VDF** converts commercial vehicles to standard axles and **LDF** allocates traffic to the design lane.

**And the geometric design counterpart** uses volumes rather than loads:

> **Design hourly volume = the 30th HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME of the year**, typically **8–12% of AADT** — not the average, and not the absolute peak.

> **Designing for the absolute peak would be uneconomic** (it occurs once a year); **designing for the average would leave the road congested for much of the time.** The 30th highest hour is the accepted compromise.

examTip.trick: **PCU measures INTERFERENCE, not size** — which is why an animal-drawn cart scores **6–8**: it is slow, and a slow vehicle disrupts a mixed stream far more than its dimensions suggest.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) names the PAVEMENT conversion — msa, via the fourth power law.** PCU is for **capacity and geometry (road SPACE)**; msa is for **pavement (axle DAMAGE)**. The two must never be swapped.
examTip.mnemonic: **A motorcycle has PCU 0.5 but does essentially ZERO pavement damage; a truck has PCU 3 but does thousands of times a car's.** Different questions: how much ROOM versus how much DAMAGE.

questions.stem: The degree of static indeterminacy of a rigid-jointed plane frame with 3 members, 4 joints and fixed supports at two joints is:
questions.solution:
**3.**

**Working.** For a **rigid-jointed PLANE FRAME**:

> **D_s = 3m + r − 3j**

| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| **m** — members | **3** |
| **r** — reaction components | **2 fixed supports × 3 = 6** |
| **j** — joints | **4** |

> **D_s = 3(3) + 6 − 3(4) = 9 + 6 − 12 = 3** ✓

**Why the formula differs from the truss one:**

| Structure | Formula | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Plane TRUSS** | **D_s = m + r − 2j** | Members carry **ONE force each (axial)**; each joint gives **2 equations** |
| **Plane FRAME** | **D_s = 3m + r − 3j** | Members carry **THREE actions (axial, shear, moment)**; each **rigid joint gives 3 equations** |

> **The 3s appear because a rigid joint transmits MOMENT as well as force.** A pin joint does not, which is why a truss uses 2s.

> **Knowing which formula belongs to which structure is the first thing to establish**, and using the truss formula here would give 3 + 6 − 8 = 1, which is wrong.

**The reaction counts:**

| Support | Reaction components |
|---|---|
| **Roller** | **1** |
| **Pin (hinge)** | **2** |
| **FIXED** | **3** |

> **A fixed support restrains two translations and one rotation** — hence 3, and hence 6 for two fixed supports.

**Reading the result:**

| D_s | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **= 0** | **Determinate** — solvable by statics alone |
| **> 0** | **INDETERMINATE** — needs compatibility conditions as well |
| **< 0** | **A MECHANISM — unstable** |

> **D_s = 3 means three redundant actions**, so three compatibility equations are needed in addition to statics.

> **A portal frame with both feet fixed is the classic D_s = 3 structure**, and it is why such frames are analysed by moment distribution, slope deflection or matrix methods rather than by statics.

**The effect of an internal hinge:**

> **Each internal hinge REDUCES the indeterminacy by 1**, because it supplies an extra equation (**ΣM = 0** at the hinge).

> **A three-hinged portal frame is therefore DETERMINATE**, which is exactly the same reasoning as for a three-hinged arch.

**Why determinacy matters — and it is not merely an analytical convenience:**

| | **DETERMINATE** | **INDETERMINATE** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Statics alone** | Statics **plus compatibility** |
| **Temperature change** | **NO stress** — it simply moves | **STRESSES induced** |
| **Support settlement** | **NO stress** | **STRESSES induced** |
| Fabrication error / lack of fit | No stress | Stresses induced |
| **Redundancy** | **None — one failure is collapse** | **ALTERNATIVE LOAD PATH** |
| Material efficiency | Less efficient | **More efficient** — smaller moments |

> **The trade-off is real on both sides.** An indeterminate structure is more efficient and has redundancy, but it is **sensitive to imposed deformations** that a determinate one simply accommodates.

> **A determinate structure develops NO stress at all from settlement, temperature or a fabrication error** — because it can move freely to accommodate them. **An indeterminate structure RESISTS that movement, and resisting it means stress.**

> **Which is why an indeterminate structure needs reliable foundations**, and why a structure on compressible ground may deliberately be articulated with joints.

**And the KINEMATIC indeterminacy** — the other count, used by displacement methods:

> **D_k = number of independent joint DISPLACEMENTS.**

| Method family | Unknowns | Number |
|---|---|---|
| **FORCE (flexibility)** | Redundant **forces** | **D_s** |
| **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** | Joint **displacements** | **D_k** |

> **Choose whichever count is SMALLER for hand analysis** — a continuous beam usually has fewer redundant forces, a multi-storey frame fewer joint rotations, which is why frames are analysed by displacement methods.

examTip.trick: **A FRAME uses 3s (D_s = 3m + r − 3j) because a rigid joint transmits MOMENT** as well as force; a **TRUSS uses 2s** because pin joints do not. Establish which formula applies first.
examTip.trap: Using the **truss** formula here gives 1 instead of 3. And count reactions carefully: **fixed = 3, pin = 2, roller = 1**, so two fixed supports give **r = 6**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Each internal HINGE reduces D_s by 1** — which is why a three-hinged portal is determinate, exactly as a three-hinged arch is. And a **determinate structure develops NO stress from settlement or temperature.**

questions.stem: In engineering economics, the term 'sunk cost' refers to a cost that:
options: Will be incurred in the future if the project proceeds
Varies with the level of output
Is shared between two or more projects
Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered by any future decision
questions.solution:
**A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered by any future decision.**

**The decisive principle:**

> **SUNK COSTS ARE IRRELEVANT TO A DECISION.**

> **A decision can only affect the FUTURE.** Since a sunk cost is unaffected by whatever is chosen now, it **cannot distinguish between the options** and must be excluded from the comparison entirely.

> **Only costs and benefits that DIFFER between the alternatives are relevant.**

**The classic error — the SUNK COST FALLACY:**

> **"We have already spent Rs 5 crore on this project, so we must continue."**

> **The Rs 5 crore is gone whatever is decided.** The only rational question is whether the **REMAINING** cost to complete is justified by the **REMAINING** benefit.

> **If it is not, continuing wastes more money on top of money already lost** — and the earlier expenditure is not a reason to continue but simply a fact about the past.

> **It is also called the "escalation of commitment"**, and it is one of the most persistent and expensive errors in project management.

**Why it is so hard to resist:**

> **Abandoning a project makes the loss VISIBLE and attributable**, while continuing defers and diffuses it. **The incentive to continue is psychological and political rather than economic** — which is precisely why the principle has to be stated as a rule.

**Worked illustration:**

| Situation | Figures |
|---|---|
| Already spent | **Rs 5 crore (SUNK)** |
| Cost to complete | **Rs 3 crore** |
| Value on completion | **Rs 2 crore** |

> **The rational decision is to ABANDON** — spending 3 to gain 2 loses a further crore, regardless of the 5 already spent.

> **Including the sunk 5 crore in the comparison would suggest continuing**, and that is exactly the fallacy.

**The related cost concepts:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SUNK cost** | **Already incurred; UNRECOVERABLE; IRRELEVANT to decisions** |
| **OPPORTUNITY cost** | **The value of the BEST ALTERNATIVE FOREGONE — always relevant** |
| **Marginal (incremental) cost** | The cost of **one more unit** |
| **Fixed cost** | Does not vary with output — **option (b) describes VARIABLE cost** |
| **Common / joint cost** | Shared between products — **option (c)** |
| **Future / avoidable cost** | **Option (a)** — and it IS relevant |

> **Each distractor names a real and different cost concept**, which makes this a clean four-way match rather than a guess.

**OPPORTUNITY COST is the instructive counterpart:**

> **It is the mirror image of a sunk cost — a cost that never appears in the accounts yet is ALWAYS relevant.**

> **Using land the organisation already owns is not free**: its opportunity cost is what it could have been sold or leased for. **The purchase price, by contrast, is sunk and irrelevant.**

> **So the same piece of land carries an irrelevant historic cost and a relevant current one** — which is the clearest illustration of why accounting cost and economic cost differ.

**Where this matters in engineering appraisal:**

| Situation | Correct treatment |
|---|---|
| **Feasibility study already paid for** | **SUNK — exclude from the project appraisal** |
| **Land already owned** | Include at **OPPORTUNITY cost**, not purchase price |
| **Existing plant being replaced** | Include its **salvage value**, not its book value |
| Abandoning a partly-built works | **Compare remaining cost with remaining benefit only** |

> **Book value is an accounting construct and is itself a sunk-cost artefact** — what matters economically is what the asset can be sold for now, not what depreciation schedules say it is worth.

**And the appraisal methods this feeds:**

> **NPV is the theoretically correct criterion**, discounting only **future incremental** cash flows. **IRR and B/C ratio share a SCALE problem** (both are ratios), and **PAYBACK ignores everything after the payback point** — a liquidity measure, not a profitability one.

> **When NPV and IRR disagree on mutually exclusive projects, NPV is right** — you cannot spend a percentage.

examTip.trick: **A decision can only affect the FUTURE.** A sunk cost is identical under every option, so it cannot distinguish between them — only costs that **DIFFER between alternatives** are relevant.
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a real cost concept**: (a) future/avoidable, (b) variable, (c) joint. All are genuine — only one is *sunk*. A four-way match, not a guess.
examTip.mnemonic: **OPPORTUNITY cost is the mirror image** — never in the accounts yet always relevant. Land you already own is not free; its purchase price is **sunk**, its current value is **opportunity cost**.
